items.stem: A respiratory therapist prepares to administer an aerosol treatment. The physician order lists albuterol every 4 hours, while the medication administration record lists every 6 hours. What should the therapist do?
options: Follow the medication administration record because it lists the schedule.
Verify the current medication order before administering the treatment.
Administer the treatment according to the previous therapist’s note.
Delay all respiratory medications until the physician evaluates the patient.

items.stem: A patient reports increasing shortness of breath during the past month. Which question provides the most useful information about the severity of functional limitation?
options: When did you last receive an influenza vaccination?
Does anyone in your family have chronic lung disease?
What activities can you no longer complete without stopping to breathe?
Have you ever been hospitalized for a breathing problem?

items.stem: A patient with asthma develops increasing chest tightness and dyspnea. Breath sounds are markedly diminished with only faint wheezing. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Air movement has improved because wheezing has decreased.
Airflow may be severely reduced despite less audible wheezing.
Secretions are obstructing the large central airways.
Fluid accumulation is limiting ventilation at the lung bases.

items.stem: A patient in severe respiratory distress initially breathes 36/min with marked accessory-muscle use. Later the rate is 18/min, respirations are shallow, and the patient is difficult to arouse. What is the best interpretation?
options: Wait for the next scheduled vital-sign check because a single change in respiratory status may represent normal variability
Increase oxygen flow first and postpone the rest of the assessment until saturation returns to baseline
Recognize the change as potential respiratory deterioration and promptly reassess oxygenation, ventilation, work of breathing, mental status, and need for escalation
Focus on auscultation alone because worsening respiratory status can be localized from breath sounds before other assessment

items.stem: A patient with COPD becomes increasingly drowsy while receiving supplemental oxygen. Respirations are shallow at 10/min and SpO₂ is 93%. Which test best evaluates ventilatory status?
options: Recommend an ABG for every patient receiving supplemental oxygen because pulse oximetry cannot provide useful oxygenation information
Recommend an ABG when the clinical question requires direct assessment of arterial oxygenation, ventilation, or acid-base status that cannot be adequately answered by noninvasive data
Use an ABG primarily to determine airway resistance when wheezing is present
Delay ABG testing until pulse oximetry falls below a fixed threshold regardless of ventilation or acid-base concerns

items.stem: A patient is rescued from an enclosed-space fire and reports headache and dizziness. The patient appears confused and SpO₂ is 99% while receiving oxygen. Which test should be recommended?
options: Pulmonary function testing
Standard arterial blood gas without CO-oximetry
Hemoximetry with carboxyhemoglobin measurement
Overnight pulse oximetry

items.stem: A postoperative patient has a weak cough. Coarse, low-pitched breath sounds over the central lung fields decrease substantially after an effective cough. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Alveolar fluid producing inspiratory crackles
Bronchospasm narrowing the small airways
Pleural fluid compressing dependent lung regions
Secretions moving within the larger airways

items.stem: Which patient requires the most immediate reassessment?
options: A patient with COPD at prescribed oxygen target who is speaking comfortably
A postoperative patient with an occasional cough and respiratory rate of 20/min
A patient whose respiratory rate rose from 22 to 34/min and who now has difficulty speaking
A patient with pneumonia whose temperature decreased after an antipyretic

items.stem: A patient has cough and dyspnea primarily at work that improve on weekends. Which question should the respiratory therapist ask next?
options: How many respiratory infections did you have during childhood?
What substances, dusts, fumes, or chemicals are you exposed to at work?
When did you receive your most recent pneumococcal vaccination?
Which medications do your parents currently take?

items.stem: A patient develops sudden dyspnea and sharp right-sided chest pain after central venous catheter placement. Breath sounds are markedly diminished on the right. Which diagnostic procedure should be recommended?
options: Order chest imaging routinely for every respiratory complaint before completing the history or physical examination
Use chest imaging primarily to determine the patient's PaCO2 when ventilation is uncertain
Recommend appropriate chest imaging when the history and examination raise concern for a structural or parenchymal process that imaging can clarify
Defer imaging whenever breath sounds are abnormal because auscultation identifies the underlying structural diagnosis

items.stem: A patient with worsening cough and dyspnea has fever, increased yellow-green sputum, long-term bronchodilator use, and a 35 pack-year smoking history. Which finding most strongly suggests an acute change?
options: Long-term bronchodilator use
Fever with increased purulent sputum
Thirty-five pack-year smoking history
Established COPD diagnosis

items.stem: A patient with worsening respiratory symptoms has RR 32/min, shallow respirations, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and difficulty speaking more than a few words. How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Normal exertional breathing
Adequate ventilation despite tachypnea
Significant respiratory distress
Primarily increased airway secretions

items.stem: A patient receiving oxygen becomes restless and repeatedly removes the device. SpO₂ falls from 93% to 86% and respiratory rate rises from 22 to 30/min. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Behavior should be addressed before respiratory reassessment.
The oxygen device is probably causing anxiety without deterioration.
The patient is most likely having difficulty understanding instructions.
The behavior may represent worsening respiratory compromise.

items.stem: During an aerosol treatment, a patient develops sudden severe chest pain, marked dyspnea, diaphoresis, and a rapid irregular pulse. What should the respiratory therapist do first?
options: Reduce aerosol flow and continue while observing.
Complete the treatment before obtaining more information.
Stop the treatment and immediately assess and escalate care.
Ask the patient to rest and resume when symptoms decrease.

items.stem: A patient has progressive exertional dyspnea, normal resting SpO₂, no acute chest radiograph abnormality, and normal hemoglobin. Symptoms become marked while walking. Which approach provides the most useful next information?
options: Sputum culture during the resting assessment
Pulmonary function and exercise assessment
Continuous ECG monitoring during sleep
Bronchoscopy to inspect the central airways

items.stem: A patient receiving oxygen by nasal cannula has an SpO2 of 86% and increased work of breathing. What should the respiratory therapist do first?
options: Change immediately to invasive ventilation without further reassessment.
Discontinue oxygen briefly to determine the patient’s room-air saturation.
Maintain the current flow until an arterial blood gas result is available.
Increase oxygen to reach the prescribed saturation target and reassess the response.

items.stem: A stable patient is receiving supplemental oxygen and the SpO2 is well above the ordered target range. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Increase the flow to provide a larger oxygen reserve.
Titrate oxygen downward while monitoring oxygenation and clinical status.
Maintain the setting because oxygen should not be reduced after initiation.
Remove the device and wait for signs of hypoxemia before restarting oxygen.

items.stem: During supervised ambulation, a patient’s SpO2 falls from 94% to 86% with dyspnea. After oxygen is increased, SpO2 rises to the prescribed range and symptoms improve. What does this response support?
options: The oxygen flow should be returned immediately to the pre-exercise setting before reassessment.
The patient no longer requires oxygen because the saturation improved with treatment.
The desaturation was caused by the pulse oximeter because symptoms improved after oxygen.
The oxygen adjustment was effective during exertion and should be documented with the response.

items.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient needs a more controlled oxygen concentration than a standard low-flow nasal cannula can provide. Which device is the best choice?
options: Reservoir mask with the reservoir bag removed
Simple mask operated at the minimum possible flow
Nasal cannula with the prongs partially occluded
Air-entrainment mask with the prescribed adapter

items.stem: The reservoir bag on a nonrebreathing mask collapses almost completely during each inspiration. What should the respiratory therapist do?
options: Decrease oxygen flow until the bag remains partially collapsed.
Increase oxygen flow so the reservoir remains adequately inflated during inspiration.
Remove the reservoir bag and continue oxygen through the mask alone.
Open the mask ports completely so room air fills the reservoir during inspiration.

items.stem: A patient receiving oxygen by tracheostomy collar has a falling SpO2. The patient is breathing comfortably, but the aerosol tubing has become disconnected from the oxygen setup. What is the best immediate action?
options: Obtain a chest radiograph before changing the oxygen equipment.
Replace the tracheostomy tube before restoring oxygen flow.
Begin chest physiotherapy because the saturation has decreased.
Reconnect the oxygen delivery system and reassess oxygenation.

items.stem: A patient is started on high-flow nasal cannula for hypoxemia. Which setup feature is essential for delivering high flows comfortably?
options: An unheated bubble humidifier connected after the cannula
A dry circuit to prevent condensation near the patient
A reservoir bag that remains inflated throughout inspiration
Active heated humidification of the delivered gas

items.stem: A patient on high-flow nasal cannula has an acceptable SpO2 but remains tachypneic with increased inspiratory effort. Which adjustment is most directly aimed at improving flow support and reducing work of breathing?
options: Decrease both flow and oxygen concentration at the same time.
Decrease the flow and increase room-air entrainment around the cannula.
Turn off humidification to reduce resistance through the circuit.
Increase the delivered flow while reassessing patient tolerance.

items.stem: Thirty minutes after high-flow nasal cannula is initiated, a patient’s SpO2 improves from 84% to 93%, respiratory rate decreases from 34 to 24/min, and accessory-muscle use lessens. How should the therapist interpret these findings?
options: The patient requires immediate intubation because the initial saturation was below 90%.
The therapy has failed because the patient still requires supplemental oxygen.
The flow should be stopped because improvement indicates the device is no longer needed.
The patient is responding to therapy and should continue to be monitored and reassessed.

items.stem: A patient with COPD and chronic hypercapnia presents with an acute exacerbation and hypoxemia. Which oxygen strategy is most appropriate?
options: Use oxygen only after the PaCO2 has returned to the patient’s baseline value.
Withhold oxygen because any increase in oxygenation will worsen carbon dioxide retention.
Give the highest available oxygen concentration until all dyspnea has resolved.
Provide controlled oxygen to the prescribed saturation target and reassess ventilation and mental status.

items.stem: A patient at risk for hypercapnic respiratory failure receives supplemental oxygen. The SpO2 improves, but the patient becomes increasingly drowsy and the respiratory rate falls. What should the therapist do next?
options: Remove all oxygen and wait for the patient to become more alert before reassessing.
Increase oxygen further because the change in mental status confirms persistent hypoxemia.
Continue the same oxygen setting because the saturation has reached the target range.
Reassess ventilation promptly and adjust respiratory support based on the clinical findings.

items.stem: Which finding is most important when evaluating a patient with COPD after oxygen therapy has been increased?
options: Whether the patient normally uses a humidifier with home oxygen
Presence of a chronic productive cough documented at admission
Number of years since the patient stopped smoking cigarettes
Change in ventilation, mental status, and gas-exchange measurements

items.stem: A patient on conventional oxygen has persistent hypoxemia, increasing respiratory rate, and worsening work of breathing despite appropriate device setup and oxygen titration. What should the respiratory therapist recommend?
options: Delay changes until the patient develops severe bradycardia or loss of consciousness.
Continue the same oxygen device because increasing work of breathing is expected during recovery.
Reduce oxygen delivery to prevent oxygen toxicity before considering another support method.
Escalate respiratory support and reassess whether high-flow, noninvasive, or invasive support is indicated.

items.stem: After an oxygen adjustment, which set of findings best indicates that therapy is effective?
options: Dyspnea persists, but the patient reports that the oxygen device feels cooler.
SpO2 rises above target while respiratory rate and confusion continue to worsen.
SpO2 is unchanged, but the oxygen flowmeter indicates a higher liter flow.
SpO2 reaches target, work of breathing decreases, and mental status remains appropriate.

items.stem: A patient receiving escalating oxygen develops worsening hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability. What is the most appropriate respiratory therapist response?
options: Wait for the next scheduled assessment before recommending a change in the care plan.
Continue increasing oxygen concentration without reassessing ventilation or circulation.
Return to the original oxygen setting because the deterioration followed a treatment change.
Recognize failure of the current strategy, reassess immediately, and recommend a higher level of support.

items.stem: A patient uses a stationary oxygen concentrator at home but desaturates during walking outside the home. Which recommendation best supports safe ambulation?
options: Increase the stationary concentrator flow before the patient leaves home.
Arrange a portable oxygen system that can provide the prescribed flow during activity.
Limit all walking outside the home so portable oxygen is unnecessary.
Use the portable system only after dyspnea becomes severe during activity.

items.stem: During home oxygen teaching, which patient statement indicates a need for additional instruction?
options: I will keep oxygen away from smoking and open flames.
I will secure oxygen cylinders so they cannot fall over.
I can use petroleum jelly around my nose when it becomes dry.
I will follow the prescribed flow rather than changing it on my own.

items.stem: A patient prescribed ambulatory oxygen reports increasing dyspnea with activity. Resting SpO2 is within the prescribed range, but SpO2 falls below target during a supervised walk. What should the respiratory therapist recommend?
options: Keep the current ambulatory setting until resting hypoxemia develops.
Discontinue ambulatory oxygen because the resting saturation remains within the target range.
Increase oxygen only at rest because exertional measurements are less useful for titration.
Reassess oxygen needs during exertion and adjust the ambulatory plan according to the prescribed target.

items.stem: An E cylinder contains oxygen at high pressure and must be connected to a flowmeter for bedside use. Which component is required to make the cylinder pressure suitable for delivery?
options: An oxygen analyzer placed between the cylinder and regulator
A pressure-reducing regulator connected to the cylinder
A humidifier connected directly to the cylinder valve
A blender connected to the cylinder without a regulator

items.stem: While assembling an oxygen system, the respiratory therapist finds that the regulator does not match the cylinder valve connection. What is the safest action?
options: Open the cylinder briefly and attach the regulator while gas is flowing
Use an adapter so the available regulator can be forced onto the valve
Lubricate the connection so the regulator can be tightened securely
Obtain the regulator designed for that cylinder and connection system

items.stem: A patient receiving a blended oxygen-air mixture has an unexpectedly low measured oxygen concentration. The ordered blender setting is correct. What should the respiratory therapist evaluate first?
options: The patient’s pulse rate before checking the delivery equipment
The gas sources, supply pressures, connections, and blender function
The humidifier temperature without assessing the gas supply
The cylinder duration calculation for the backup oxygen source

items.stem: An oxygen cylinder has 1,500 psi remaining. The cylinder factor is 0.28 L/psi, the flow is 6 L/min, and a 200-psi reserve must remain. Approximately how long can the cylinder be used?
options: 84 minutes
70 minutes
51 minutes
61 minutes

items.stem: A transport is expected to last 45 minutes. A cylinder has 1,000 psi, a factor of 0.28 L/psi, and oxygen will run at 5 L/min. A 200-psi reserve is required. What should the respiratory therapist conclude?
options: The supply is adequate because the calculated duration exceeds 45 minutes
The available supply is insufficient for the planned transport with reserve
The supply is adequate if the reserve pressure is ignored during transport
The supply is sufficient only if the flow is increased during transport

items.stem: A patient’s oxygen flow is increased from 4 L/min to 8 L/min while the same cylinder is in use. If cylinder pressure is unchanged at that moment, how will the estimated remaining duration change?
options: It will decrease only after the cylinder pressure reaches the reserve level
It will remain unchanged because cylinder pressure did not change
It will double because a higher flow empties the cylinder more efficiently
It will decrease to approximately one-half of the previous duration

items.stem: A patient has marked upper-airway obstruction with turbulent airflow and increased work of breathing while definitive treatment is being arranged. Which therapy may temporarily reduce airway resistance?
options: A higher-density oxygen-nitrogen mixture
A helium-oxygen mixture
Inhaled nitric oxide as the primary airway dilator
Aerosolized sterile water delivered at high flow

items.stem: A patient who may benefit from heliox also requires a higher oxygen concentration because of hypoxemia. Which consideration is most important when selecting the mixture?
options: Use pure helium first, then add oxygen after airway resistance decreases
Choose the mixture with the highest helium concentration regardless of oxygenation
Deliver 80/20 heliox and add room air until the oxygen saturation improves
Choose a mixture that provides enough oxygen while retaining a useful helium concentration

items.stem: A 70/30 heliox mixture is delivered through a conventional oxygen flowmeter set at 10 L/min. If the correction factor is 1.6, what is the approximate actual flow?
options: 10 L/min
16 L/min
6 L/min
26 L/min

items.stem: A patient receiving inhaled nitric oxide develops evidence of worsening pulmonary irritation. Which therapy-related measurement should the respiratory therapist verify promptly?
options: Absolute humidity at the room-air intake
Helium concentration in the inspiratory mixture
Cylinder duration for the oxygen backup supply
Nitrogen dioxide concentration in the delivered gas

items.stem: A patient receiving inhaled nitric oxide is improving and the team plans to discontinue therapy. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Stop the therapy abruptly once the oxygen saturation reaches the target
Taper the therapy while monitoring oxygenation and pulmonary hemodynamic response
Increase the dose immediately before discontinuation to prevent methemoglobinemia
Replace nitric oxide with heliox at the same flow before stopping therapy

items.stem: A patient receiving inhaled epoprostenol develops new systemic hypotension. What is the most appropriate respiratory therapy response?
options: Stop all supplemental oxygen while continuing the same epoprostenol dose
Increase the epoprostenol dose because hypotension indicates improved pulmonary vasodilation
Reassess the patient and therapy promptly and communicate the adverse response for treatment adjustment
Switch immediately to heliox because it produces the same pulmonary vascular effect

items.stem: An intubated patient develops increasingly thick secretions after several hours of ventilation. Which change best addresses the loss of normal upper-airway conditioning?
options: Remove humidification to reduce secretion production
Increase circuit dead space to retain exhaled moisture
Lower inspired-gas temperature as much as possible
Provide adequate humidification to the inspired gas

items.stem: A patient with an artificial airway is receiving gas that is inadequately warmed and humidified. Which finding is most consistent with this problem?
options: Rapid development of excessive oral salivation
Thick secretions with increasing difficulty clearing the airway
Improved mucociliary clearance with thinner secretions
Reduced need for airway suctioning over time

items.stem: Inspired gas is warmed without adding additional water vapor. What happens to its relative humidity?
options: It remains unchanged because absolute humidity increases equally
It increases because warming creates additional water vapor
It decreases because warmer gas can hold more water vapor
It reaches 100% because warmed gas becomes fully saturated

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient has copious thick secretions and requires frequent suctioning. Which humidification approach is most appropriate?
options: Use an unheated dry circuit to reduce airway resistance
Use an HME because heavy secretions improve its efficiency
Remove humidification until the secretion burden decreases
Use an active heated humidifier to provide greater humidification

items.stem: A patient using an HME develops increasing airway resistance and the device is visibly contaminated with secretions. What should the respiratory therapist do?
options: Increase ventilator pressure while leaving the contaminated HME in place
Replace the HME and reassess whether passive humidification remains appropriate
Add sterile water directly into the HME and continue using it
Decrease humidification because secretions indicate excessive moisture

items.stem: Which patient factor makes an HME a less appropriate choice for humidification?
options: A short period of uncomplicated mechanical ventilation
A stable airway with minimal secretion production
A large secretion burden requiring frequent airway clearance
A closed circuit with otherwise stable ventilatory needs

items.stem: Water is collecting in the dependent limb of a heated ventilator circuit. What is the best action?
options: Disconnect humidification and leave the circuit dry for the remainder of ventilation
Empty the condensate toward the patient so humidity is not lost
Increase the water level until the condensate returns to the chamber
Drain the condensate away from the patient using appropriate infection-control precautions

items.stem: An intubated patient develops tenacious secretions, mucus plugging, and repeated suctioning needs. Which equipment issue should be evaluated first?
options: Whether the oxygen analyzer is calibrated to room air
Whether the humidification system is providing adequate airway conditioning
Whether the expiratory alarm volume is set above baseline
Whether the flowmeter has been replaced with a pressure regulator

items.stem: A heated humidifier is delivering gas at an unexpectedly high temperature. What is the safest immediate response?
options: Bypass the temperature probe while keeping the heater at the same setting
Continue therapy because higher temperature always improves humidification
Assess the patient and correct the humidifier temperature or equipment problem
Increase circuit insulation so the patient receives the same high temperature

items.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient with a tracheostomy requires a high-humidity interface. Which setup is most appropriate?
options: A nonrebreather mask placed over the patient's nose and mouth
A dry nasal cannula positioned beside the tracheostomy tube
A metered-dose inhaler attached continuously to the tracheostomy
A large-volume aerosol system connected to a tracheostomy collar

items.stem: A tracheostomy collar aerosol setup produces little visible mist and the patient reports increasing airway dryness. What should the therapist assess first?
options: The patient's pulse oximeter alarm limits only
Gas flow, water supply, and the aerosol generator for proper operation
The cuff pressure of an unrelated endotracheal tube
The dose counter on the patient's rescue inhaler

items.stem: Which interface is designed to deliver bland aerosol directly to a patient with a tracheostomy?
options: Simple oxygen mask
Nasal cannula
Tracheostomy collar
Metered-dose inhaler mouthpiece

items.stem: A patient inhales an aerosol treatment with rapid, turbulent breaths. Which coaching change is most likely to improve lower-airway deposition?
options: Take only very small tidal breaths to keep particles in the upper airway
Increase inspiratory turbulence by inhaling as rapidly as possible
Exhale forcefully through the aerosol generator during medication delivery
Use a slower controlled inhalation pattern appropriate for the device

items.stem: Aerosol particles are depositing mainly in the mouth and large central airways. Which factor most likely contributes to this pattern?
options: A controlled inhalation that reduces turbulent flow
High inspiratory flow that increases inertial impaction
A breath hold after inhalation that promotes sedimentation
A device technique that minimizes oropharyngeal deposition

items.stem: Two patients receive the same aerosol dose from the same device. One has severe airway obstruction. Why might lung deposition differ?
options: Airway obstruction prevents all aerosol from entering the respiratory tract
The nominal device dose guarantees identical lung deposition
Airway geometry and breathing pattern can change where particles deposit
Only medication concentration determines pulmonary deposition

items.stem: A patient actuates an MDI after completing the inhalation. Which correction should the therapist teach?
options: Actuate several doses into the mouth before beginning to inhale
Actuate only after holding the breath for several seconds
Inhale rapidly first and actuate during exhalation
Coordinate actuation with the beginning of a slow inhalation

items.stem: A patient has difficulty coordinating MDI actuation with inhalation. Which change is most appropriate?
options: Replace the MDI with a dry-powder device regardless of inspiratory ability
Use a valved holding chamber and reinforce correct technique
Remove all accessory devices so the medication travels faster
Ask the patient to actuate repeated doses before taking a breath

items.stem: A patient's MDI appears to function normally, but symptom control remains poor. What should the respiratory therapist assess before recommending a different device?
options: Increase the prescribed dose without assessing device use
Assume the medication is ineffective because the canister sprays
Observe the patient's complete inhaler technique and correct errors
Replace the inhaler solely because the patient still has symptoms

items.stem: A frail patient cannot generate an adequate inspiratory flow through a dry-powder inhaler. What is the best response?
options: Store the DPI in a humid environment to make the powder easier to inhale
Tell the patient to exhale forcefully through the DPI before each dose
Continue the DPI because inspiratory flow does not affect powder dispersion
Select a delivery device that does not depend on the same inspiratory-flow requirement

items.stem: Which instruction is most important for protecting a dry-powder inhaler from a common technique-related problem?
options: Rinse the powder chamber with water immediately before every dose
Avoid exhaling into the device and keep the powder protected from moisture
Store the device open in a humid bathroom between treatments
Use a slow weak inhalation to prevent powder from leaving the device

items.stem: A patient loads a DPI correctly but takes a very slow, weak inhalation. What is the primary concern?
options: The device will automatically convert the powder into a pressurized aerosol
The medication will be delivered more efficiently because flow is lower
Insufficient inspiratory energy may reduce powder dispersion and drug delivery
The dose will bypass the airway and enter the bloodstream directly

items.stem: A jet nebulizer produces no aerosol after it is connected for treatment. What should the therapist check first?
options: Switch to continuous therapy without evaluating the setup
Increase the medication dose before checking the equipment
Replace the patient's pulse oximeter probe
Verify the driving-gas source, flow, tubing, and nebulizer assembly

items.stem: A therapist is comparing jet and mesh nebulizers for a patient. Which consideration is most relevant?
options: Whether both devices have the same external color and shape
Device technology, setup requirements, output, and the patient's clinical situation
Whether the patient has previously used an oxygen cylinder
Whether the treatment room has a wall suction regulator

items.stem: A patient with severe airflow obstruction is prescribed continuous aerosolized bronchodilator therapy. What is most important during administration?
options: Use the lowest possible driving flow regardless of device performance
Stop reassessment because continuous therapy guarantees a stable dose
Ensure continuous delivery is functioning and monitor the patient's clinical response
Disconnect the aerosol source whenever the patient becomes tachypneic

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient has a poor response to an aerosol treatment. Which equipment factor should be evaluated?
options: The location of the ventilator power cord in the room
The patient's room lighting and monitor brightness
The brand of pulse oximeter used at the bedside
Aerosol-device placement and circuit configuration relative to the artificial airway

items.stem: When administering aerosol through an artificial airway, why should the therapist consider the airway and circuit when evaluating treatment response?
options: An artificial airway guarantees that the entire nominal dose reaches the lungs
The artificial airway and circuit can alter how much aerosol reaches the lower respiratory tract
Ventilator circuits eliminate the effects of device placement on aerosol delivery
Humidity and circuit configuration have no effect on aerosol delivery

items.stem: A ventilated patient repeatedly receives aerosol therapy with little clinical improvement. What is the best next step before assuming the medication itself has failed?
options: Increase the medication dose first because repeated poor response usually indicates inadequate prescribed drug strength
Change medications before checking delivery because ventilator circuits provide consistent aerosol deposition once connected
Evaluate drug delivery by checking the device, circuit position, humidification effects, ventilator settings, synchrony, and whether the aerosol is actually reaching the patient
Disconnect the patient from the ventilator for every treatment because spontaneous aerosol delivery is predictably more efficient

items.stem: A patient with acute bronchospasm needs rapid relief of airflow obstruction. Which medication class is most appropriate for immediate bronchodilation?
options: A leukotriene modifier used as controller therapy
A long-acting muscarinic antagonist used for maintenance
An inhaled corticosteroid used for airway inflammation
A short-acting beta agonist

items.stem: After repeated beta-agonist treatments, a patient develops tremor and tachycardia while wheezing has improved. How should the therapist interpret these findings?
options: Administer the scheduled respiratory medication first and review contraindications only if the patient reports an adverse effect
Confirm the medication, indication, dose, route, allergies, relevant contraindications, and patient-specific factors before administration
Verify the drug name and dose; indication and comorbidities can be reviewed after treatment because the medication is already ordered
Use the prior treatment response as the main safety check because previously tolerated respiratory medications remain appropriate

items.stem: A patient asks why a long-acting bronchodilator is prescribed even when breathing feels comfortable. What is the best explanation?
options: It replaces the need to reassess symptoms and airflow
It is intended only for sudden severe bronchospasm
It provides maintenance bronchodilation rather than serving as the primary rapid-relief treatment
It works by directly dissolving retained airway secretions

items.stem: A patient with persistent asthma uses a rescue bronchodilator frequently despite prescribed controller therapy. Which issue should be evaluated?
options: Judge effectiveness from heart-rate increase because tachycardia confirms adequate beta-agonist delivery
Repeat the treatment automatically if wheezing remains, without reassessing airflow or adverse effects
Use improvement in SpO2 alone as the primary measure of bronchodilator response in obstructive disease
Assess response to the bronchodilator using symptoms, breath sounds, airflow measures when appropriate, vital signs, and adverse effects

items.stem: Which response best indicates that an inhaled corticosteroid is being used for its intended role in asthma?
options: Immediate reversal of severe bronchospasm within seconds
Reduced airway inflammation and improved long-term symptom control
Mechanical removal of thick mucus from the central airway
Direct stimulation of respiratory drive during apnea

items.stem: A patient with severe asthma remains poorly responsive to initial bronchodilator therapy. Which medication may be considered as an adjunct in severe exacerbation management?
options: Naloxone
Dornase alfa
Magnesium sulfate
Inhaled nitric oxide

items.stem: A patient has severe asthma despite optimized standard therapy. Before advanced biologic therapy is selected, what information is most important?
options: The size of the patient's home oxygen cylinder
The color and brand of the patient's current inhaler
Whether the patient prefers nebulizers to oxygen masks
The patient's inflammatory phenotype and clinical eligibility for the targeted therapy

items.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for consideration of asthma biologic therapy?
options: A patient with occasional symptoms controlled by infrequent rescue medication
A patient with severe persistent asthma that remains uncontrolled despite optimized conventional therapy
A patient needing one bronchodilator treatment for an isolated viral illness
A patient whose only problem is incorrect metered-dose inhaler technique

items.stem: After phenotype-directed biologic therapy is started, which approach is most appropriate?
options: Stop all other asthma therapy after the first biologic dose
Assume the treatment is effective without further clinical evaluation
Reassess exacerbations, symptoms, medication needs, and overall clinical response
Judge effectiveness only by whether the injection caused discomfort

items.stem: A patient has very thick airway secretions that are difficult to clear. Which medication concept most directly targets mucus characteristics?
options: A sedative reversal agent
A neuromuscular blocking agent
A pulmonary vasodilator
A mucolytic or airway-secretion therapy

items.stem: A patient with cystic fibrosis is prescribed dornase alfa. What is the intended respiratory-care goal?
options: Use an inhaled corticosteroid as the preferred rescue medication because anti-inflammatory effects occur within minutes
Recognize that inhaled corticosteroids are controller therapy aimed at reducing airway inflammation and future risk, not rapid relief of acute bronchospasm
Stop controller corticosteroid whenever symptoms improve because continued use increases acute bronchospasm
Reserve inhaled corticosteroids for episodes when a short-acting bronchodilator fails to produce immediate relief

items.stem: Why is a patient's CFTR mutation relevant when considering a CFTR-modulator medication?
options: Use systemic corticosteroids primarily for immediate bronchodilation when inhaled beta-agonists do not normalize airflow
Withhold systemic corticosteroids until infection is excluded because corticosteroids are contraindicated whenever infection is possible
Recognize systemic corticosteroids as anti-inflammatory therapy used in appropriate exacerbations, while monitoring for clinically relevant adverse effects
Continue systemic corticosteroids indefinitely after an exacerbation because longer treatment consistently prevents relapse

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient receives a neuromuscular blocking agent. Which statement is most important when evaluating the medication plan?
options: A paralytic should be used as the primary treatment for patient anxiety
Neuromuscular blockade automatically provides pain relief and amnesia
Paralysis eliminates the need to monitor ventilation and oxygenation
Paralysis does not provide analgesia or sedation, so those needs must be addressed separately

items.stem: A patient becomes markedly hypoventilated after receiving an opioid analgesic. Which reversal-agent concept is most relevant?
options: Flumazenil is the standard reversal agent for opioid effects
Naloxone may reverse opioid-related respiratory depression
Dornase alfa reverses opioid-induced hypoventilation
Ipratropium directly reverses opioid sedation

items.stem: During moderate sedation, a patient's respiratory rate falls and ventilation becomes shallow. What is the respiratory therapist's priority?
options: Increase the sedative dose so breathing becomes more regular
Wait for oxygen saturation to fall before assessing ventilation
Assess and support airway and ventilation while the sedation-related change is addressed
Assume shallow breathing is expected and requires no reassessment

items.stem: A drowsy patient has snoring respirations, poor air movement, and intermittent oxygen desaturation. Which problem should the respiratory therapist address first?
options: Chronic metabolic alkalosis
Excessive pulmonary surfactant
Isolated diffusion impairment
Loss of upper-airway patency

items.stem: A patient with a depressed level of consciousness has repeated vomiting and cannot manage oral secretions. Which finding is most concerning?
options: The patient requires long-term bronchodilator maintenance
The patient may be unable to protect the airway
The patient has excessive inspiratory muscle strength
The patient is ready for immediate airway-device removal

items.stem: Before an urgent intubation, the therapist identifies limited mouth opening and restricted neck movement. How should these findings affect preparation?
options: Remove rescue airway equipment to simplify the bedside setup
Proceed as though routine direct laryngoscopy is guaranteed to succeed
Anticipate a difficult airway and ensure backup airway strategies are available
Delay oxygenation until the airway difficulty has been fully classified

items.stem: An unresponsive adult without suspected cervical spine injury has upper-airway obstruction from loss of muscle tone. Which initial maneuver is appropriate?
options: Apply continuous positive pressure without assessing airway patency
Insert an endotracheal tube without first opening the airway
Place the patient prone and avoid manual airway positioning
Open the airway with head-tilt/chin-lift positioning

items.stem: An unconscious patient has no gag reflex and needs a temporary adjunct to help maintain upper-airway patency. Which device is appropriate?
options: A speaking valve
An oropharyngeal airway
A dry-powder inhaler
A tracheostomy collar

items.stem: During bag-mask ventilation, the chest is not rising and a large leak is heard around the mask. What should the therapist do first?
options: Continue squeezing the bag at the same rate despite absent chest rise
Increase medication delivery through the mask before correcting the leak
Reposition the airway and improve the mask seal before reassessing ventilation
Remove the mask and wait for spontaneous ventilation to improve

items.stem: A patient is deteriorating and endotracheal intubation is planned. Which preparation best supports a safe first attempt?
options: Disconnect physiologic monitoring until the airway procedure is complete
Withhold oxygen until after tube placement so saturation can confirm success
Prepare only the laryngoscope because backup equipment is unnecessary
Preoxygenate and verify airway equipment, suction, monitoring, and a backup plan

items.stem: Why should functional suction be immediately available before intubation?
options: Suction is required to inflate the endotracheal tube cuff
Secretions or emesis may need rapid removal to improve visualization and protect the airway
Suction replaces the need for preoxygenation before laryngoscopy
Suction is used to verify endotracheal placement after every attempt

items.stem: The team is preparing for an anticipated difficult intubation. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Attempt direct laryngoscopy first and assemble backup equipment only if the initial attempt fails
Use the device most familiar to the operator without preparing a rescue oxygenation strategy
Prepare a difficult-airway plan with appropriate personnel, preoxygenation, primary and backup devices, rescue oxygenation options, and a clear escalation strategy
Delay preoxygenation until airway equipment is fully assembled because oxygen reserve is best preserved immediately before laryngoscopy

items.stem: Immediately after endotracheal intubation, which finding provides the strongest ongoing evidence that the tube is in the trachea?
options: An oxygen saturation value obtained before the intubation
Condensation appearing somewhere inside the endotracheal tube
Equal movement of the patient's upper extremities
A persistent waveform capnography tracing with exhaled carbon dioxide

items.stem: After intubation, breath sounds are markedly decreased on the left and the tube depth is greater than expected. What should the therapist suspect?
options: A correctly positioned tube at the usual tracheal depth
Right mainstem bronchus intubation
An isolated failure of the pulse oximeter probe
A cuff leak caused only by insufficient humidification

items.stem: A previously stable intubated patient develops an unexpected cuff leak and the centimeter marking at the teeth has changed. What is the best response?
options: Assume the ventilator is malfunctioning and ignore the airway marking
Increase cuff pressure without checking tube depth or position
Assess for endotracheal tube migration and reconfirm position
Remove capnography because it may interfere with tube assessment

items.stem: Multiple intubation attempts have failed and the patient cannot be adequately oxygenated with bag-mask ventilation. What is the priority?
options: Remove all airway adjuncts so the patient can breathe without assistance
Continue identical laryngoscopy attempts until the original technique succeeds
Delay rescue ventilation while waiting for radiographic confirmation
Move promptly to the established rescue-airway pathway to restore oxygenation

items.stem: A supraglottic airway is placed after unsuccessful endotracheal intubation. What is its immediate purpose?
options: Measure endotracheal tube cuff pressure
Provide a rescue route for ventilation and oxygenation
Deliver long-term invasive ventilation through the trachea
Confirm the location of a surgically created airway

items.stem: An airway procedure will involve an ignition source near an oxygen-enriched field. Which principle is most important?
options: Ignore the oxidizer source because only the ignition device affects airway-fire risk
Increase oxygen concentration routinely because higher oxygen reduces ignition risk
Minimize the elements that support airway fire while maintaining safe oxygenation and coordinating with the team
Place combustible materials near the airway so equipment remains easy to reach

items.stem: A patient requires a definitive airway for prolonged invasive ventilatory support. Which airway type is most consistent with that need after the acute endotracheal phase?
options: A valved holding chamber
A nasopharyngeal airway
A simple oxygen mask
A tracheostomy tube

items.stem: A patient with difficult upper-airway anatomy needs a temporary rescue device to permit ventilation after failed intubation. Which device category best fits this purpose?
options: A tracheostomy speaking valve
A supraglottic airway
A heat-moisture exchanger
A dry-powder inhaler

items.stem: A standard tracheostomy tube does not adequately fit a patient because of unusual neck and tracheal anatomy. What is the best next consideration?
options: Use an oropharyngeal airway as the long-term tracheal device
Increase cuff pressure until the standard tube reaches farther
Evaluate whether a specialty or extended-length airway is indicated
Remove the artificial airway and rely on supplemental oxygen alone

items.stem: An intubated patient develops an audible leak and a low exhaled tidal volume. What should the therapist assess as part of the airway evaluation?
options: Increase tidal volume first because low exhaled volume confirms inadequate ventilator output
Advance the endotracheal tube until the audible leak stops without first checking tube position
Increase cuff pressure substantially above the recommended range because any audible leak indicates underinflation
Check cuff inflation/pressure, pilot system, tube position, circuit connections, and the patient for a source of leak

items.stem: Why is cuff manometry preferred to estimating cuff inflation by feel alone?
options: It confirms endotracheal placement without any other assessment
It provides an objective measurement that can guide adequate sealing while limiting pressure injury
It measures the patient's intrinsic PEEP during spontaneous breathing
It determines the exact depth of the tube on a chest radiograph

items.stem: The centimeter marking of an endotracheal tube has changed after patient repositioning. What is the best action?
options: Ignore the change if the ventilator remains powered on
Add air to the cuff without evaluating the tube position
Reassess tube position and security before assuming ventilation is unchanged
Remove the securing device so the tube can return to position on its own

items.stem: A tracheostomy patient develops thick secretions and increasing difficulty clearing the airway. Which aspect of routine care should be reassessed?
options: Whether the tracheostomy should remain uncovered to dry secretions
Whether the upper airway is providing normal humidification
Whether the patient should avoid all airway clearance
Humidification and secretion-management adequacy

items.stem: During routine tracheostomy care, which assessment best supports ongoing airway safety?
options: Assess only the patient's oral cavity because the tracheostomy bypasses the airway
Evaluate tube position, stoma condition, secretions, humidification, and airway patency
Avoid evaluating secretions unless oxygen saturation falls below the target
Remove the tracheostomy tube routinely to inspect the distal airway

items.stem: A tracheostomy patient requires increasingly frequent suctioning for tenacious secretions. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Frequent suction need confirms that the tracheostomy can be removed
The increased secretions prove humidification should be discontinued
The airway-care plan should be reassessed for secretion clearance and adequate conditioning
The finding is unrelated to artificial-airway management

items.stem: Before placing a one-way speaking valve on a tracheostomy tube, what must be ensured?
options: The tracheostomy tube is connected to continuous suction
The cuff is fully inflated so all exhaled gas exits through the valve
The upper airway is completely bypassed during both inspiration and expiration
The cuff is deflated and the patient can exhale through a patent upper airway

items.stem: Shortly after speaking-valve placement, a patient develops distress and cannot exhale effectively. What should the therapist do?
options: Inflate the cuff further while leaving the valve in place
Remove the valve and reassess cuff status and upper-airway patency
Increase oxygen flow through the valve and ignore the expiratory problem
Secure the valve more tightly so exhalation cannot escape around it

items.stem: Why can an inflated tracheostomy cuff make a one-way speaking valve dangerous?
options: It converts the speaking valve into a bidirectional airway
It directs all exhaled gas safely through the vocal cords
It can prevent exhaled gas from escaping through the upper airway
It automatically reduces airway resistance during exhalation

items.stem: A tracheostomy patient suddenly becomes distressed, and a suction catheter cannot be passed through the tube. What problem should be suspected first?
options: Normal progression toward decannulation
Isolated failure of the pulse oximeter
Excessive bronchodilator response
Tracheostomy tube obstruction or malposition

items.stem: A newly created tracheostomy becomes accidentally decannulated and the patient is in respiratory distress. Which factor is especially important when planning the response?
options: Reinsert the same tracheostomy tube immediately because a fresh tract is easier to identify before it begins to close
Consider how recently the tracheostomy was created because an immature tract increases the risk of false passage during attempted reinsertion
Occlude the stoma and ventilate through the upper airway in every patient regardless of the indication for tracheostomy
Probe the stoma with a suction catheter to define the tract before assessing oxygenation or ventilation

items.stem: A tracheostomy patient develops acute respiratory distress with suspected tube blockage. What is the immediate priority?
options: Wait for imaging before attempting to restore airflow
Complete routine stoma care before assessing ventilation
Restore airway patency and effective oxygenation or ventilation while identifying the obstruction
Increase cuff pressure as the only intervention for any tracheostomy emergency

items.stem: A patient with a total laryngectomy develops apnea. Where should emergency ventilation be directed?
options: Through the mouth with the stoma occluded
Through the nose using a nasopharyngeal airway
Through the mouth and stoma simultaneously
Through the laryngectomy stoma

items.stem: Why is distinguishing a tracheostomy from a total laryngectomy critical during an airway emergency?
options: Both conditions permanently disconnect the mouth and nose from the lungs
It determines whether the upper airway remains connected to the lungs and where ventilation should be delivered
Both conditions require ventilation only through the mouth during emergencies
The distinction affects communication but has no effect on emergency oxygenation

items.stem: An unresponsive patient has a neck stoma, and staff are uncertain whether the patient has a tracheostomy or total laryngectomy. What information is most important to establish rapidly?
options: Whether the patient prefers humidification during sleep
Whether the patient normally uses an inhaled corticosteroid
Whether the upper airway is anatomically connected to the lungs
Whether the stoma dressing was changed earlier in the day

items.stem: A tracheostomy patient is being evaluated for decannulation. Which combination most strongly supports readiness?
options: Repeated respiratory distress whenever the tracheostomy is occluded
Copious secretions, weak cough, and inability to tolerate cuff deflation
Persistent upper-airway obstruction with increasing suction requirements
Adequate cough and secretion control, upper-airway patency, and tolerance of cuff deflation or capping progression

items.stem: A patient tolerates cuff deflation and a speaking valve but develops marked distress during capping. What is the best interpretation?
options: The distress confirms immediate decannulation is appropriate
Further evaluation is needed before decannulation because full upper-airway breathing is not yet tolerated
Capping intolerance is unrelated to upper-airway patency
The cuff should be reinflated and decannulation performed immediately

items.stem: A tracheostomy patient has a strong cough but requires frequent suctioning for a large secretion burden. How should this affect decannulation planning?
options: A strong cough is sufficient for decannulation because secretion volume does not affect airway-management needs
Frequent suctioning supports decannulation because removing the tube improves secretion clearance
A high secretion burden and frequent suction requirement suggest the patient may not yet be ready for decannulation despite a strong cough
Decannulation readiness should be based on oxygen requirement rather than secretion management or cough effectiveness

items.stem: An intubated patient has coarse breath sounds, visible secretions in the tube, and a sawtooth pattern on the ventilator waveform. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Delay airway clearance until oxygen saturation decreases
Suction on a fixed schedule regardless of clinical findings
Increase cuff pressure to eliminate the secretion sounds
Suction the artificial airway and reassess the patient

items.stem: An intubated patient has clear breath sounds, stable ventilator pressures, and no visible airway secretions. How should suctioning be approached?
options: Perform deep suctioning routinely because an artificial airway is present
Continue assessment and suction when clinical evidence indicates retained secretions
Instill saline and suction at every scheduled respiratory treatment
Suction until a cough occurs even when no secretion evidence is present

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient develops coarse rhonchi and a sudden rise in peak inspiratory pressure while plateau pressure is unchanged. Which finding best supports suctioning?
options: Evidence that the endotracheal cuff pressure is too low
Evidence of worsening lung compliance without airway involvement
Evidence of increased airway resistance from retained secretions
Evidence that the patient no longer needs an artificial airway

items.stem: During endotracheal suctioning, a patient develops marked bradycardia and oxygen desaturation. What should the therapist do first?
options: Repeat suction passes immediately without allowing recovery
Continue suctioning until all secretions are removed
Increase suction pressure while keeping the catheter inserted
Stop suctioning, oxygenate the patient, and reassess

items.stem: Why should a suction catheter be appropriately sized for an artificial airway?
options: A larger catheter always improves oxygenation during the procedure
An oversized catheter can excessively obstruct airflow and increase suction-related complications
Catheter diameter determines the required endotracheal cuff pressure
Catheter size has no effect when suction pressure is properly adjusted

items.stem: A ventilated patient requires high PEEP and frequent airway suctioning. Which consideration favors use of a closed suction system?
options: It prevents all suction-related hypoxemia and airway trauma
It eliminates the need to monitor the patient during suctioning
It can permit suctioning while limiting interruption of the ventilator circuit and loss of support
It allows unlimited suction duration without physiologic consequences

items.stem: A patient with neuromuscular weakness has retained secretions despite adequate hydration and humidification because the cough is ineffective. Which strategy best addresses the primary problem?
options: Avoid positioning or airway-clearance assistance because the cough is weak
Increase oxygen concentration as the only secretion-clearance intervention
Reduce humidification so secretions become easier to mobilize
Use an assisted-cough strategy appropriate to the patient's condition

items.stem: A patient has thick secretions but a strong spontaneous cough. Which approach best reflects secretion management beyond suctioning?
options: Schedule invasive suctioning even when the patient clears secretions independently
Optimize hydration and humidification and use appropriate airway-clearance strategies
Use neuromuscular blockade to reduce secretion production
Discontinue airway conditioning so mucus becomes less mobile

items.stem: Two patients both retain secretions. One has dehydrated, tenacious mucus; the other has a weak cough from neuromuscular disease. Why might their airway-clearance plans differ?
options: Cough strength matters only when supplemental oxygen is unavailable
All retained secretions require the same suctioning schedule
Secretion characteristics and cough effectiveness should guide the selected interventions
Hydration and assisted cough have identical purposes in airway clearance

items.stem: A patient has bronchiectasis, a large daily secretion burden, and an effective cough but needs help mobilizing peripheral secretions. Which treatment goal should guide therapy selection?
options: Use lung expansion alone because secretion clearance is unnecessary
Increase inspired oxygen concentration regardless of secretion burden
Suppress cough so secretions remain in smaller airways
Mobilize retained secretions toward the central airways for effective clearance

items.stem: Before selecting an airway-clearance technique, which information is most important to consider?
options: The volume of sputum produced during the previous treatment because secretion quantity determines the appropriate technique
Airway patency, secretion location/amount, cough effectiveness, disease process, contraindications, tolerance, and the patient's ability to participate
The patient's oxygen device because airway-clearance techniques are selected primarily from delivered FiO2
The most familiar technique available to staff because effectiveness is similar when secretion retention is present

items.stem: After an airway-clearance treatment, which finding best supports that the therapy was effective?
options: Increased airway obstruction with reduced secretion movement
A higher oxygen flow despite unchanged secretion retention
Improved secretion expectoration with clearer breath sounds and easier breathing
A need for progressively more assistance without clinical improvement

items.stem: A patient has retained secretions in a specific lung segment and can tolerate position changes. What is the purpose of selecting the appropriate postural-drainage position?
options: Prevent all movement of secretions during percussion and vibration
Increase airway resistance so mucus remains in the affected segment
Replace the patient's cough with passive oxygen administration
Use gravity to assist movement of secretions from the targeted bronchopulmonary segment

items.stem: During chest physiotherapy, when is vibration typically coordinated with the patient's breathing pattern?
options: During a prolonged breath hold to prevent secretion movement
During exhalation to help move secretions toward larger airways
Only during maximal inspiration to increase airway closure
Continuously without regard to the respiratory cycle

items.stem: A patient needs secretion clearance but cannot tolerate a traditional head-down drainage position. What is the best approach?
options: Cancel all secretion-clearance therapy regardless of available alternatives
Use the contraindicated position because drainage requires an exact posture
Modify positioning while preserving the secretion-clearance goal and patient safety
Increase percussion force to compensate for unsafe positioning

items.stem: A cooperative patient with chronic mucus retention needs a portable technique that combines positive expiratory pressure with airway oscillation. Which option best fits this goal?
options: A nonrebreather mask
A simple oxygen flowmeter
An incentive spirometer used only for sustained inspiration
An oscillatory PEP device

items.stem: A patient with neuromuscular weakness has a very poor cough despite mobilized secretions. Which device most directly addresses the ineffective cough?
options: A dry-powder inhaler
Mechanical insufflation-exsufflation
A large-volume aerosol mask
A simple bubble humidifier

items.stem: A patient using an oscillatory PEP device produces little expiratory pressure because air is leaking around the mouthpiece. What should the therapist do first?
options: Replace the therapy with suction regardless of cough effectiveness
Increase oxygen concentration without correcting the leak
Correct the seal and technique, then reassess device performance
Continue unchanged because leaks do not affect PEP therapy

items.stem: A postoperative patient is taking shallow breaths and has dependent atelectatic changes with minimal secretions. Which therapeutic goal is most appropriate?
options: Use suctioning as the primary treatment despite minimal secretions
Focus exclusively on mobilizing copious retained secretions
Suppress deep breathing to reduce transpulmonary pressure
Promote lung expansion and alveolar recruitment

items.stem: A patient rapidly inhales through an incentive spirometer and cannot sustain the maneuver. Which coaching is most appropriate?
options: Use repeated rapid shallow breaths through the device
Use a slow deep inspiration followed by an appropriate inspiratory hold
Exhale forcefully into the device to raise the inspiratory indicator
Perform the maneuver only when secretions are visible in the airway

items.stem: Which patient problem is most directly targeted by lung-expansion therapy rather than secretion-clearance therapy?
options: An ineffective cough caused by neuromuscular weakness
Copious mucus requiring movement from peripheral to central airways
Reduced alveolar expansion with postoperative atelectatic change
A mucus plug requiring removal from an artificial airway

items.stem: A patient with severe respiratory muscle fatigue has worsening hypercapnia, declining mental status, and an ineffective breathing pattern despite initial support. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reduce monitoring to decrease the patient's work of breathing
Increase oxygen concentration alone and continue observation
Begin secretion-clearance therapy as the primary treatment
Initiate invasive ventilatory support to provide adequate ventilation and airway protection

items.stem: A patient is intubated because of severe ventilatory failure. Which goal most directly addresses the reason for support?
options: Eliminate all spontaneous respiratory effort in every patient
Provide adequate ventilation while reducing excessive work of breathing
Maintain the highest possible airway pressure throughout ventilation
Normalize every blood gas value immediately regardless of lung injury risk

items.stem: A patient has acceptable oxygenation but cannot protect the airway because of progressive neurologic deterioration. Why may invasive ventilation still be indicated?
options: Acceptable oxygenation means invasive ventilation is unnecessary until PaCO2 becomes elevated
Neurologic deterioration is an indication for NIV rather than intubation because spontaneous breathing is still present
Loss of airway protection creates aspiration and airway-patency risk that may require an artificial airway and ventilatory support even when oxygenation is currently acceptable
Airway protection can be assessed from SpO2, so normal saturation indicates that intubation can be deferred

items.stem: A ventilator breath begins when the patient creates a sufficient change in flow or pressure. Which breath variable is being described?
options: Baseline
Limit
Cycle
Trigger

items.stem: In a pressure-support breath, inspiratory flow falls to the ventilator's cycling threshold and inspiration ends. Which phase variable determined the end of inspiration?
options: Cycle
Trigger
Baseline
Limit

items.stem: A ventilator returns to 8 cm H2O of PEEP after each breath. In phase-variable terminology, the PEEP represents which component?
options: Assess the patient and ventilator, verify airway/circuit integrity, and determine whether the change reflects resistance, compliance, or another cause before making targeted adjustments
Increase tidal volume first because rising airway pressure most often indicates inadequate minute ventilation
Reduce alarm limits so ventilation can continue while the cause of the pressure change is observed
Increase inspiratory pressure until the previous delivered volume returns, then evaluate the patient if pressures remain high

items.stem: A patient receiving volume-controlled ventilation develops worsening lung compliance. If the set tidal volume is unchanged, which ventilator variable is most likely to increase?
options: Airway pressure required to deliver the set volume
Delivered tidal volume because pressure is fixed
PEEP automatically decreases to preserve minute ventilation
Inspiratory flow becomes zero regardless of the set pattern

items.stem: A patient receiving pressure-controlled ventilation develops worsening compliance while the inspiratory pressure remains unchanged. What change should the therapist expect?
options: Delivered tidal volume may decrease
Delivered tidal volume must remain exactly constant
Peak pressure must rise above the set inspiratory pressure
Respiratory rate must automatically double

items.stem: Which statement best compares volume- and pressure-targeted ventilation?
options: Volume targeting prioritizes delivered volume while pressure targeting limits inspiratory pressure and allows volume to vary
Both strategies guarantee identical tidal volume and airway pressure
Pressure targeting fixes tidal volume while allowing pressure to vary freely
Volume targeting prevents airway pressure from changing when compliance worsens

items.stem: A ventilator mode provides mandatory breaths but also allows the patient to breathe spontaneously between them. Which concept is most important for interpreting this mode?
options: Mandatory and spontaneous breath types can coexist within the same mode
Every breath in any ventilator mode must be identical
Spontaneous breathing is impossible whenever mandatory breaths are present
A mode name alone determines patient synchrony without assessing breath behavior

items.stem: A patient triggers a breath and the ventilator then provides the preset support for that breath. How should the breath be classified?
options: Patient-triggered and ventilator-assisted
Ventilator-triggered and completely spontaneous
Unassisted because the patient initiated the breath
Apneic because the ventilator supplied support

items.stem: Why is it safer to describe a ventilator mode by its breath types and control variables rather than relying only on a manufacturer's mode name?
options: Evaluate readiness using the patient's overall stability, oxygenation/ventilatory support, ability to initiate breaths, airway protection, secretion burden, and appropriate liberation criteria
Begin a spontaneous breathing trial whenever the patient is awake, even if oxygen and hemodynamic requirements are increasing
Delay all liberation assessment until ventilator settings reach room-air FiO2 and zero PEEP
Use respiratory rate alone to determine readiness because it reflects both oxygenation and ventilatory reserve

items.stem: Before connecting a newly assembled ventilator circuit to a patient, what should the therapist do?
options: Complete the required pre-use verification, including circuit integrity, alarms, oxygen supply, and leak checks
Connect the patient first and test alarms only if a problem develops
Disable alarms during initial connection to avoid nuisance alerts
Skip circuit checks when the ventilator passed inspection on a previous patient

items.stem: A ventilator fails its pre-use leak test after a circuit change. What is the best next action?
options: Recognize signs of spontaneous-breathing-trial intolerance, return appropriate support, identify reversible causes, and reassess readiness later
Continue the trial until the planned duration is complete because early distress can resolve with continued effort
Extubate promptly because increased respiratory effort demonstrates adequate spontaneous drive
Reduce monitoring during the trial so anxiety-related changes do not trigger premature termination

items.stem: Which action best reflects quality-control practice before mechanical ventilation begins?
options: Verify that required sensors, alarms, gas supply, humidification, and circuit components function as intended
Assume factory calibration eliminates the need for bedside verification
Silence all alarms permanently once the circuit is assembled
Reuse single-patient circuit components without following processing standards

items.stem: An adult with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure is newly intubated. Which approach best reflects an appropriate initial ventilator strategy?
options: Use a lung-protective initial strategy with appropriate VT based on predicted body weight, suitable PEEP/FiO2, and reassessment of pressures, gas exchange, and patient response
Use a large tidal volume to normalize PaCO2 quickly, then reduce VT only if barotrauma develops
Set PEEP to zero initially so oxygenation changes can be attributed entirely to FiO2
Choose tidal volume from actual body weight and avoid plateau-pressure assessment during the first several hours

items.stem: Shortly after ventilation begins, the patient has an acceptable oxygen saturation but hypotension develops and airway pressures are higher than expected. What should the therapist do?
options: Reassess ventilator strategy and patient response rather than judging success by oxygen saturation alone
Continue unchanged because adequate oxygen saturation confirms safe ventilation
Increase PEEP immediately without evaluating the hemodynamic change
Delay reassessment until the first scheduled ventilator check

items.stem: After initial settings are applied, exhaled tidal volume is lower than intended and the patient appears asynchronous. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Evaluate the patient, airway, circuit, settings, and synchrony before making a targeted adjustment
Increase every ventilator setting simultaneously until the tidal volume rises
Ignore the finding if the ventilator remains in the selected mode
Change FiO2 alone because oxygen concentration controls tidal volume

items.stem: A ventilated patient receives a tidal volume of 500 mL at 12 breaths/min. What is the minute ventilation?
options: 6.0 L/min
4.2 L/min
8.3 L/min
12.0 L/min

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient has an elevated PaCO2 caused by inadequate ventilation. Which change would most directly increase minute ventilation if otherwise appropriate?
options: Increase respiratory rate or tidal volume while reassessing safety
Decrease respiratory rate and tidal volume together
Increase FiO2 without changing ventilation
Decrease inspiratory flow while leaving minute ventilation unchanged

items.stem: After a ventilator adjustment, PaCO2 falls well below the target and pH rises. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Alveolar ventilation is excessive for the patient's current CO2 production
Oxygenation is inadequate because FiO2 is too low
Airway resistance must have increased substantially
The patient requires a larger minute ventilation

items.stem: Two patients have the same minute ventilation, but one has substantially more dead-space ventilation. Which patient will generally have less effective alveolar ventilation?
options: The patient with greater dead-space ventilation
The patient with lower dead-space ventilation
Both patients must have identical alveolar ventilation
Dead space affects oxygenation but cannot affect CO2 clearance

items.stem: A ventilated patient's dead-space fraction increases while total minute ventilation remains unchanged. What trend is most likely if CO2 production is stable?
options: PaCO2 may rise because effective alveolar ventilation has fallen
PaCO2 must fall because dead space removes additional CO2
PaCO2 cannot change unless FiO2 changes
PaCO2 will equal the inspired oxygen concentration

items.stem: A patient has persistent hypercapnia despite an apparently adequate total minute ventilation. Which concept should be evaluated before simply increasing support?
options: How much of the delivered ventilation reaches gas-exchanging alveoli rather than dead space
Whether the oxygen analyzer displays exactly 21%
Whether PEEP can be eliminated from every breath
Whether the humidifier temperature matches room temperature

items.stem: A volume breath delivers 600 mL with a constant inspiratory flow of 60 L/min. Approximately how long is inspiratory time?
options: 0.6 second
1.0 second
1.7 seconds
6.0 seconds

items.stem: A patient with obstructive lung disease has incomplete exhalation before the next ventilator breath begins. Which adjustment most directly increases expiratory time?
options: Reduce respiratory rate or shorten inspiratory time as clinically appropriate
Increase respiratory rate while prolonging inspiratory time
Decrease inspiratory flow so inspiration lasts longer
Increase tidal volume without changing rate or inspiratory flow

items.stem: A patient receiving volume-controlled ventilation appears air hungry during inspiration, and the set inspiratory flow is low. Which change may better meet inspiratory demand while also shortening inspiratory time?
options: Increase inspiratory flow and reassess patient response
Decrease inspiratory flow further
Increase expiratory resistance in the circuit
Reduce trigger sensitivity until the patient stops initiating breaths

items.stem: A patient with severe hypoxemia remains below the oxygenation target on a high FiO2. Which ventilator strategy should be considered while monitoring hemodynamics and overdistention?
options: Evaluate an appropriate increase in PEEP/recruitment strategy within a lung-protective plan while monitoring oxygenation, hemodynamics, and overdistention
Increase tidal volume substantially because refractory hypoxemia is best corrected by increasing minute ventilation
Reduce PEEP and compensate with higher FiO2 because PEEP primarily affects ventilation rather than oxygenation
Shorten expiratory time to create intrinsic PEEP because auto-PEEP is preferred to set PEEP for severe hypoxemia

items.stem: After PEEP is increased, oxygenation improves but blood pressure falls significantly. What should the therapist do?
options: Reassess the PEEP strategy and hemodynamic response rather than evaluating oxygenation alone
Continue increasing PEEP because improved oxygenation proves the setting is optimal
Decrease FiO2 to room air without reassessing the patient
Ignore the blood pressure because PEEP does not affect circulation

items.stem: A patient's oxygenation is stable well above the prescribed target on a high FiO2. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Titrate oxygen support downward as tolerated while maintaining the target and reassessing
Maintain unnecessarily high FiO2 because oxygen toxicity is unrelated to exposure
Decrease minute ventilation because PaCO2 controls oxygen toxicity
Remove PEEP before considering any reduction in FiO2

items.stem: A patient has VT 500 mL, plateau pressure 25 cm H2O, and PEEP 5 cm H2O. What is the static compliance?
options: 25 mL/cm H2O
20 mL/cm H2O
50 mL/cm H2O
100 mL/cm H2O

items.stem: Peak inspiratory pressure rises from 28 to 40 cm H2O while plateau pressure remains 22 cm H2O. Which problem is most likely?
options: Increased airway resistance
Worsening static compliance
Increased driving pressure from alveolar overdistention
A decrease in resistive pressure

items.stem: A patient's plateau pressure is 27 cm H2O and total PEEP is 10 cm H2O. What is the driving pressure?
options: 17 cm H2O
10 cm H2O
27 cm H2O
37 cm H2O

items.stem: On the ventilator flow-time waveform, expiratory flow has not returned to baseline before the next breath begins. What should the therapist suspect?
options: Incomplete exhalation with dynamic hyperinflation and possible auto-PEEP
Complete lung emptying with excessive expiratory time
A normal pattern that rules out intrinsic PEEP
An isolated oxygen-analyzer calibration problem

items.stem: A patient with severe airflow obstruction has auto-PEEP and dynamic hyperinflation. Which ventilator change is most likely to help?
options: Increase available expiratory time by reducing rate and/or shortening inspiratory time as appropriate
Increase respiratory rate and prolong inspiratory time
Increase tidal volume while reducing expiratory time
Add unnecessary circuit resistance during exhalation

items.stem: Why does a patient with high airway resistance often require more time for exhalation?
options: An increased respiratory-system time constant slows filling and emptying of affected lung units
High resistance shortens the time constant and causes instant lung emptying
Airway resistance affects oxygen concentration but not lung emptying
Time constants apply only to spontaneous breathing and not mechanical ventilation

items.stem: On a flow-time waveform, inspiratory flow appears above baseline and expiratory flow below baseline. What should the therapist evaluate first when using this graphic?
options: Whether the shape and timing of inspiratory and expiratory flow match the patient's ventilatory pattern
Whether the oxygen cylinder contains enough gas for transport
Whether the cuff pressure was documented during the previous shift
Whether the humidifier chamber contains sterile water

items.stem: A ventilated patient's pressure waveform changes at the same time that delivered volume falls. What is the best use of the ventilator graphics?
options: Compare pressure, flow, and volume together to identify the likely change before adjusting support
Interpret each waveform independently and ignore simultaneous changes
Change FiO2 because waveform abnormalities primarily reflect oxygen concentration
Silence alarms because graphics cannot provide clinically useful information

items.stem: Why is comparing current ventilator waveforms with the patient's prior pattern useful?
options: A new waveform change may reveal evolving patient, airway, or circuit problems
Normal waveforms remain identical in every patient and mode
Only numeric ventilator values can demonstrate a change in mechanics
