Waveform trends are useful only after the patient is extubated

items.stem: A pressure-volume loop develops a pronounced flattening or beaking near the upper end of inspiration. What should the therapist suspect?
options: Possible overdistention at the current inspiratory pressure or volume
A guaranteed improvement in compliance
Complete elimination of airway resistance
A normal finding that confirms additional tidal volume is required

items.stem: On a flow-volume loop, the expiratory limb repeatedly fails to return to the starting volume. Which problem should be considered?
options: A leak in the patient-airway or ventilator system
An increase in delivered tidal volume with no leak
A perfectly sealed circuit with complete volume return
A change in FiO2 without any effect on circuit volume

items.stem: A patient's pressure-volume loop shifts in a way consistent with greater pressure required for the same delivered volume. What physiologic change should be considered?
options: Reduced respiratory-system compliance
Reduced airway resistance with improved mechanics
Increased compliance with easier lung inflation
A change in oxygen concentration without a mechanics change

items.stem: Peak inspiratory pressure rises substantially while plateau pressure remains near baseline. Which mechanical problem best fits this pattern?
options: Increased airway resistance
Decreased lung compliance
Increased chest-wall compliance
Reduced resistive pressure

items.stem: Peak and plateau pressures both rise by a similar amount while tidal volume is unchanged. Which problem is most likely?
options: Reduced respiratory-system compliance
Isolated increase in airway resistance
A circuit leak causing loss of pressure
Improved compliance with less distending pressure

items.stem: A ventilated patient develops a sawtooth appearance on the flow waveform along with coarse breath sounds. What should the therapist assess?
options: Secretions or condensate causing airway or circuit obstruction
A perfectly clear airway with improved laminar flow
An isolated decrease in FiO2
A normal waveform caused by adequate humidification

items.stem: A pressure waveform shows repeated patient effort deflections that do not result in ventilator breaths. What should the therapist suspect?
options: Ineffective triggering from factors such as sensitivity, auto-PEEP, weakness, or support mismatch
Autotriggering caused by breaths delivered without patient effort
Normal synchrony because every effort should remain unsupported
Excessive delivered tidal volume as the only possible cause

items.stem: The ventilator repeatedly delivers breaths even though no patient effort is visible. Which cause should be investigated?
options: An overly sensitive trigger or circuit-related disturbance causing autotriggering
An insensitive trigger preventing ventilator activation
A prolonged expiratory time that prevents all triggering
A low FiO2 causing mandatory breaths

items.stem: A patient must generate a large inspiratory effort before each assisted breath begins. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Evaluate trigger sensitivity and patient factors that are making breath initiation difficult
Make the trigger less sensitive so an even larger effort is required
Increase expiratory resistance without assessing the trigger
Disable patient triggering and ignore spontaneous effort

items.stem: During volume-controlled ventilation, the pressure waveform becomes concave during inspiration while the patient appears to demand more flow. What should the therapist suspect?
options: Inspiratory flow is insufficient for the patient's demand
Expiratory time is excessive because inspiratory flow is too high
The patient is receiving excessive flow with no spontaneous effort
A circuit leak is the only possible cause of the waveform shape

items.stem: Two ventilator breaths occur in rapid succession with little exhalation between them during a strong patient inspiratory effort. What is the most likely problem?
options: Double triggering with breath stacking from patient-ventilator mismatch
Normal cycling with complete exhalation between breaths
Autotriggering caused only by condensate despite visible patient effort
An isolated oxygenation problem unrelated to breath timing

items.stem: In pressure support, the ventilator ends inspiration while the patient is still actively inhaling. Which dyssynchrony is most likely?
options: Premature cycling
Delayed triggering
Autotriggering
Late cycling

items.stem: Expiratory flow remains below baseline when the next mechanical breath begins. What does this graphic suggest?
options: Incomplete exhalation with dynamic hyperinflation and intrinsic PEEP
Complete exhalation with no possibility of air trapping
A normal flow pattern proving expiratory time is excessive
An isolated oxygen analyzer malfunction

items.stem: A passive ventilated patient has a flow waveform suggesting incomplete exhalation. Which maneuver can help quantify intrinsic PEEP when appropriate?
options: Perform an end-expiratory hold and evaluate total PEEP
Perform only an inspiratory hold and call the result auto-PEEP
Disconnect all pressure monitoring before measuring intrinsic PEEP
Increase respiratory rate until expiratory flow reaches baseline

items.skill: Correcting graphic evidence of air trapping
items.stem: A patient with obstructive disease shows persistent expiratory flow at the start of each new breath. Which ventilator change may reduce the problem?
options: Increase available expiratory time and reassess the waveform and patient
Increase respiratory rate and prolong inspiratory time
Increase tidal volume while shortening expiratory time
Add expiratory circuit resistance to slow lung emptying

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient suddenly becomes cyanotic and hypotensive while multiple ventilator alarms activate. What should the respiratory therapist do first?
options: Wait for the alarm message to identify the exact equipment fault
Replace the expiratory filter before assessing the patient
Assess the patient and provide manual ventilation with oxygen if effective ventilation is uncertain
Open the ventilator settings menu and review every alarm limit

items.stem: The patient is stable during a ventilator alarm. After assessing the patient, which sequence best organizes further troubleshooting?
options: Change the ventilator mode before inspecting the airway or circuit
Evaluate the airway, circuit, ventilator, and gas or power source systematically
Disconnect monitoring equipment to determine whether alarms persist
Increase all alarm limits, then reassess after the alarm stops

items.stem: During troubleshooting, the therapist disconnects the patient from the ventilator and begins manual ventilation. The bag is very difficult to compress and the patient's chest barely rises. What should be evaluated next?
options: The humidifier temperature because manual ventilation bypasses the airway
The ventilator alarm settings because the ventilator remains the likely cause
The patient and artificial airway for obstruction or severe mechanical impairment
The electrical outlet because bag resistance indicates loss of power

items.stem: A ventilated patient develops a high-pressure alarm. Peak pressure has increased, plateau pressure is unchanged, and coarse rhonchi are present. Which cause is most likely?
options: Worsening lung compliance from pulmonary edema
A circuit disconnection causing loss of pressure
A large cuff leak reducing delivered volume
Retained airway secretions increasing resistance

items.stem: Peak and plateau pressures both rise suddenly in a patient receiving a constant tidal volume. Breath sounds are diminished on one side and blood pressure is falling. What should the therapist suspect?
options: A low-pressure alarm caused by circuit disconnection
An isolated increase in airway resistance from secretions
A harmless increase in inspiratory flow demand
An acute compliance problem such as pneumothorax requiring immediate assessment

items.stem: A high-pressure alarm begins immediately after the ventilator tubing is repositioned. The patient is stable but delivered tidal volume has fallen. What should the therapist check first?
options: The low-pressure alarm limit for excessive sensitivity
The cuff for a large leak around the artificial airway
The circuit for kinking, compression, or pooled condensate
The oxygen analyzer calibration for a low FiO2 reading

items.stem: A low-pressure alarm sounds and exhaled tidal volume abruptly falls to near zero. The patient is no longer receiving visible ventilator breaths. What should the therapist assess immediately?
options: The airway for bronchospasm causing excessive resistance
The circuit and artificial airway for a disconnection or major leak
The lungs for reduced compliance causing elevated plateau pressure
The inspiratory limb for obstruction causing excessive peak pressure

items.stem: A ventilated patient has a persistent low-volume alarm, an audible leak around the endotracheal tube, and lower exhaled than inspired tidal volume. Which problem is most likely?
options: Severe bronchospasm with increased airway resistance
A mucus plug producing a high-pressure condition
Decreased compliance causing higher plateau pressure
An endotracheal tube cuff or airway-system leak

items.stem: After patient repositioning, a low-volume alarm occurs and the endotracheal tube marking at the teeth has changed. What should the therapist do?
options: Assume a ventilator sensor failure because repositioning cannot affect the airway
Assess for tube displacement and promptly reconfirm airway position
Increase cuff pressure without checking tube depth
Increase the low-volume alarm limit until the alarm stops

items.stem: A patient on a spontaneous ventilator mode develops recurrent apnea alarms shortly after receiving additional sedative medication. What should the therapist evaluate first?
options: Whether inspiratory flow should be increased to treat the apnea
Whether the high-pressure alarm should be disabled
The patient's respiratory drive and need for adequate backup ventilation
Whether PEEP should be removed to stimulate spontaneous breathing

items.stem: A patient remains awake and appears to make inspiratory efforts, but several efforts fail to trigger supported breaths and the low-minute-ventilation alarm activates. What should the therapist assess?
options: Increase the low-minute-volume alarm limit because the alarm indicates the ventilator is underestimating delivered ventilation
Increase mandatory rate first because ineffective triggering is primarily caused by insufficient set frequency
Trigger sensitivity, auto-PEEP, leaks, circuit/airway factors, patient effort, and other causes of ineffective triggering
Decrease inspiratory time because missed triggers occur when supported breaths are too long

items.stem: A patient receiving spontaneous support is at risk for intermittent apnea. Which ventilator feature is most important for safety?
options: Appropriately configured backup ventilation that activates when spontaneous breathing is absent
An excessively wide low-minute-volume alarm range
A fixed high-pressure limit unrelated to the patient's airway pressures
A permanently disabled apnea alarm to prevent nuisance alarms

items.stem: A stable patient's normal exhaled tidal volume is 450 to 500 mL. The low-volume alarm is set at 100 mL and would not identify a clinically important decrease promptly. What should the therapist do?
options: Set the alarm to a clinically appropriate limit based on the patient's expected ventilation
Leave the alarm unchanged because alarm limits should be identical for all adults
Set the alarm below the smallest volume the ventilator can measure
Disable the alarm because the patient is currently stable

items.stem: A patient repeatedly triggers nuisance alarms during coughing, but the alarms are otherwise clinically appropriate. What is the best response?
options: Address the cause and adjust limits appropriately without eliminating essential alarm protection
Silence all ventilator alarms until the patient stops coughing
Disable the alarm permanently so coughing does not disturb the patient
Set every alarm to its widest possible limit regardless of patient condition

items.stem: A patient's ventilator support is substantially reduced during recovery. How should this affect alarm management?
options: Keep every alarm limit unchanged until extubation
Use manufacturer default limits without considering the patient's current status
Reassess alarm limits so they remain appropriate for the patient's new ventilatory pattern
Disable low-volume alarms because spontaneous breathing has increased

items.stem: A patient with severe COPD is intubated for acute ventilatory failure. The flow-time waveform shows expiratory flow continuing when the next breath begins. Which ventilator change is most appropriate?
options: Prolong inspiratory time and increase mandatory breath frequency
Decrease inspiratory flow and increase respiratory rate to raise mean airway pressure
Increase inspiratory flow and reduce respiratory rate to allow more expiratory time
Increase tidal volume and respiratory rate to normalize PaCO2 rapidly

items.stem: An intubated patient with status asthmaticus has severe airflow obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation. PaCO2 remains elevated, but pH and hemodynamics are acceptable. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Increase tidal volume until peak airway pressure reaches the ventilator alarm limit
Shorten expiratory time so more mandatory breaths can be delivered each minute
Increase respiratory rate until PaCO2 reaches the normal range regardless of air trapping
Prioritize adequate expiratory time and limitation of hyperinflation rather than aggressively normalizing PaCO2

items.stem: After a ventilator change for severe asthma, peak pressure remains high but plateau pressure is acceptable and expiratory flow now returns to baseline before the next breath. How should the therapist interpret these findings?
options: High resistive pressure may persist despite improved expiratory emptying and limited alveolar distending pressure
The patient has worsening compliance because peak pressure remains elevated
Returning expiratory flow to baseline confirms the respiratory rate should be increased further
An acceptable plateau pressure indicates airway resistance has returned to normal

items.stem: A patient with ARDS requires invasive ventilation. Which approach best reflects a lung-protective strategy?
options: Normalize PaCO2 with progressively larger tidal volumes regardless of airway pressure
Minimize PEEP in all patients to avoid any increase in mean airway pressure
Use a large tidal volume based on actual body weight to prevent atelectasis
Use a low tidal volume based on predicted body weight and monitor plateau pressure and oxygenation

items.stem: An ARDS patient receiving lung-protective ventilation has a plateau pressure above the desired safety range. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Increase tidal volume to improve alveolar recruitment despite the plateau pressure
Ignore plateau pressure if oxygen saturation remains within the target range
Reassess tidal volume and the overall ventilator strategy to reduce injurious distending pressure
Increase respiratory rate and tidal volume together until PaCO2 is normal

items.stem: An ARDS patient remains hypoxemic despite a high FiO2. Which approach best supports oxygenation while limiting prolonged exposure to excessive oxygen?
options: Use an appropriate PEEP strategy to support recruitment while monitoring pressure and hemodynamic effects
Increase tidal volume until oxygen saturation normalizes regardless of plateau pressure
Reduce PEEP to zero because PEEP does not influence oxygenation in ARDS
Continue increasing FiO2 without reassessing PEEP or lung recruitment

items.stem: A patient with cardiogenic pulmonary edema requires invasive ventilation and has diffuse alveolar flooding with severe hypoxemia. Which ventilator intervention can improve oxygenation by helping recruit flooded or unstable alveoli?
options: Apply appropriate PEEP while monitoring oxygenation and hemodynamic response
Increase respiratory rate as the primary method of alveolar recruitment
Eliminate PEEP so venous return is never affected
Reduce mean airway pressure until oxygenation improves

items.stem: After PEEP is increased in a ventilated patient with pulmonary edema, oxygenation improves but blood pressure falls substantially. What should the therapist recommend?
options: Reassess the level of PEEP and the patient's cardiovascular response while preserving needed oxygenation support
Continue increasing PEEP because improved oxygenation outweighs any blood pressure change
Increase tidal volume because larger breaths reliably correct PEEP-related hypotension
Remove all oxygen and PEEP simultaneously to restore venous return

items.stem: A ventilated patient with cardiogenic pulmonary edema improves after treatment, with better oxygenation and decreasing support requirements. What is the best respiratory care response?
options: Increase PEEP routinely because prior pulmonary edema requires permanently elevated pressure
Avoid reassessment because cardiac treatment determines all respiratory support decisions
Maintain the highest initial support until extubation regardless of response
Reassess and titrate ventilatory and oxygen support as the underlying condition improves

items.stem: A patient with progressive neuromuscular weakness develops shallow breathing, declining vital capacity, rising PaCO2, and increasing fatigue. Which problem is most directly causing the respiratory failure?
options: Inadequate ventilatory pump function despite potentially normal lung parenchyma
Severe intrapulmonary shunt from diffuse alveolar flooding
Excessive pulmonary compliance causing refractory hypoxemia
Primary airway obstruction producing dynamic hyperinflation

items.stem: A patient with neuromuscular disease is ventilated because respiratory muscle strength is inadequate. Which ventilator goal is most important?
options: Create prolonged expiratory time to treat severe bronchospasm
Use high PEEP primarily to correct diffuse alveolar collapse in every case
Maintain spontaneous ventilation without assistance despite progressive hypercapnia
Provide sufficient ventilatory support while monitoring secretion clearance and ability to protect the airway

items.stem: A ventilated patient with neuromuscular weakness has adequate gas exchange but cannot generate an effective cough. What additional respiratory problem should be addressed?
options: Impaired secretion clearance requiring an appropriate cough-assistance strategy
Dynamic hyperinflation requiring a shorter expiratory time
Excessive airway resistance requiring a lower inspiratory flow
Refractory shunt requiring immediate escalation to maximal PEEP

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient with acute brain injury has adequate oxygenation and no signs of impending herniation. Which PaCO2 strategy is generally most appropriate?
options: Maintain prophylactic hypocapnia because cerebral vasoconstriction routinely prevents intracranial-pressure elevation
Allow marked hypercapnia because higher PaCO2 consistently improves cerebral perfusion without increasing intracranial pressure
Set ventilation from oxygenation targets alone because PaCO2 has little influence on cerebral blood flow
Target normocapnia unless a specific temporary indication calls for a different PaCO2 strategy

items.stem: Why is prevention of hypoxemia especially important in a patient with acute brain injury?
options: Secondary cerebral injury can worsen when oxygen delivery is inadequate
Oxygenation targets are unrelated to neurologic outcomes
Cerebral tissue does not depend on arterial oxygen once mechanical ventilation begins
Hypoxemia reliably lowers intracranial pressure without harming brain tissue

items.stem: A brain-injured patient's ventilator settings produce marked hypocapnia while oxygenation is adequate. What should the therapist do?
options: Reassess the ventilation target and avoid unnecessary sustained hypocapnia unless a specific temporary indication exists
Maintain marked hypocapnia because lower PaCO2 consistently improves cerebral perfusion in brain injury
Increase minute ventilation further because cerebral vasoconstriction protects injured brain tissue from ischemia
Ignore PaCO2 when oxygenation is adequate because ventilation has little effect on cerebral blood flow

items.stem: A patient with severe respiratory failure remains profoundly hypoxemic despite an optimized lung-protective conventional ventilator strategy. What is the best next step?
options: Remove PEEP because refractory hypoxemia indicates excessive recruitment
Recognize failure of conventional support and evaluate an appropriate rescue strategy
Continue unchanged because rescue support should begin only after cardiac arrest
Increase tidal volume repeatedly until oxygenation normalizes

items.stem: A ventilated patient's oxygenation continues to worsen while FiO2 and PEEP requirements rise and safe pressure limits constrain further conventional adjustments. How should the therapist interpret this trend?
options: The patient should receive less monitoring until oxygenation stabilizes
The patient may be reaching the limits of conventional ventilation and needs prompt escalation planning
Pressure limits should be ignored so conventional ventilation can always be intensified
The rising support requirement confirms that the current strategy is succeeding

items.stem: Which finding most strongly supports early discussion of rescue support rather than repeated potentially injurious conventional ventilator changes?
options: Stable oxygenation on decreasing FiO2 and PEEP
Persistent gas-exchange failure despite optimized support within acceptable safety limits
A single mildly abnormal blood gas immediately after intubation
Improving compliance with lower airway pressures

items.stem: A patient with severe diffuse lung injury remains markedly hypoxemic despite an appropriate ventilator strategy. Which advanced oxygenation intervention may improve ventilation-perfusion matching and recruitment?
options: Routine supine positioning with progressive removal of PEEP
Reducing monitoring during position changes to prevent alarm fatigue
Prone positioning with close monitoring and a coordinated team
Increasing tidal volume above lung-protective targets

items.stem: During prone positioning of an intubated patient, which concern requires particular attention?
options: Securing the airway and lines while monitoring oxygenation, pressure injury, and hemodynamic response
Removing vascular access before repositioning
Deflating the endotracheal cuff so the tube can move freely
Disabling ventilator alarms during the turn

items.stem: A recruitment maneuver produces transient improvement in oxygenation but causes significant hypotension. What should the therapist do?
options: Continue the maneuver because oxygenation improvement proves it is safe
Stop or modify the maneuver and reassess because hemodynamic intolerance limits the strategy
Ignore the hypotension because recruitment affects only the lungs
Increase recruitment pressure until blood pressure returns to baseline

items.stem: A patient receiving high-frequency oscillatory ventilation needs improved oxygenation. Which variable is most closely associated with lung recruitment and oxygenation in HFOV?
options: Endotracheal cuff pressure
Suction catheter diameter
Mean airway pressure
Oscillatory amplitude alone

items.stem: During HFOV, carbon dioxide clearance is inadequate. Which adjustment concept most directly targets ventilation?
options: Modify oscillatory amplitude and/or frequency according to the patient's response
Increase mean airway pressure as the only method of removing CO2
Adjust FiO2 alone because oxygen concentration controls CO2 elimination
Decrease all oscillatory pressure changes to increase ventilation

items.stem: Which statement best distinguishes high-frequency jet ventilation from conventional ventilation?
options: It uses conventional adult tidal volumes at a slower respiratory rate
It delivers very small rapid gas pulses through a specialized jet system while gas exchange depends on high-frequency principles
It functions only as a form of noninvasive mask ventilation
It eliminates the need to monitor oxygenation and ventilation

items.stem: A patient has severe isolated respiratory failure with potentially recoverable lungs and adequate cardiac function despite maximal conventional and rescue respiratory support. Which extracorporeal concept is most relevant?
options: ECMO replaces the need for any ongoing lung-protective ventilator strategy
VV ECMO can provide extracorporeal respiratory support when appropriately indicated
Extracorporeal support is used only when respiratory function has already recovered
VA ECMO is required whenever the primary problem is isolated lung failure

items.stem: A patient's severe refractory respiratory failure is worsening despite optimized rescue therapy. What is the most appropriate respiratory-care action regarding ECMO?
options: Recognize the need for early specialty-center evaluation rather than waiting for irreversible deterioration
Delay referral until all organ systems have failed
Increase injurious ventilator pressures because ECMO should never be considered while ventilation is possible
Discontinue respiratory support while determining ECMO eligibility

items.stem: After VV ECMO is initiated for severe respiratory failure, what remains an important respiratory-care responsibility?
options: Remove the artificial airway immediately after extracorporeal flow begins
Stop all respiratory assessment because ECMO completely replaces lung care
Continue monitoring and providing an appropriate lung-support strategy while extracorporeal gas exchange is used
Use maximal ventilator pressures because extracorporeal support prevents ventilator injury

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient suddenly becomes hypotensive and hypoxemic with unilateral absent breath sounds and rapidly increasing airway pressure. What should the therapist suspect?
options: Improved compliance after recruitment
An isolated oxygen-analyzer calibration problem
A simple cuff leak causing low airway pressure
Tension pneumothorax requiring immediate emergency response

items.stem: New crepitus is palpated across the upper chest and neck of a ventilated patient after airway pressures increased. What complication should be considered?
options: Subcutaneous emphysema associated with an air-leak syndrome
Improved alveolar recruitment
Isolated mucus retention without air leak
A normal effect of heated humidification

items.stem: A ventilated patient with a chest tube develops a persistent large air leak consistent with a bronchopleural fistula. What respiratory-care goal is most appropriate?
options: Maintain adequate gas exchange while limiting pressures and volumes that may worsen flow through the fistula
Increase tidal volume solely to compensate for every lost milliliter of gas
Increase airway pressures until bubbling in the drainage system stops
Clamp the chest tube routinely during positive-pressure ventilation

items.stem: A ventilated patient suddenly has a large difference between inspired and exhaled tidal volume. An audible leak is heard at the mouth. What should the therapist evaluate first?
options: Increase tidal volume until exhaled volume matches the set value
Assume a bronchopleural fistula without checking the artificial airway
Increase PEEP before evaluating the airway
Endotracheal tube position, cuff integrity, and airway connections

items.stem: A large ventilator leak persists after the circuit connections, tube position, and cuff are verified. Continuous bubbling is also present in the chest drainage system. What should the therapist suspect?
options: A normal cuff leak that does not affect ventilation
An intrathoracic air leak such as a bronchopleural fistula
A high-pressure alarm caused by mucus plugging
A disconnected ventilator circuit that has already been verified intact

items.stem: A patient with a known bronchopleural fistula is losing substantial delivered volume through the air leak. Which approach best balances ventilation with limiting further leak?
options: Use the lowest effective airway pressures and volumes while monitoring gas exchange and the leak
Increase tidal volume substantially to force all lost volume through the fistula
Increase inspiratory pressure until the air leak becomes continuous
Ignore exhaled volume because intrathoracic leaks do not affect ventilation

items.stem: A patient receives bilevel NIV with IPAP 14 cm H2O and EPAP 6 cm H2O. What is the pressure support?
options: 14 cm H2O
6 cm H2O
8 cm H2O
20 cm H2O

items.stem: A patient needs assistance with ventilation in addition to airway splinting. Which feature of bilevel NIV provides direct inspiratory pressure assistance?
options: Mask dead space without positive pressure
The pressure difference between IPAP and EPAP
The oxygen flowmeter setting alone
EPAP alone with no inspiratory pressure difference

items.stem: Why might a backup rate be important for a patient receiving bilevel NIV?
options: It converts EPAP directly into delivered tidal volume
It can provide supported breaths when spontaneous breathing becomes inadequate
It prevents every possible mask leak
It eliminates the need to assess airway protection

items.stem: A cooperative patient with an acute COPD exacerbation has respiratory acidosis, increased work of breathing, and can protect the airway. Which support should be strongly considered?
options: Immediate tracheostomy
Room air without ventilatory support
Noninvasive ventilation
Incentive spirometry as the primary ventilatory treatment

items.stem: A patient has severe respiratory distress, repeated vomiting, declining consciousness, and poor airway protection. Which respiratory support is most appropriate?
options: Begin mask NIV because vomiting improves mask tolerance
Proceed toward invasive airway and ventilatory support rather than relying on NIV
Use CPAP alone because airway protection is unrelated to NIV selection
Delay escalation until the patient becomes apneic

items.stem: A patient considered for NIV has copious secretions and an ineffective cough. Why is this clinically important?
options: Secretion burden affects oxygen therapy but has little relevance to NIV selection
An ineffective cough is corrected automatically by EPAP
Poor secretion clearance can make NIV unsafe or ineffective and may favor another airway strategy
Secretions improve mask seal and therefore increase NIV success

items.stem: A patient on bilevel NIV remains hypercapnic with inadequate tidal volumes but oxygenation is acceptable. Which adjustment most directly increases ventilatory assistance?
options: Reduce the pressure difference between IPAP and EPAP
Increase the difference between IPAP and EPAP as clinically appropriate
Increase EPAP and IPAP equally so pressure support is unchanged
Decrease IPAP while maintaining EPAP

items.stem: A patient on NIV has adequate ventilation but persistent hypoxemia. Which approach best targets oxygenation?
options: Decrease all airway pressures regardless of oxygenation response
Reduce IPAP until respiratory rate rises
Adjust oxygen and/or EPAP as appropriate while reassessing the patient's response
Decrease EPAP and remove supplemental oxygen

items.stem: Shortly after NIV begins, which combination best indicates a favorable response?
options: Increasing distress despite escalating support
Progressively larger mask leak with falling tidal volume
Lower respiratory rate and work of breathing with improving gas exchange and comfort
Increasing somnolence with worsening acidosis

items.stem: A patient receiving NIV has a large unintentional leak around the mask and poor breath triggering. What should the therapist do first?
options: Correct the interface leak and reassess fit, comfort, triggering, and delivered support before making unrelated setting changes
Increase inspiratory pressure to compensate for the leak before adjusting the interface
Increase trigger sensitivity to its maximum setting because mask leak does not affect synchrony once sensitivity is increased
Change to invasive ventilation solely because an unintentional mask leak is present

items.stem: A patient needs prolonged NIV and develops redness over the bridge of the nose. What is the best response?
options: Relieve interface pressure, reassess fit, and consider an alternate interface or protective strategy
Tighten the mask further to prevent movement
Stop all respiratory support solely because redness is present
Continue unchanged until open skin breakdown occurs

items.stem: A patient is making visible inspiratory efforts, but NIV breaths are inconsistently triggered. A large mask leak is present. Which factor should be corrected first?
options: The unintentional leak because it can interfere with triggering and effective support
FiO2 because oxygen concentration determines trigger sensitivity
Humidifier temperature because it directly controls breath initiation
EPAP should always be set to zero before evaluating synchrony

items.stem: After an appropriate NIV trial, a patient becomes more somnolent, respiratory acidosis worsens, and work of breathing remains severe. What should the therapist recommend?
options: Reduce monitoring because anxiety may be causing the abnormal findings
Switch to incentive spirometry while maintaining the same mask
Continue the same NIV settings for several more hours
Escalate promptly toward invasive ventilatory support

items.stem: A patient initially improves on NIV but then develops increasing secretion burden, inability to protect the airway, and worsening hypoxemia. What is the best response?
options: Increase mask pressure indefinitely despite loss of airway protection
Remove ventilatory support and reassess after the patient rests
Continue NIV because initial improvement guarantees ongoing success
Recognize evolving NIV failure and prepare for invasive airway management

items.stem: A patient's respiratory rate, pH, PaCO2, mental status, and work of breathing all improve during NIV. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Stop all monitoring because the initial response predicts the entire course
Increase pressure support until PaCO2 falls below the normal range
Intubate immediately because improvement indicates NIV has reached its limit
Continue support with ongoing reassessment and titrate as the patient's condition improves

items.stem: A patient using bilevel NIV reports severe dryness of the nose and mouth after several hours of therapy. Gas exchange and mask fit are otherwise acceptable. What should the therapist evaluate?
options: Evaluate heated humidification and other modifiable causes of upper-airway dryness while maintaining effective NIV
Reduce inspiratory pressure until dryness resolves even if the lower pressure no longer provides adequate ventilation
Increase mask leak intentionally so room air reduces oral and nasal dryness
Discontinue humidification because water vapor increases mucosal irritation during bilevel therapy

items.stem: A patient receiving NIV develops abdominal distention and discomfort while pressures have been progressively increased. Which problem should the therapist consider?
options: Aerophagia related to positive-pressure delivery and the current pressure/interface strategy
Loss of intentional leak from the exhalation system
A low oxygen concentration caused by heated humidification
A normal sign that pressure support is improving ventilation

items.stem: A patient on NIV becomes increasingly uncomfortable. The mask leak is minimal, but the patient repeatedly tries to inhale before supported breaths begin and appears asynchronous. What should the therapist assess?
options: Evaluate trigger sensitivity, timing, leaks, patient effort, and other causes of patient-ventilator asynchrony
Increase EPAP first because delayed inspiratory support is primarily caused by insufficient expiratory pressure
Reduce inspiratory pressure until the patient stops initiating breaths before the ventilator
Increase backup rate above the patient's spontaneous rate so patient triggering is no longer necessary

items.stem: A ventilated patient's pneumonia is improving. The patient is awake, hemodynamically stable, oxygenating adequately on modest support, and initiating breaths. What is the best next step?
options: Wait for every laboratory value to normalize before considering liberation
Increase sedation so spontaneous breathing does not interfere with ventilation
Evaluate the patient for progression into a ventilator-liberation protocol
Increase mandatory support because spontaneous effort delays liberation

items.stem: A patient is awake and initiating breaths but requires rapidly increasing vasopressor support and has worsening oxygenation. How should liberation readiness be interpreted?
options: The endotracheal tube should be removed before reassessing hemodynamics
The current instability argues against proceeding with a spontaneous breathing trial
Vasopressor requirement and oxygenation have little relevance to liberation readiness
Spontaneous effort alone establishes readiness for liberation

items.stem: What is the main value of a respiratory-driven liberation protocol?
options: It promotes consistent daily screening and timely progression when evidence-based readiness criteria are met
It requires extubation whenever a patient triggers a spontaneous breath
It replaces clinical assessment with a single ventilator number
It delays spontaneous breathing trials until a physician changes every ventilator setting manually

items.stem: During a spontaneous breathing trial, a patient develops marked tachypnea, diaphoresis, accessory-muscle use, and falling oxygen saturation. What should the therapist conclude?
options: The endotracheal tube should be removed immediately before fatigue worsens
The trial is successful because spontaneous breathing continues
The patient is showing SBT intolerance and should be returned to appropriate support while the cause is reassessed
The trial should continue unchanged because respiratory rate does not reflect tolerance

items.stem: A stable patient meets readiness criteria for a spontaneous breathing trial. Which approach best reflects the purpose of the trial?
options: Deeply sedate the patient so respiratory demand remains low
Increase mandatory rate to test whether the ventilator can maintain gas exchange
Use an accepted low-support spontaneous breathing method and monitor whether the patient can sustain adequate breathing
Provide enough pressure support to eliminate nearly all work of breathing

items.stem: A patient completes an SBT with stable gas exchange, respiratory pattern, hemodynamics, and comfort. What should happen next?
options: Repeat increasingly difficult SBTs until respiratory distress develops
Automatically extubate without assessing the airway or secretion burden
Evaluate extubation readiness, including airway protection, cough, secretions, and airway patency
Return to full ventilator support for another day regardless of the successful trial

items.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient has a respiratory rate of 24/min and tidal volume of 0.40 L. What is the RSBI?
options: 60 breaths/min/L
9.6 breaths/min/L
96 breaths/min/L
24 breaths/min/L

items.stem: A patient has a favorable RSBI but develops increasing distress and hypoxemia during the SBT. How should the therapist use the RSBI result?
options: Use the RSBI as an absolute pass criterion and continue toward extubation
Treat it as supporting data and prioritize the patient's overall SBT response
Ignore the clinical deterioration because the calculated value predicts success
Repeat the calculation until it overrides the bedside findings

items.stem: Why should VC, MIP/NIF, minute ventilation, tidal volume, and respiratory rate be interpreted together with the clinical picture?
options: Clinical appearance has little value when respiratory mechanics are available
Any one normal measurement guarantees successful extubation
Liberation measurements are useful only after extubation
No single liberation measurement reliably functions as an absolute pass/fail gate

items.stem: A patient passes an SBT but has a weak cough, copious secretions requiring frequent suctioning, and fluctuating mental status. What is the best interpretation?
options: The secretion burden becomes relevant only after the tube is removed
Ventilatory readiness is present, but airway-protection and secretion concerns make extubation risky
Passing the SBT establishes complete extubation readiness
A weak cough is unimportant when oxygenation is adequate

items.stem: A patient has passed an SBT but has substantial concern for upper-airway edema after prolonged intubation. What should the therapist do?
options: Increase cuff pressure and proceed directly to extubation
Evaluate airway patency and edema risk as part of the extubation decision
Extubate immediately because the SBT evaluates upper-airway patency
Ignore airway edema risk when gas exchange is acceptable

items.stem: Which finding most strongly supports airway readiness for extubation after a successful SBT?
options: An effective cough with manageable secretions and adequate ability to protect the airway
Frequent suctioning with a weak cough and progressive somnolence
Copious secretions that the patient cannot clear
Increasing airway obstruction whenever support is reduced

items.stem: Shortly after extubation, a patient develops inspiratory stridor and increasing work of breathing. What is the priority?
options: Rapidly assess upper-airway obstruction and provide appropriate airway support while monitoring for deterioration
Focus only on secretion clearance because stridor indicates mucus in the distal bronchi
Assume the sound is lower-airway wheezing and delay airway assessment
Encourage prolonged breath holding before reassessing

items.stem: Which assessment is most appropriate immediately after extubation?
options: Avoid listening for stridor because upper-airway findings are expected after extubation
Evaluate breathing pattern, oxygenation, ventilation, airway sounds, cough, secretions, mental status, and work of breathing
Assess only oxygen saturation because other findings can wait until the next scheduled check
Delay respiratory assessment so the patient can rest after tube removal

items.stem: A recently extubated patient develops progressively increasing respiratory rate, accessory-muscle use, and worsening gas exchange. How should the therapist interpret the trend?
options: Increasing work of breathing confirms the patient needs less respiratory monitoring
The findings demonstrate normal recovery from mechanical ventilation
Worsening gas exchange is expected and does not affect the post-extubation plan
The patient may be developing post-extubation respiratory failure and needs prompt reassessment and escalation

items.stem: A high-risk patient is extubated successfully but still requires substantial oxygen and has increased work of breathing without immediate evidence of airway failure. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Select post-extubation support such as HFNC or appropriately indicated NIV based on the patient's physiology and risk, then reassess
Use room air initially so the need for support can be proven
Choose support based only on which device is closest to the bedside
Reintubate every high-risk patient immediately after planned extubation

items.stem: A recently extubated patient has persistent hypoxemia and increased inspiratory demand but is alert and protecting the airway. Which support may provide heated humidified high-flow oxygen while meeting inspiratory flow demand?
options: Incentive spirometry as the sole oxygen-delivery method
A dry-powder inhaler
An unpressurized aerosol mask with no oxygen source
High-flow nasal cannula

items.stem: A patient at high risk for extubation failure has chronic hypercapnic respiratory disease and successfully completes extubation criteria. Which post-extubation strategy may be appropriate when clinically indicated?
options: Deep sedation to reduce spontaneous respiratory effort
Immediate reintubation despite successful extubation criteria
Planned NIV with close reassessment
Routine removal of all respiratory support

items.stem: Several hours after extubation, a patient develops worsening respiratory acidosis, severe work of breathing, and declining mental status despite appropriate noninvasive support. What should the therapist recommend?
options: Prompt reintubation rather than allowing noninvasive support to delay definitive airway management
Continue the same noninvasive support until respiratory arrest occurs
Reduce monitoring so the patient can rest
Use incentive spirometry as the primary treatment for the worsening acidosis

items.stem: A post-extubation patient initially receives HFNC but develops progressive hypoxemia, inability to clear secretions, and loss of airway protection. What is the best next step?
options: Escalate to invasive airway management because the patient now has established failure features
Continue observation because secretion clearance is unrelated to extubation failure
Switch repeatedly among noninvasive devices to postpone reintubation
Increase HFNC indefinitely despite loss of airway protection

items.stem: A recently extubated patient has mild increased work of breathing but remains alert, hemodynamically stable, and is improving on appropriately selected noninvasive support. What is the best plan?
options: Continue the selected support with close reassessment for improvement or signs of failure
Increase support to maximal levels regardless of the improving trajectory
Reintubate immediately because any post-extubation support represents failure
Stop support because improvement means monitoring is no longer needed

items.stem: Before interpreting a patient's spirometry, the therapist notices inconsistent efforts and poor repeatability between acceptable-looking maneuvers. What should be done first?
options: Interpret only the maneuver with the largest FVC regardless of quality
Average all efforts and diagnose from the mean values
Address test quality and obtain repeatable acceptable maneuvers before interpreting the pattern
Classify the pattern from the flow-volume loop without considering effort

items.stem: A patient stops exhaling prematurely during repeated forced vital-capacity maneuvers. How can this affect interpretation?
options: FEV1 must increase and confirms obstruction
FVC may be underestimated, making the results unreliable for pattern interpretation
The maneuver becomes more accurate because fatigue is avoided
Early termination has no effect on measured vital capacity

items.stem: A spirometry tracing shows a hesitant start and variable effort. What is the best response?
options: Report the test as normal because variable effort lowers sensitivity
Diagnose restriction from the tracing alone
Correct technique and repeat the maneuver rather than assigning a disease pattern to poor-quality data
Proceed directly to bronchodilator interpretation without repeating baseline spirometry

items.stem: Quality spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC below the patient's lower limit of normal. Which ventilatory pattern is supported?
options: Isolated diffusion impairment
Confirmed restriction regardless of TLC
Airflow obstruction
Normal spirometry by definition

items.stem: Why is the FEV1/FVC ratio compared with an appropriate lower limit of normal or z-score rather than relying only on a fixed ratio?
options: A fixed ratio is used only to measure diffusion capacity
The lower limit of normal determines total lung capacity directly
Every healthy adult has exactly the same FEV1/FVC ratio
Expected normal ratios vary with patient characteristics, so reference limits improve interpretation

items.stem: A patient with asthma has a substantial decline in peak expiratory flow from the patient's established best value along with worsening symptoms. How should this information be used?
options: Treat the decline as evidence of worsening airflow limitation in the clinical context
Interpret the decline as proof of restrictive lung disease
Ignore the change because peak flow cannot be trended
Use peak flow alone to measure total lung capacity

items.stem: Spirometry shows a preserved FEV1/FVC ratio with a reduced FVC. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Restriction is confirmed by spirometry alone
The pattern proves diffusion capacity is normal
Restriction is suspected, but lung-volume measurement is needed to confirm a low TLC
Obstruction is confirmed because FVC is reduced

items.stem: A patient has reduced FVC, preserved FEV1/FVC, and a TLC below the reference range. Which pattern is confirmed?
options: Isolated upper-airway obstruction
Restrictive ventilatory defect
Normal pulmonary function
Pure obstructive defect

items.stem: Quality testing demonstrates an abnormally low FEV1/FVC and a confirmed low TLC. Which interpretation best fits?
options: Pure restriction without obstruction
A mixed obstructive-restrictive ventilatory defect
Normal spirometry with isolated diffusion impairment
Pure obstruction with normal lung volume

items.stem: A patient with obstructive disease has a markedly elevated RV/TLC ratio. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: Reduced residual volume from restriction
Isolated diffusion impairment
Air trapping
Normal expiratory emptying

items.stem: Which lung-volume finding most directly supports hyperinflation?
options: A normal FRC with reduced RV
A reduced residual volume with normal TLC
A reduced TLC
An increased total lung capacity

items.stem: Why can measurement method matter when evaluating lung volumes in severe obstructive disease?
options: Gas trapping can cause different measurement methods to estimate communicating and trapped gas differently
All lung-volume methods measure trapped gas identically in every patient
Measurement technique matters only when diffusion capacity is high
Spirometry directly measures residual volume, so another method is unnecessary

items.stem: A patient has airflow obstruction and a reduced DLCO. Which additional process should be considered when interpreting the low gas-transfer value?
options: Loss or dysfunction of the alveolar-capillary gas-exchange surface
An isolated increase in respiratory muscle strength
Improved diffusion from increased hemoglobin
A guaranteed normal pulmonary vascular bed

items.stem: A patient is significantly anemic when DLCO is measured. Why is hemoglobin relevant to interpretation?
options: Low hemoglobin can reduce measured carbon-monoxide uptake and influence the DLCO result
Hemoglobin determines FEV1/FVC but not diffusion
Hemoglobin has no role in carbon-monoxide transfer during DLCO testing
Anemia always causes an abnormally high DLCO

items.stem: A DLCO result is higher than expected. What is the best interpretive approach?
options: Interpret the elevated DLCO in clinical context and consider factors that can increase measured diffusing capacity rather than assuming the result is erroneous
Classify the study as restrictive because DLCO above predicted indicates reduced alveolar volume
Repeat spirometry until FEV1 falls into the expected range, then reinterpret the DLCO
Diagnose pulmonary vascular disease because elevated DLCO is characteristic of reduced pulmonary capillary blood volume

items.stem: Pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry are available. What is the best way to determine whether a significant response occurred?
options: Use the post-bronchodilator FEV1 alone; the pre-bronchodilator value is not needed
Compare the pre/post values using the accepted bronchodilator-response criteria for the measured spirometric variables
Call any increase in FEV1 a significant response regardless of its magnitude
Determine response from symptom improvement rather than the measured spirometric change

items.stem: A patient demonstrates meaningful improvement after bronchodilator administration but still has residual airflow obstruction. How should this be interpreted?
options: Any remaining obstruction invalidates the post-bronchodilator test
A response proves the patient has no chronic obstructive disease
Residual obstruction means there was no bronchodilator response
Bronchodilator responsiveness can be present even when obstruction does not completely normalize

items.stem: Why should an RTE candidate recognize both current bronchodilator-response interpretation and older threshold language?
options: Current and older criteria are always numerically identical
Bronchodilator response is no longer assessed with spirometry
Current practice may use updated criteria while older-style thresholds can still appear in legacy educational or exam-oriented material
Older criteria are required for all current clinical testing

items.stem: A flow-volume loop shows flattening of both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs. Which pattern should be considered?
options: Isolated small-airway obstruction with no upper-airway involvement
Fixed upper-airway obstruction
Normal maximal expiratory flow
Pure restriction confirmed without lung volumes

items.stem: A flow-volume loop demonstrates prominent flattening of the inspiratory limb with relatively preserved expiration. Which process should be considered?
options: Isolated restrictive disease
Normal loop morphology
Fixed obstruction affecting both limbs equally
Variable extrathoracic upper-airway obstruction

items.stem: A patient with unexplained dyspnea has reproducible flow-volume loops suggesting significant upper-airway obstruction. What is the most appropriate implication?
options: Treat the loop as proof of isolated parenchymal restriction
Recognize a potentially difficult airway and recommend appropriate further airway evaluation
Repeat spirometry indefinitely without considering airway assessment
Dismiss the finding if FEV1 is near predicted

items.stem: A patient with suspected neuromuscular respiratory weakness has reduced MIP and MEP. What do these findings support?
options: Reduced inspiratory and expiratory respiratory-muscle strength
Normal respiratory muscle function
Confirmed airflow obstruction based on FEV1/FVC
Isolated impairment of pulmonary diffusion

items.stem: During a 6-minute walk test, a patient develops substantial exertional desaturation and dyspnea despite acceptable resting oxygenation. What does the test provide?
options: Confirmation of bronchodilator reversibility
A direct measurement of residual volume
A measurement of upper-airway resistance
Functional information about exercise tolerance and the patient's oxygen response during exertion

items.stem: A patient's MVV is markedly reduced. Which factors should be considered when interpreting the result?
options: Interpret the largest isolated value as the patient's true function even when repeated maneuvers are not reproducible
Classify the defect from FEV1 alone because acceptability and repeatability affect severity but not pattern recognition
Average all attempts, including technically unacceptable maneuvers, to reduce variability in the final interpretation
Assess test quality and reproducibility, then interpret the pattern using appropriate reference values and the full set of measured variables

items.stem: Before patient spirometry, a laboratory's volume verification with a 3-L syringe is outside the acceptable range. What should the therapist do?
options: Proceed with patient testing and correct the values afterward
Change the patient's predicted values to match the spirometer
Troubleshoot the equipment and resolve the quality-control problem before patient testing
Ignore the result if the previous day's verification passed

items.stem: A spirometer repeatedly fails volume verification. Inspection reveals a loose connection in the testing circuit. What is the best action?
options: Record the failure as normal variation and continue testing
Increase the patient's expiratory effort to compensate for the leak
Use the equipment because leaks affect only inspiratory measurements
Correct the leak and repeat the required verification before clinical use

items.stem: Why are calibration or verification and documented quality-control procedures essential in pulmonary function testing?
options: They eliminate the need to assess patient effort or test quality
They guarantee every abnormal test represents disease
They allow reference equations to be ignored
They help establish that equipment measurements are reliable before clinical decisions are based on them

items.stem: A patient's pulse oximeter suddenly reads 78%, but the patient is comfortable and the pleth waveform is erratic during hand movement. What should the therapist do first?
options: Document severe hypoxemia solely from the displayed number
Assess the patient and improve signal quality by addressing motion and probe placement before accepting the value
Immediately intubate because every SpO2 below 80% is accurate
Increase oxygen to maximum without checking the signal

items.stem: A patient in shock has cool extremities and a weak pulse-oximetry pleth waveform. Why should the displayed SpO2 be interpreted cautiously?
options: A weak pleth proves arterial oxygenation is normal
Low peripheral perfusion can reduce pulse-oximeter signal reliability
Peripheral perfusion affects only respiratory rate monitoring
Shock causes pulse oximeters to directly measure PaO2 instead of saturation

items.stem: A patient with suspected carbon monoxide exposure has an SpO2 of 99% but headache, confusion, and a concerning exposure history. What is the best interpretation?
options: Pulse oximetry directly measures carboxyhemoglobin concentration
Standard pulse oximetry may be misleading in dyshemoglobinemia, so additional appropriate testing is needed
A normal SpO2 proves tissue oxygen delivery is adequate
The SpO2 excludes clinically important carbon monoxide exposure

items.stem: On a normal time capnogram, where is end-tidal CO2 measured?
options: Near the end of the alveolar plateau just before inspiration begins
Only during the initial rapid expiratory upstroke
At the beginning of exhalation before alveolar gas reaches the sensor
At the lowest point of the inspiratory baseline

items.stem: Why is PaCO2 normally somewhat higher than PetCO2?
options: The gradient exists because pulse oximetry lowers exhaled CO2
Exhaled end-tidal gas is influenced by physiologic dead space and may not perfectly represent average arterial CO2
PetCO2 is measured directly from arterial blood
PaCO2 excludes perfused alveoli while PetCO2 includes only shunted blood

items.stem: A critically ill patient develops a larger PaCO2-PetCO2 gradient while minute ventilation is unchanged. Which physiologic change should be considered?
options: A guaranteed improvement in pulmonary perfusion
Elimination of all physiologic dead space
An isolated increase in hemoglobin concentration
Increased dead-space ventilation or worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch

items.stem: A capnogram develops a prolonged sloping expiratory upstroke and alveolar plateau often described as a shark-fin appearance. What should the therapist suspect?
options: Normal rapid alveolar emptying
Esophageal intubation with no exhaled CO2
Complete circuit disconnection
Expiratory airflow obstruction such as bronchospasm

items.stem: The inspiratory baseline of a capnogram no longer returns to zero between breaths. Which problem should be considered?
options: A normal capnogram during hyperventilation
Rebreathing of carbon dioxide
Improved elimination of apparatus dead space
Complete absence of pulmonary perfusion

items.stem: Continuous capnography on an intubated patient abruptly becomes nearly flat. What should the therapist assess immediately?
options: The patient, airway, breathing circuit, and perfusion for causes such as disconnection, extubation, obstruction, or circulatory collapse
The pulse-oximeter probe before assessing the airway
Whether the patient needs a bronchodilator because a flat tracing confirms bronchospasm
Only the oxygen flowmeter because CO2 waveforms do not reflect airway continuity

items.stem: After endotracheal intubation, which capnography finding most strongly supports tracheal placement when adequate circulation is present?
options: A single transient color change without a continuing waveform
Absence of exhaled CO2 with progressive gastric distention
An SpO2 reading obtained before intubation
A persistent exhaled CO2 waveform over successive breaths

items.stem: During CPR, PetCO2 abruptly and persistently rises while compressions continue. What should the team consider?
options: Return of spontaneous circulation and the need to assess for a pulse and organized circulation
A reason to stop waveform monitoring
Immediate confirmation of esophageal intubation
Worsening airway obstruction as the only explanation

items.stem: During cardiac arrest, waveform capnography shows persistently very low PetCO2 despite a patent airway. What should the respiratory therapist help the team evaluate?
options: The quality of chest compressions, ventilation, and overall perfusion during resuscitation
Whether increasing respiratory rate will always correct the low PetCO2
Whether the capnography should be disconnected until a pulse returns
Whether oxygen saturation alone confirms adequate circulation

items.stem: A patient needs noninvasive trending of ventilation over an extended period. Which monitor can provide a continuous estimate of CO2 through the skin?
options: Peak expiratory flow monitoring
Standard pulse oximetry alone
Incentive spirometry
Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring

items.stem: A transcutaneous CO2 value changes substantially, but the patient's clinical status does not. What should the therapist do?
options: Adjust ventilation immediately to the transcutaneous value because continuous trends are more reliable than the bedside assessment
Ignore the transcutaneous value until the next scheduled blood gas because abrupt changes are usually artifact
Move the sensor to a new site and accept the new reading without checking the patient or device conditions
Assess the patient and verify sensor placement, site perfusion/temperature, calibration or device factors, and comparison data before accepting the change as physiologic

items.stem: A noninvasive pulse CO-oximeter suggests an elevated SpCO in a symptomatic patient after smoke exposure. How should the therapist use the result?
options: Use it as an infallible replacement for all laboratory CO-oximetry
Treat it as useful screening/trending information while obtaining appropriate clinical confirmation when indicated
Assume SpCO and SpO2 measure the same hemoglobin species
Dismiss the exposure history if standard SpO2 is normal

items.stem: A patient with acute dyspnea has cool extremities, weak peripheral pulses, hypotension, and delayed capillary refill. What do these findings most strongly suggest?
options: Impaired systemic perfusion
Normal cardiovascular function
Adequate cardiac output with isolated bronchospasm
Improved left-ventricular performance

items.stem: A dyspneic patient has jugular venous distention, bilateral dependent edema, and inspiratory crackles. Which process should the respiratory therapist consider?
options: Uncomplicated dehydration
Isolated upper-airway obstruction
Cardiac dysfunction with volume congestion affecting the cardiopulmonary system
Normal findings caused by supplemental oxygen

items.stem: A patient reports chest pressure and increasing shortness of breath. Blood pressure is falling and new crackles are present. What is the best response?
options: Assume the crackles exclude a cardiac cause
Treat the findings as an isolated secretion problem
Delay cardiovascular evaluation until oxygen saturation falls
Recognize possible cardiovascular deterioration and escalate assessment and care promptly

items.stem: When evaluating an ECG rhythm strip, which approach is most appropriate?
options: Identify the rhythm primarily from heart rate because rate distinguishes most clinically important dysrhythmias
Evaluate QRS morphology first and classify the rhythm before checking atrial activity or regularity
Compare the strip with a normal sinus template and diagnose the rhythm from whichever feature differs most
Use a systematic approach that evaluates rate, regularity, P waves, PR interval, QRS width, and the relationship among complexes

items.stem: A monitor suddenly displays an irregular chaotic tracing, but the patient is awake, speaking, and has a strong regular pulse. What should the therapist consider first?
options: Artifact and the need to verify electrodes, leads, and the patient's actual rhythm
Asystole because the patient is conscious
Pulseless electrical activity despite the palpable pulse
Ventricular fibrillation requiring immediate defibrillation without further assessment

items.stem: An ECG shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm with a visible P wave before every QRS and a consistent PR interval. Which rhythm is most consistent with these findings?
options: Ventricular fibrillation
Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Sinus rhythm
Asystole

items.stem: A patient has a rapid tachyarrhythmia with hypotension, altered mental status, and ischemic chest discomfort. Which treatment pathway should be anticipated?
options: Transcutaneous pacing as the first treatment for rapid tachycardia
Routine observation because tachycardia is present
Unsynchronized defibrillation for every tachyarrhythmia with a pulse
Synchronized cardioversion for an unstable tachyarrhythmia

items.stem: A patient has a narrow-complex tachycardia but remains alert with adequate blood pressure and no shock, ischemic discomfort, or acute heart failure. What should guide the next step?
options: Begin chest compressions despite the presence of a pulse
Perform immediate synchronized cardioversion solely because the heart rate is elevated
Use transcutaneous pacing to slow the rhythm
Follow the appropriate stable-tachycardia evaluation and medication pathway while monitoring for deterioration

items.stem: Why is synchronization used when electrically cardioverting an appropriate tachyarrhythmia with a pulse?
options: It converts the procedure into transcutaneous pacing
It times shock delivery to the QRS complex to reduce the risk of delivering energy during a vulnerable repolarization period
It increases oxygen concentration during the shock
It guarantees the patient will not require sedation

items.stem: A patient has a heart rate of 34/min with hypotension, altered mental status, and signs of shock. How should the rhythm be interpreted?
options: A shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm
A stable tachyarrhythmia
An asymptomatic rhythm requiring no further assessment
Clinically significant symptomatic bradycardia requiring prompt treatment and escalation

items.stem: A patient with symptomatic bradycardia does not improve adequately with initial medication therapy. Which intervention may be needed next?
options: Transcutaneous pacing with appropriate escalation of bradycardia management
No further treatment until the patient becomes pulseless
Synchronized cardioversion to increase the heart rate
Defibrillation because all slow rhythms are shockable

items.stem: An ECG shows atrial activity and ventricular activity occurring independently with no consistent PR relationship. Which conduction problem should be suspected?
options: First-degree AV block
Normal sinus rhythm
Third-degree atrioventricular block
Sinus tachycardia

items.stem: A pulseless patient is in ventricular fibrillation. What is the priority rhythm-specific intervention?
options: Transcutaneous pacing
Atropine as the only treatment
Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation while high-quality CPR and the arrest algorithm continue

items.stem: A pulseless patient has organized electrical activity on the monitor. Which arrest rhythm category applies?
options: Stable sinus rhythm requiring observation
A tachyarrhythmia requiring synchronized cardioversion
Pulseless electrical activity, a nonshockable rhythm requiring CPR and treatment of reversible causes
Ventricular fibrillation requiring immediate defibrillation

items.stem: Immediately before delivering a defibrillation shock, what is essential?
options: Continue touching the patient to assess the pulse during shock delivery
Place oxygen-delivery equipment directly across the patient's chest
Use synchronized mode for ventricular fibrillation
Confirm that no one is in contact with the patient or equipment that could transmit the shock and follow device safety procedures

items.stem: During adult cardiac arrest, which medication is a core component of the current resuscitation pathway regardless of whether the initial rhythm is shockable or nonshockable?
options: Atropine
Diltiazem
Epinephrine
Adenosine

items.stem: A patient remains in ventricular fibrillation after appropriate defibrillation attempts and CPR. Which antiarrhythmic may be considered in the arrest algorithm?
options: Amiodarone or lidocaine
A calcium-channel blocker to terminate pulseless VF
Atropine as the preferred VF antiarrhythmic
Adenosine for every refractory VF episode

items.stem: During a cardiac arrest, the team suspects severe hypoxia as a reversible cause. What should the respiratory therapist prioritize?
options: Delay rhythm-specific treatment until a 12-lead ECG is completed even if the patient is becoming hemodynamically unstable
Treat the monitor rhythm first without assessing the patient because electrical instability determines management
Administer an unsynchronized shock for any tachyarrhythmia associated with hypotension
Assess the patient for perfusion and symptoms, identify the rhythm, and determine whether immediate synchronized cardioversion or another urgent intervention is indicated

items.stem: After an advanced airway is established during CPR, what is the respiratory therapist's priority?
options: Provide effective controlled ventilation without excessive rate or volume while compressions continue
Remove waveform capnography because the airway is already secured
Hyperventilate continuously to maximize PaO2
Pause compressions for every breath

items.stem: During CPR with an advanced airway, a sudden sustained increase in PetCO2 occurs. What should the team assess?
options: Resume high-quality CPR immediately after shock delivery and continue according to the resuscitation algorithm before the next rhythm check
Pause compressions after the shock to obtain a 12-lead ECG before deciding whether CPR should resume
Check for a pulse continuously for 30 seconds after each shock because return of circulation must be excluded before compressions
Deliver a second shock immediately without resuming CPR because persistent ventricular fibrillation is likely

items.stem: During resuscitation, the team leader says, 'Ventilate once every 6 seconds.' Which response best demonstrates closed-loop communication?
options: The therapist waits for another team member to interpret the instruction
The therapist discusses unrelated equipment options before acting
The respiratory therapist repeats the instruction, confirms it, performs it, and reports relevant changes
The therapist silently changes ventilation and assumes the leader noticed

items.stem: A patient with acute ischemic ECG changes develops severe dyspnea, diffuse crackles, and hypoxemia. What complication should be considered?
options: A normal respiratory response to myocardial ischemia
Isolated upper-airway obstruction
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema requiring prompt cardiopulmonary support
Uncomplicated hyperventilation with no cardiac consequence

items.stem: A patient with suspected myocardial infarction has an SpO2 of 98% on room air and no respiratory distress. How should oxygen therapy be approached?
options: Start high-concentration oxygen because suspected myocardial ischemia requires maximal arterial oxygen tension even with normal SpO2
Give low-flow oxygen routinely because any increase in dissolved oxygen improves myocardial oxygen delivery regardless of saturation
Withhold oxygen monitoring because a normal initial SpO2 excludes later hypoxemia during myocardial infarction
Do not give routine supplemental oxygen solely for suspected MI when oxygenation is adequate; continue monitoring and treat hypoxemia if it develops

items.stem: A patient with myocardial ischemia develops worsening hypoxemia and increased work of breathing from pulmonary edema. What is the respiratory therapist's role?
options: Delay respiratory intervention until the cardiac diagnosis is fully resolved
Treat only the ECG abnormality because respiratory support cannot affect the patient's immediate condition
Use incentive spirometry as the primary treatment for acute pulmonary edema
Recognize the cardiogenic respiratory deterioration and provide or recommend appropriate respiratory support while the cardiac condition is treated

items.stem: A patient's heart rate is 80/min and stroke volume is 70 mL. What is the approximate cardiac output?
options: 8.0 L/min
15.0 L/min
1.1 L/min
5.6 L/min

items.stem: A patient's MAP is falling while urine output, mental status, and peripheral perfusion are worsening. What is the best interpretation?
options: Normal oxygen saturation excludes a perfusion problem
MAP should be interpreted without considering organ-perfusion findings
The pressure trend is clinically concerning because tissue perfusion appears inadequate
A falling MAP proves preload is excessive

items.stem: Which change would most directly increase cardiac workload by increasing resistance against ventricular ejection?
options: An increase in afterload
A reduction in ventricular filling
A lower arterial pressure
A decrease in systemic vascular resistance

items.stem: A patient's CVP is elevated. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Use CVP alone to determine whether additional fluid will improve cardiac output
Assume the patient is always fluid overloaded
Assume the patient cannot have right-ventricular dysfunction
Interpret it with the overall clinical picture because CVP is a pressure measurement and not a direct measurement of intravascular volume

items.stem: A patient with acute dyspnea has an elevated pulmonary artery wedge pressure along with diffuse crackles and pulmonary edema. What does this pattern support?
options: Use CVP as the primary measure of left-ventricular preload and adjust therapy until it reaches a normal reference value
Treat a low arterial pressure as proof of inadequate intravascular volume regardless of cardiac function or vascular tone
Evaluate preload, afterload, contractility, rhythm, perfusion, and the clinical context rather than interpreting a single pressure in isolation
Use cardiac output alone because filling pressures and systemic vascular resistance add little to hemodynamic interpretation

items.stem: A patient has markedly elevated right-sided pressures and signs of systemic venous congestion. Which finding would fit this pattern?
options: Flat neck veins with severe volume depletion
Low right-sided pressure by definition
Isolated low hemoglobin without circulatory findings
Jugular venous distention and peripheral edema

items.stem: A hypotensive patient has cool skin, low filling pressures, and evidence of reduced cardiac output after major fluid loss. Which shock pattern is most consistent?
options: Cardiogenic shock from left-ventricular failure
Distributive shock with vasodilation
Obstructive shock from increased pulmonary vascular load
Hypovolemic shock

items.stem: A septic patient is hypotensive with warm extremities early in the course and markedly reduced systemic vascular resistance. Which shock pattern is most likely?
options: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Distributive shock
Obstructive shock

items.stem: A patient after a large myocardial infarction has hypotension, pulmonary edema, elevated left-sided filling pressure, and reduced cardiac output. Which shock pattern is most consistent?
options: Isolated hypovolemia
Cardiogenic shock
Uncomplicated distributive shock
Normal hemodynamic adaptation

items.stem: Why can severe pulmonary hypertension lead to right-ventricular failure?
options: Pulmonary artery pressure has no effect on right-ventricular work
The right ventricle must eject against an abnormally high pulmonary vascular load
Pulmonary hypertension eliminates right-ventricular afterload
The condition directly reduces systemic vascular resistance to zero

items.stem: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension develops increasing JVD, peripheral edema, hypotension, and worsening perfusion. What should be suspected?
options: Isolated upper-airway obstruction
Decompensating right-ventricular failure
Normal adaptation to pulmonary hypertension
Improved right-ventricular function

items.stem: A patient with pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction becomes hypoxemic. Why is correction of clinically significant hypoxemia important?
options: Hypoxemia improves RV ejection by increasing preload
Hypoxemia reliably lowers pulmonary vascular resistance
Hypoxemia can worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction and increase right-ventricular load
Oxygenation has no relationship to pulmonary vascular tone

items.stem: A hypotensive patient has an uncertain volume status. Why might a dynamic assessment be more useful than relying on one static filling pressure?
options: It evaluates whether cardiovascular performance changes with a reversible preload challenge or physiologic variation
Dynamic indices eliminate the need for clinical reassessment
Dynamic assessment directly measures total body water
A static pressure always predicts the response to fluid perfectly

items.stem: After a reversible preload challenge, a patient's stroke volume rises meaningfully and blood pressure improves. What does this response suggest?
options: Additional fluid can never increase cardiac output
The patient is likely fluid responsive in the current clinical state
Static filling pressure is the only relevant measurement
The patient has proven cardiogenic pulmonary edema

items.stem: A patient has a low CVP, but a dynamic assessment shows no meaningful improvement in stroke volume with a preload challenge. What is the best interpretation?
options: The low CVP guarantees a beneficial response to unlimited fluid
The dynamic result should be ignored because CVP is always definitive
The patient must have pulmonary hypertension
The low static pressure alone should not be used to assume that additional fluid will improve flow

items.stem: A patient’s arterial oxygen saturation remains 97%, but central venous oxygen saturation falls from 68% to 52% while cardiac output decreases. What is the best interpretation?
options: Arterial oxygenation proves tissue oxygen delivery is adequate.
The falling venous saturation may reflect increased extraction as oxygen delivery falls.
Central venous saturation directly measures arterial oxygen content.
The change is insignificant because pulse oximetry is unchanged.

items.stem: After treatment, a patient’s mean arterial pressure rises from 58 to 70 mm Hg, but lactate rises, urine output falls, and capillary refill becomes slower. What should the respiratory therapist conclude?
options: The improved pressure confirms adequate tissue perfusion.
