The perfusion findings remain concerning despite the improved blood pressure.
The rising lactate identifies the exact type of shock.
Normal arterial pressure makes cardiac output irrelevant.

items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) from central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2)?
options: SvO2 is obtained from the pulmonary artery, while ScvO2 is obtained from a central venous site.
SvO2 is measured by pulse oximetry, while ScvO2 is measured from arterial blood.
Both values are interchangeable regardless of sampling site.
ScvO2 directly measures oxygen leaving the lungs.

items.stem: An arterial pressure transducer is positioned well below the appropriate reference level. How can this affect the displayed pressure?
options: It has no effect after the system is zeroed
It can only lower the measured pressure
It converts arterial pressure into venous pressure
It can produce a falsely high pressure reading

items.stem: An arterial-line waveform becomes unusually flattened and the systolic pressure appears lower than expected. What should the therapist assess?
options: Whether the patient needs a bronchodilator
Only the pulse-oximeter probe because arterial-line shape is unrelated to the monitoring system
The monitoring system for damping causes such as air, clot, tubing problems, or an impaired pressure-flush setup
Whether the transducer should be placed on the floor

items.stem: An invasive arterial pressure suddenly differs greatly from the patient's cuff pressure and clinical appearance. What is the best first approach?
options: Treat the invasive pressure as correct because direct arterial measurements take priority over cuff pressure regardless of waveform quality
Treat the cuff pressure as correct and remove the arterial catheter because disagreement proves the invasive system has failed
Assess the patient and compare systems, then inspect the arterial line for leveling/zeroing, damping, tubing, and waveform problems before accepting the invasive value
Average the invasive and cuff pressures and use the result until the next scheduled calibration

items.stem: After a substantial increase in PEEP, a patient develops hypotension and reduced cardiac output. Which mechanism should be considered?
options: The pressure change must increase preload in every patient
Positive pressure has no cardiovascular effects
PEEP always increases venous return
Increased intrathoracic pressure can reduce venous return and alter ventricular loading

items.stem: In a patient with severe right-ventricular dysfunction, excessive lung inflation and airway pressure may worsen hemodynamics by doing what?
options: Increasing pulmonary vascular load and impairing right-ventricular output
Preventing all changes in venous return
Guaranteeing increased cardiac output
Eliminating right-ventricular afterload

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient becomes hypotensive immediately after PEEP is increased. What should the respiratory therapist do?
options: Reassess oxygenation, airway pressures, blood pressure, perfusion, and the hemodynamic response to determine whether the new PEEP is tolerated
Increase PEEP further without reassessment
Ignore blood pressure if oxygen saturation improved
Assume the hypotension is unrelated to ventilation

items.stem: Why should a respiratory therapist use a consistent sequence when reviewing a chest radiograph?
options: It guarantees a diagnosis without clinical assessment
It reduces the chance of overlooking image quality, airway, cardiac, diaphragmatic, lung, pleural, or device findings
It makes image quality irrelevant
It eliminates the need to compare with prior images

items.stem: Before interpreting lung findings on a chest radiograph, what should be assessed first?
options: Begin with the lung fields because technical factors rarely alter apparent cardiopulmonary findings
Assess image quality and technical factors such as projection, rotation, inspiration, and exposure before interpreting lung findings
Identify the cardiac silhouette first and use its apparent size to determine whether the film is technically adequate
Compare the film with the written radiology report before evaluating image quality so technical limitations do not influence interpretation

items.stem: A chest radiograph appears unchanged, but the patient has rapidly worsening dyspnea and hypoxemia. What is the best response?
options: Assume the patient is stable because the radiograph is unchanged
Delay reassessment until another routine radiograph is scheduled
Prioritize the patient's clinical deterioration and continue evaluation rather than relying on the image alone
Treat the image as more important than the bedside assessment

items.stem: A chest radiograph shows increased opacity with signs of volume loss and displacement of nearby structures toward the affected area. Which process is most consistent?
options: Normal lung expansion
Pleural air without volume loss
Atelectasis
Hyperinflation

items.stem: A dyspneic patient has bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities and an enlarged cardiac silhouette in a clinical setting of heart failure. Which process should be considered?
options: Isolated pneumothorax
Uncomplicated hyperinflation
Normal aging
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

items.stem: Which radiographic pattern is most consistent with pulmonary hyperinflation?
options: Pleural fluid layering at the lung base
Increased lung volumes with diaphragmatic flattening
A focal dense opacity with air bronchograms only
Reduced lung volume with mediastinal shift toward collapse

items.stem: A chest image shows a visible pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings beyond it. Which finding is most likely?
options: Lobar consolidation
Pleural effusion
Pulmonary edema
Pneumothorax

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient suddenly becomes hypotensive and hypoxemic. Imaging shows a large unilateral pneumothorax with mediastinal displacement. What should be suspected?
options: Chronic hyperinflation without acute consequence
Stable atelectasis requiring routine follow-up
Tension pneumothorax requiring urgent escalation
Uncomplicated small pleural effusion

items.stem: Which imaging finding is most consistent with a pleural effusion?
options: A pleural line with absent markings peripheral to it
Diffuse hyperlucency with flattened diaphragms
A normally positioned endotracheal tube
Dependent pleural opacity with blunting of the costophrenic region

items.stem: A post-intubation chest radiograph shows the endotracheal tube extending into a mainstem bronchus. What complication should the therapist anticipate?
options: A pleural effusion caused solely by tube depth
Guaranteed normal oxygenation
Improved bilateral ventilation by definition
Preferential ventilation of one lung with inadequate ventilation of the other

items.stem: After placement of a thoracic device, the patient develops new respiratory distress and the radiograph shows an unexpected device position. What is the best approach?
options: Correlate the image with the patient's condition and promptly escalate the suspected malposition
Ignore the image if the device was recently placed
Wait for symptoms to resolve before reporting the finding
Assume every visible device position is acceptable

items.stem: When reviewing a chest radiograph containing multiple tubes and lines, what should the respiratory therapist do?
options: Trace each tube and line along its course, verify tip position and complications, and relate the findings to the patient's clinical status
Confirm only the endotracheal tube because other tubes and lines are outside respiratory assessment
Use the radiology report alone for device position because bedside clinicians should not independently inspect tubes and lines
Judge placement from where each device enters the body because the internal tip position is less important than the insertion site

items.stem: Which imaging study is specifically designed to evaluate the pulmonary arteries when pulmonary embolism is suspected?
options: Standard bedside pulse oximetry
CT pulmonary angiography
Incentive spirometry
Routine noncontrast chest radiography

items.stem: Which statement best describes lung ultrasound in respiratory evaluation?
options: It can evaluate only cardiac rhythm
It can provide bedside information about selected pleural and pulmonary abnormalities
It cannot be used at the bedside
It replaces every form of thoracic imaging

items.stem: A clinician is evaluating possible pulmonary embolism and needs information about the relationship between regional ventilation and perfusion. Which study addresses that relationship?
options: Electrocardiography
Routine sinus radiography
Standard spirometry
Ventilation-perfusion imaging

items.stem: A patient has findings concerning for pulmonary embolism. Which principle should guide selection of the next imaging study?
options: Avoid additional imaging whenever oxygen saturation is normal
Select imaging without considering the suspected pathology
Choose an appropriate pulmonary vascular imaging strategy based on the clinical question, urgency, and test limitations
Order a chest radiograph and assume a normal result excludes pulmonary embolism

items.stem: A patient has suspected pleural fluid that may require further characterization before a pleural procedure. Which imaging approach is most appropriate?
options: Avoid imaging because pleural abnormalities cannot be evaluated radiographically
Use the same imaging study for every respiratory diagnosis
Recommend imaging suited to the suspected pleural process while considering bedside availability and procedural needs
Base the choice only on which test was performed most recently

items.stem: Why should urgency and test limitations be considered when recommending respiratory imaging?
options: Test limitations do not affect clinical decision-making
Every imaging modality provides identical information
The best study depends on the clinical question and whether the test can provide useful information safely and promptly
A more complex study is always the correct choice

items.stem: A patient has persistent lobar atelectasis with suspected mucus plugging despite routine airway-clearance measures. Why might bronchoscopy be recommended?
options: It replaces all chest imaging
It is used only to obtain arterial blood
It directly measures total lung capacity
It can be used therapeutically to inspect the airway and remove obstructing secretions

items.stem: Before bronchoscopy, which respiratory-therapy action best supports safe preparation?
options: Wait until sedation is given before checking oxygen or suction equipment
Assess respiratory status and risks and ensure required oxygen, suction, monitoring, and airway-support equipment are ready
Assume airway equipment is unnecessary for diagnostic bronchoscopy
Remove monitoring because it interferes with the procedure

items.stem: A patient scheduled for bronchoscopy has rapidly worsening hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability. What should the therapist do?
options: Reduce monitoring so abnormal values do not delay the procedure
Assume moderate sedation will correct the instability
Recognize the increased procedural risk and promptly communicate the instability before proceeding
Proceed routinely because bronchoscopy has no important cardiopulmonary risks

items.stem: Which procedure is specifically used to obtain ultrasound-guided samples from structures adjacent to the tracheobronchial tree, such as mediastinal lymph nodes?
options: Routine sputum induction
Incentive spirometry
EBUS with transbronchial needle aspiration
Thoracentesis

items.stem: Which situation is more likely to require rigid rather than routine flexible bronchoscopy?
options: Collection of a routine expectorated sputum specimen
Measurement of peak expiratory flow
Routine pulse-oximetry monitoring
A need for a large working channel and advanced airway intervention such as management of a major central-airway obstruction

items.stem: What is the main purpose of navigational bronchoscopy?
options: Provide continuous high-frequency chest-wall oscillation during bronchoscopy to mobilize peripheral secretions
Use advanced navigation to help guide bronchoscopy toward a targeted pulmonary lesion for diagnostic evaluation or sampling
Replace rigid bronchoscopy when a large central foreign body requires removal
Measure diffusing capacity by sampling gas from multiple bronchopulmonary segments

items.stem: A submitted sputum specimen is mostly saliva with little lower-respiratory material. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Saliva is always equivalent to a lower-airway specimen
The sample should be diluted with tap water before transport
Specimen appearance has no effect on interpretation
Poor specimen quality can limit the usefulness of the result and recollection may be needed

items.stem: Which statement best distinguishes mini-BAL from expectorated sputum collection?
options: Mini-BAL is another name for incentive spirometry
Mini-BAL is a blood test for infection
Mini-BAL measures only upper-airway flora
Mini-BAL obtains a lower-airway sample using an airway sampling technique rather than relying on spontaneous expectoration

items.stem: After obtaining a respiratory specimen, what is an essential next step?
options: Use appropriate biohazard handling, labeling, and transport procedures to preserve safety and specimen integrity
Open the container repeatedly to assess odor
Leave the specimen unlabeled until laboratory staff identify the patient
Store every respiratory specimen at the bedside indefinitely

items.stem: During bronchoscopy through an endotracheal tube, airway pressures rise and delivered volumes fall. What mechanism should the therapist consider?
options: The bronchoscope automatically increases endotracheal-tube diameter
The bronchoscope occupies part of the artificial-airway lumen and increases resistance to gas flow
The procedure eliminates the need for ventilator monitoring
Airway resistance cannot change during bronchoscopy

items.stem: An intubated patient's oxygen saturation falls during bronchoscopy. What is the best respiratory-therapy response?
options: Continue bronchoscopy while increasing suction because transient desaturation is expected during all procedures
Withdraw the bronchoscope immediately and extubate the patient before reassessing oxygenation
Reduce inspired oxygen to limit absorption atelectasis while the bronchoscopy continues
Assess the patient and airway, increase oxygen/support as needed, and communicate with the bronchoscopist so the procedure can be paused or modified if instability persists

items.stem: Why should the ventilator circuit and bronchoscopy adapter be checked before bronchoscopy in an intubated patient?
options: Leaks or an improper setup can interfere with ventilation and procedural safety
A circuit leak improves delivered tidal volume
The adapter is used only to measure blood pressure
Circuit integrity is unrelated to bronchoscopy

items.stem: After bronchoscopy with biopsy, a patient develops sudden pleuritic pain, dyspnea, hypoxemia, and decreased breath sounds on one side. What complication should be suspected?
options: Expected sedation recovery
Improved airway patency
Normal postprocedure fever
Pneumothorax

items.stem: After bronchoscopy, a patient develops increasing hemoptysis and respiratory distress. What is the best response?
options: Encourage vigorous coughing without evaluating the bleeding
Delay reassessment until the next scheduled vital signs
Recognize possible significant bleeding, reassess immediately, and escalate care
Treat the finding as routine regardless of severity

items.stem: A patient becomes increasingly somnolent with hypoventilation after bronchoscopy performed with moderate sedation. What should the therapist prioritize?
options: Assume sleepiness cannot affect ventilation
Remove oxygen and monitoring to stimulate the patient
Wait for hypercapnia to resolve without reassessment
Airway, ventilation, oxygenation, monitoring, and prompt management of the sedation-related deterioration

items.stem: Before brain-death apnea testing begins, why must prerequisites and baseline physiologic conditions be reviewed?
options: Baseline PaCO2 and pH have no relevance to interpretation
Prerequisites are unnecessary if the patient is mechanically ventilated
The test is designed to begin during uncontrolled hypoxemia and hypotension
The test requires appropriate preconditions so absence of respiratory effort and the resulting gas changes can be interpreted safely and correctly

items.stem: During an apnea test, what respiratory finding is specifically observed?
options: Whether peak expiratory flow reaches predicted
Whether any spontaneous respiratory effort occurs while the protocol's oxygenation and monitoring strategy is maintained
Whether the patient can cough on command
Whether FEV1 increases after bronchodilator

items.stem: During apnea testing, the patient develops severe instability meeting the protocol's abort criteria. What should be done?
options: Continue the test until the target PaCO2 is reached because physiologic instability is expected
Reduce monitoring intensity so transient instability does not interrupt the test
Restart the test immediately after a brief pause without first restoring physiologic stability
Abort the apnea test according to protocol, stabilize the patient, and use the established alternative evaluation pathway if needed

items.stem: A patient has sudden unilateral pleuritic pain, dyspnea, decreased breath sounds, and imaging that shows pleural air. Which disorder best fits?
options: Pneumothorax
Pleural effusion
Chylothorax
Empyema

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient suddenly develops severe hypoxemia, hypotension, unilateral absent breath sounds, and rapidly worsening distress. What should be suspected?
options: Tension pneumothorax requiring urgent intervention
Uncomplicated chylothorax
Stable transudative pleural effusion
Chronic pleural thickening

items.stem: Why is distinguishing an exudative from a transudative pleural effusion clinically useful?
options: It identifies the exact chest-tube size required in every case
It eliminates the need to consider the clinical history
It determines the patient's FEV1/FVC ratio
It helps narrow the underlying mechanism and guides further diagnostic evaluation

items.stem: A patient has a new unexplained pleural effusion and the team needs fluid for diagnostic evaluation. Which procedure may be appropriate?
options: Peak-flow measurement
Routine spirometry
Thoracentesis
Endotracheal suctioning

items.stem: During a pleural drainage procedure, the patient develops acute dyspnea and hypoxemia. What should the respiratory therapist do?
options: Remove all monitoring until the procedure is finished
Continue drainage without reassessment because respiratory symptoms are expected
Recognize possible complication, reassess immediately, and communicate the deterioration so the procedure can be modified or stopped
Assume the symptoms prove the pleural fluid has resolved

items.stem: Which action best reflects the respiratory therapist's role when assisting with a provider-performed pleural procedure?
options: Assume procedural responsibility once respiratory monitoring begins because the therapist is managing oxygenation
Assist within scope by preparing/monitoring respiratory support, observing the patient, maintaining safety, and promptly communicating changes during the provider-performed procedure
Limit involvement to equipment setup and leave physiologic monitoring to the proceduralist
Adjust procedural medications independently when respiratory status changes so the procedure can continue

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of the water-seal component of a traditional chest drainage system?
options: To humidify inspired oxygen
To collect all pleural fluid for laboratory analysis
To allow gas to leave the pleural space while limiting its return through the drainage system
To determine the patient's arterial oxygen tension

items.stem: Where does fluid draining from the patient's pleural space primarily accumulate in a chest drainage system?
options: The inspiratory limb of the ventilator circuit
The oxygen blender
The collection chamber
The pulse-oximetry sensor

items.stem: When comparing wet and dry suction-control chest drainage systems, what should the therapist recognize?
options: Both systems require identical water levels in every chamber
Wet suction eliminates the need for a water seal
The systems regulate suction differently, so the device-specific setup and expected behavior must be understood
Dry suction systems cannot be connected to wall suction

items.stem: Continuous bubbling is observed in the water-seal chamber of a chest drainage system. What should the therapist consider?
options: A direct measurement of pleural pressure
An air leak somewhere from the patient through the drainage-system connections
Normal fluid collection with no possibility of an air leak
Proof that the chest tube is completely occluded

items.stem: Previously visible tidaling in a chest drainage system suddenly stops. What is the best interpretation?
options: Clamp the chest tube immediately because absent tidaling confirms an air leak
Increase wall suction because absent tidaling proves suction pressure is inadequate
Assess the patient and system because loss of tidaling may reflect lung re-expansion or an obstruction/kink in the drainage pathway
Replace the drainage system because absent tidaling always indicates equipment failure

items.stem: A chest tube that had been draining a small amount of serous fluid suddenly produces a large amount of fresh bloody drainage. What should the therapist do?
options: Recognize an important change, assess the patient, and promptly report/escalate the finding
Raise the drainage system above the patient's chest
Assume all bloody drainage is expected and take no action
Clamp the tube indefinitely without an order or clinical assessment

items.stem: A patient with a chest tube becomes dyspneic. The tubing is visibly kinked between the patient and drainage unit. What is the safest initial action?
options: Clamp the tube on both sides of the kink and leave it clamped
Place the drainage system above chest level
Correct the kink while assessing the patient and restoring unobstructed drainage
Increase wall suction without correcting the tubing obstruction

items.stem: The chest tube becomes disconnected from the drainage-system tubing. What principle should guide the immediate response?
options: Clamp the chest tube and leave it clamped until a new drainage unit is available
Place the open chest tube end below sterile water and delay reconnecting it until the next scheduled assessment
Increase wall suction on the disconnected drainage unit before reconnecting the patient
Re-establish a safe closed drainage pathway promptly according to protocol while assessing the patient and system

items.stem: A patient's chest tube is accidentally pulled completely out of the chest. What should the therapist prioritize?
options: Insert the same tube back through the tract without assistance
Ignore the site if the patient initially appears comfortable
Connect the empty drainage tubing to wall oxygen
Immediately assess the patient, protect the insertion site according to emergency protocol, provide respiratory support, and summon appropriate help

items.stem: A patient has prolonged expiration, wheezing, air trapping, and reduced expiratory flow. Which physiologic pattern is most consistent?
options: Obstructive airflow limitation
Pure restrictive physiology
Isolated diffusion impairment without airflow limitation
Normal pulmonary mechanics

items.stem: Why can a patient with severe expiratory airflow obstruction develop dynamic hyperinflation?
options: Pulmonary compliance must always be absent
All exhaled gas leaves the lungs faster than normal
The next breath begins before the lungs have fully emptied, progressively trapping gas
Inspiratory resistance becomes zero

items.stem: Which combination most strongly supports obstructive rather than restrictive lung disease?
options: Isolated anemia with normal respiratory mechanics
Reduced expiratory flow with air trapping and hyperinflation clues
Normal spirometry and normal imaging
Reduced total lung capacity with preserved expiratory flow ratio as the only findings

items.stem: A long-term smoker reports progressive exertional dyspnea and chronic cough. Which additional information is most important when evaluating possible COPD?
options: A single normal resting oxygen saturation alone
Objective evidence of persistent airflow obstruction together with symptom and exposure history
Whether the patient has ever used incentive spirometry
Only the patient's current temperature

items.stem: Why should prior exacerbations and hospitalizations be reviewed when assessing a patient with COPD?
options: They prove the patient requires invasive ventilation
They eliminate the need to assess current symptoms
They help characterize future exacerbation risk and guide chronic management priorities
They determine the patient's blood type

items.stem: A patient with stable COPD is using an inhaler incorrectly and continues to smoke. Which management priorities are most appropriate?
options: Escalate maintenance medication first because technique and smoking behavior have little effect on treatment response
Stop maintenance inhalers until smoking cessation is achieved so response can be measured accurately
Correct inhaler technique, reinforce evidence-based smoking cessation, assess adherence and symptoms, and optimize maintenance therapy within the care plan
Focus on rescue medication use because baseline COPD management does not require technique reassessment

items.stem: A patient with COPD has increasing dyspnea, accessory-muscle use, worsening gas exchange, and declining mental status despite initial therapy. What is the best interpretation?
options: Only chronic outpatient management should be considered
The patient is improving because respiratory effort increased
The exacerbation is worsening and respiratory support should be escalated promptly
No change in the care plan is needed until cardiac arrest occurs

items.stem: A patient with a COPD exacerbation remains acidemic and hypercapnic with marked work of breathing despite controlled oxygen and bronchodilator therapy. What should be considered?
options: Discharge based only on the diagnosis of COPD
Escalation of ventilatory support, including NIV when clinically appropriate
Stopping all respiratory support because hypercapnia is expected in COPD
Increasing oxygen without reassessing ventilation

items.stem: After treatment for a COPD exacerbation, which finding best indicates that the respiratory care plan should be reassessed rather than simply continued unchanged?
options: A documented smoking history
Persistent or worsening dyspnea, gas-exchange abnormality, or work of breathing
Correct inhaler technique
A stable patient whose symptoms and gas exchange are improving

items.stem: A patient with asthma reports frequent symptoms and repeated rescue-inhaler use. Why is this important?
options: Controller therapy should automatically be stopped
It suggests inadequate control and should prompt reassessment of controller therapy, technique, adherence, and triggers
Frequent rescue use proves asthma is fully controlled
Symptoms are unrelated to asthma-control assessment

items.stem: A patient's peak expiratory flow has fallen substantially below the patient's usual personal-best value while symptoms are increasing. What should the therapist conclude?
options: Only oxygen saturation should be considered
The patient is necessarily improving
The objective decline supports worsening airflow obstruction and should be interpreted with symptoms and the action plan
Peak flow cannot provide useful information about airflow change

items.stem: Which approach best reflects guideline-based long-term asthma management?
options: Increase controller therapy whenever rescue medication has been used, without first assessing adherence or inhaler technique
Base long-term asthma treatment only on today's wheezing because prior exacerbations and symptom pattern do not alter risk
Assess severity, current therapy, adherence/technique, triggers, exacerbation history, and risk before recommending an evidence-based step-up or other change
Reduce controller therapy during an exacerbation so the response to rescue bronchodilator can be assessed more clearly

items.stem: A patient with severe asthma was initially tachypneic with a low PaCO2. The patient is now exhausted, has very poor air movement, and the PaCO2 is rising. What does this change suggest?
options: Worsening ventilatory failure and need for urgent escalation
Resolution of airflow obstruction
A reason to stop monitoring
Reliable improvement because PaCO2 moved toward normal

items.stem: A patient in a severe asthma attack becomes quieter on auscultation, but work of breathing and distress worsen. How should the quieter chest be interpreted?
options: As a normal finding unrelated to severity
As evidence that bronchodilator therapy should be stopped
As proof that bronchospasm has resolved
As a dangerous sign of severely reduced airflow rather than automatic improvement

items.stem: Despite aggressive bronchodilator treatment, a patient with status asthmaticus develops fatigue, worsening gas exchange, and declining mental status. What should be anticipated?
options: Routine discharge because wheezing may be less audible
Waiting for complete apnea before preparing advanced airway support
Urgent escalation of ventilatory support while continuing appropriate severe-asthma management
Stopping bronchodilator therapy and observation only

items.stem: A patient has chronic daily productive cough, recurrent respiratory infections, and large amounts of sputum. Which disease pattern should be considered?
options: Pure restrictive chest-wall disease
Uncomplicated isolated pleural effusion
Bronchiectasis with chronic secretion burden
Normal airway physiology

items.stem: A patient with bronchiectasis develops increased sputum volume, purulence, dyspnea, and systemic symptoms. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Interpret the sputum change as expected chronic bronchiectasis unless hemoptysis develops
Recognize a likely bronchiectasis exacerbation and evaluate severity, oxygenation/ventilation, airway-clearance needs, microbiology, and escalation of treatment
Reduce airway clearance because increased sputum volume indicates excessive treatment-related secretion mobilization
Delay evaluation until symptoms persist for several weeks because bronchiectasis exacerbations are defined by prolonged symptom duration

items.stem: Which respiratory-management priority is most consistent with chronic bronchiectasis and secretion disease?
options: Support effective secretion clearance and reassess changes in sputum, symptoms, infection pattern, and respiratory status
Avoid evaluating sputum characteristics
Suppress all cough regardless of secretion burden
Use oxygen as the sole treatment for retained secretions

items.stem: Which combination best reflects pulmonary management priorities in cystic fibrosis?
options: Avoidance of airway-clearance therapy
Airway clearance, management of chronic airway infection, mucoactive therapy when indicated, and disease-specific modern therapy
Routine discontinuation of all inhaled therapies
Treatment based only on resting oxygen saturation

items.stem: Why may dornase alfa be used in cystic fibrosis pulmonary care?
options: It is a pulmonary vasodilator
It is a disease-specific mucoactive therapy used to reduce secretion viscosity and support airway clearance
It replaces all airway-clearance techniques in every patient
It is used primarily to increase pleural fluid drainage

items.stem: What is an important principle regarding CFTR-modulator therapy?
options: CFTR modulators are selected primarily from the patient's current FEV1 regardless of genotype
All patients with cystic fibrosis receive the same modulator because CFTR mutations have equivalent drug response
CFTR modulators replace airway-clearance and other supportive therapies once treatment begins
CFTR modulators are genotype-specific therapies, so eligibility depends on the patient's CFTR variants and the approved indication

items.stem: A patient has reduced lung volumes. Which additional finding most strongly supports intrinsic parenchymal rather than extrapulmonary restriction?
options: Evidence of impaired diffusion and parenchymal lung disease
Marked kyphoscoliosis without parenchymal disease
Severe respiratory muscle weakness with otherwise normal lung tissue
Obesity-related chest-wall loading

items.stem: Which pattern is most consistent with restrictive physiology?
options: Air trapping with prolonged expiration as the defining abnormality
Isolated increased airway resistance with normal lung volumes
Reduced lung volumes with limited expansion rather than primary expiratory airflow obstruction
Dynamic hyperinflation caused by incomplete exhalation

items.stem: Two patients have similarly reduced vital capacities. One has fibrotic lung disease and the other has severe neuromuscular weakness. Why is the distinction important?
options: Use the pattern of lung volumes, spirometry, diffusing capacity, imaging, and clinical context to determine whether restriction is present and what may be causing it
Diagnose restriction from a reduced FVC alone because lung-volume measurement is unnecessary when spirometry is abnormal
Use an elevated FEV1/FVC ratio as definitive evidence of restrictive lung disease regardless of TLC
Classify all low-volume patterns as parenchymal restriction because extrapulmonary causes do not reduce measured lung volumes

items.stem: A patient with interstitial lung disease has progressive exertional dyspnea, reduced lung volumes, impaired diffusion, and exertional desaturation. What does this pattern support?
options: Isolated large-airway obstruction
Normal pulmonary function
Parenchymal restrictive disease with impaired gas transfer
Pure chest-wall restriction with guaranteed normal diffusion

items.stem: Why can interstitial parenchymal disease substantially increase the work of breathing?
options: Stiff lungs with reduced compliance require greater effort to expand
Respiratory muscles no longer participate in ventilation
Airway resistance must always fall to zero
The lungs become excessively compliant and easy to inflate

items.stem: A patient with fibrotic interstitial disease maintains acceptable SpO2 at rest but desaturates substantially while walking. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Normal resting SpO2 excludes significant parenchymal disease
The walking result should be ignored if resting saturation is acceptable
Exercise desaturation proves upper-airway obstruction
Exertion can reveal clinically important gas-exchange impairment not apparent at rest

items.stem: A patient with progressive neuromuscular disease has a falling vital capacity and increasingly weak maximal inspiratory pressure over serial measurements. What should the therapist conclude?
options: Declining values indicate stronger respiratory muscles
Only oxygenation should be monitored in neuromuscular disease
The trend proves lung compliance is improving
Respiratory muscle performance is worsening and ventilatory failure risk is increasing

items.stem: A patient with neuromuscular weakness has a weak cough and increasing secretion burden despite acceptable resting oxygen saturation. Why is this concerning?
options: Secretions are clinically unimportant in neuromuscular disease
Cough strength is unrelated to respiratory muscle function
Normal SpO2 proves airway clearance is adequate
Weak cough can impair airway clearance and contribute to respiratory deterioration even before resting hypoxemia appears

items.stem: Why should bulbar function be assessed in a patient with neuromuscular respiratory weakness?
options: Bulbar dysfunction can affect airway protection, secretion handling, and the safety/effectiveness of respiratory support strategies
Bulbar function determines pulmonary artery pressure
Bulbar weakness guarantees normal swallowing
It is relevant only to spirometer calibration

items.stem: Which respiratory pattern is most concerning in a patient with myasthenia gravis?
options: Progressive fatigable weakness with declining ventilatory muscle performance
Fixed hyperinflation caused only by smoking
Improving vital capacity with stronger cough
An isolated pleural effusion

items.stem: A patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome develops rapidly progressive weakness and declining respiratory muscle measurements. What is the priority implication?
options: Use oxygen saturation alone to judge respiratory adequacy because neuromuscular weakness primarily affects oxygenation
Delay ventilatory assessment until hypercapnia is severe because early weakness is best followed by symptoms alone
Emphasize bronchodilator escalation because declining respiratory muscle strength usually reflects reversible airflow obstruction
Recognize the increased risk of hypoventilation/respiratory failure and assess ventilation, cough effectiveness, secretion clearance, and need for assisted support

items.stem: A patient with ALS develops weaker cough, difficulty handling secretions, orthopnea, and declining vital capacity. What should these findings suggest?
options: Resolution of neuromuscular respiratory involvement
Normal expected findings that do not affect respiratory care
Progressive respiratory muscle and airway-protection impairment requiring reassessment of support needs
Isolated bronchospasm as the only problem

items.stem: A patient with progressive neuromuscular weakness develops nocturnal hypoventilation but can still protect the airway and cooperate with therapy. Which support may be appropriate?
options: Oxygen alone as a guaranteed correction for hypoventilation
Chest drainage
Noninvasive ventilation with reassessment of effectiveness and tolerance
Immediate discontinuation of all ventilatory support

items.stem: A patient with neuromuscular disease has retained secretions because the cough is too weak to clear them effectively. Which intervention directly addresses this problem?
options: Increasing oxygen concentration without addressing secretion clearance
Assisted cough or an appropriate cough-augmentation strategy
Routine defibrillation
Stopping all airway-clearance therapy

items.stem: A patient using NIV for neuromuscular respiratory failure develops worsening gas exchange, inability to protect the airway, and ineffective secretion clearance. What should the therapist anticipate?
options: Increase NIV pressure repeatedly as long as oxygen saturation remains measurable, even if airway protection is lost
Recognize NIV failure and prepare for escalation to invasive airway/ventilatory support while addressing reversible causes
Continue NIV and add sedatives to improve tolerance despite ineffective secretion clearance
Switch to low-flow oxygen because worsening ventilation indicates that positive-pressure support is no longer needed

items.stem: How can severe kyphoscoliosis produce restrictive respiratory impairment?
options: It guarantees increased total lung capacity
Chest-wall deformity can limit thoracic expansion and reduce effective ventilation
It primarily causes excessive expiratory airflow from enlarged airways
It eliminates the work of breathing

items.stem: A patient with severe obesity has daytime hypercapnia, sleep-related worsening of ventilation, and restrictive mechanics. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Only airway resistance should be assessed
Hypercapnia proves intrinsic pulmonary fibrosis
Obesity cannot affect respiratory mechanics
Extrapulmonary mechanical loading can contribute to hypoventilation and may create a need for ventilatory support

items.stem: A patient has low lung volumes, normal-appearing lung parenchyma, marked chest-wall deformity, and chronic hypoventilation. Which interpretation best fits?
options: The low lung volumes are clinically irrelevant
Primary obstructive disease is the only possible cause
Intrinsic interstitial disease is proven despite normal parenchyma
Extrapulmonary restriction from chest-wall limitation should be considered

items.stem: A patient has fever, productive cough, focal crackles, leukocytosis, and a new focal infiltrate. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
options: Stable chronic hyperinflation
Uncomplicated neuromuscular weakness
Isolated pneumothorax
Lower respiratory infection with pneumonia

items.stem: An older patient with dysphagia develops cough, fever, hypoxemia, and a new dependent-lung infiltrate after a witnessed choking episode. Which cause should be strongly considered?
options: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Aspiration-related lower respiratory infection
Isolated upper-airway obstruction
Pulmonary hypertension without infection

items.stem: A patient with suspected pneumonia produces a new purulent sputum sample. How should the therapist use this information?
options: Treat purulent appearance as sufficient evidence of bacterial pneumonia and select therapy before microbiologic evaluation
Reject the specimen because purulent sputum is usually contaminated and has no diagnostic value
Assess specimen quality and integrate Gram stain/culture findings with the clinical picture rather than treating sputum appearance alone as diagnostic
Use sputum color to determine the likely organism because specific colors reliably identify common pathogens

items.stem: Which respiratory-care approach best supports prevention of ventilator-associated complications?
options: Change the ventilator circuit on a fixed frequent schedule because routine circuit replacement is the primary prevention strategy
Use evidence-based prevention measures such as minimizing unnecessary ventilator exposure, appropriate positioning/oral care, hand hygiene, and readiness-to-liberate practices
Keep the patient deeply sedated to reduce coughing and circuit contamination
Disconnect the circuit regularly to drain condensation and reduce microbial colonization

items.stem: An intubated patient is at high risk for aspiration. Which principle is most appropriate?
options: Disconnect the airway repeatedly to reduce pneumonia risk
Use appropriate aspiration-prevention and airway-management practices while following the patient's care protocol
Place the patient flat for all feeding and airway care
Assume the endotracheal tube completely prevents aspiration

items.stem: Why should a respiratory therapist distinguish a pneumonia diagnosis from a ventilator-associated event?
options: Every ventilator-associated event is pneumonia by definition
Ventilator-associated events are diagnosed only from sputum color
They are related concepts but use different clinical/surveillance frameworks and should not automatically be treated as identical
Pneumonia cannot occur in a mechanically ventilated patient

items.stem: A patient has chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and a significant tuberculosis exposure history. What should the therapist recommend?
options: Routine peak-flow testing as the only diagnostic study
No further evaluation if resting SpO2 is normal
Appropriate tuberculosis evaluation/testing while airborne precautions are maintained as indicated
Immediate discontinuation of respiratory precautions

items.stem: When pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected, which type of respiratory testing may be part of the diagnostic evaluation?
options: An incentive-spirometry volume as confirmation
A bronchodilator response as proof of infection
A single pulse-oximetry reading as definitive TB testing
Appropriate respiratory specimens for mycobacterial testing according to the diagnostic protocol

items.stem: A patient being evaluated for pulmonary tuberculosis requires a respiratory procedure that may generate aerosols. What should the therapist consider?
options: Respiratory procedures eliminate the need for isolation
Aerosol generation decreases transmission risk
Airborne infection-control requirements and procedure-specific precautions before proceeding
Standard precautions are never needed during respiratory procedures

items.stem: A patient has severe hypoxemia with a low PaO2 but no primary elevation in PaCO2. Which physiologic category best fits?
options: Change antimicrobial therapy whenever any organism grows, even when the specimen is likely colonized or contaminated
Continue the initial antimicrobial regimen regardless of susceptibility results if the patient's temperature has improved
Select therapy from Gram-stain morphology alone because culture and susceptibility data rarely change respiratory infection management
Use microbiologic results, susceptibility data, specimen quality, and the patient's clinical response together when evaluating therapy

items.stem: A somnolent patient has inadequate ventilation with a markedly elevated PaCO2 and respiratory acidemia. Which category best fits?
options: Hypercapnic ventilatory respiratory failure
Isolated hypoxemic failure with normal ventilation
Normal ventilation with metabolic acidosis
Pure oxygenation failure without CO2 retention

items.stem: A patient has severe hypoxemia plus rising PaCO2 and respiratory acidemia as respiratory effort fails. What is the best classification?
options: Pure compensated metabolic alkalosis
Normal gas exchange
Isolated diffusion impairment without respiratory failure
Mixed oxygenation and ventilatory respiratory failure

items.stem: A patient with pneumonia becomes hypotensive, confused, tachypneic, and poorly perfused with an increasing lactate. What should the therapist recognize?
options: An isolated inhaler-technique problem
Stable infection because oxygen saturation is measurable
Routine improvement after pneumonia treatment
Possible sepsis with systemic hypoperfusion requiring urgent escalation

items.stem: A patient being treated for infection needs progressively more oxygen and has increasing work of breathing over several hours. What is the most important interpretation?
options: Interpret the rising oxygen need as an expected response to antimicrobial therapy unless hypotension also develops
Delay escalation until culture results identify the organism because treatment response cannot be assessed earlier
Increase oxygen flow and continue the same plan because work of breathing is not a marker of infection severity
Recognize possible clinical deterioration/sepsis or worsening respiratory failure and escalate assessment and support promptly

items.stem: A patient with severe infection has cool mottled skin, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, and falling blood pressure. What do these findings suggest?
options: Resolution of systemic illness
An isolated upper-airway problem
Worsening perfusion and possible shock
Adequate tissue perfusion

items.stem: A patient with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains significantly hypoxemic and tachypneic despite conventional oxygen. What should the therapist consider?
options: Using only incentive spirometry regardless of severity
Waiting for cardiac arrest before changing support
Escalating oxygenation support, such as HFNC when clinically appropriate, with close reassessment
Stopping oxygen because conventional therapy did not fully correct the problem

items.stem: A cooperative patient has acute ventilatory failure with hypercapnia, respiratory acidemia, and increased work of breathing but can protect the airway. Which support may be appropriate?
options: Oxygen alone as a guaranteed correction for inadequate ventilation
Noninvasive ventilation with close reassessment for response or failure
Chest-tube drainage
Immediate removal of all respiratory support

items.stem: A patient on noninvasive support becomes increasingly somnolent, cannot protect the airway, and has worsening gas exchange. What should the therapist recommend?
options: Treat only the oxygen saturation and ignore mental status
Reduce monitoring to improve tolerance
Prompt escalation toward invasive airway and ventilatory support as clinically appropriate
Continue unchanged noninvasive support despite clear failure

items.stem: A patient develops acute severe hypoxemia after a major inflammatory insult. Imaging shows bilateral diffuse opacities, and the lungs are poorly compliant. Which process should be considered?
options: ARDS with acute lung injury physiology
Isolated upper-airway obstruction
Uncomplicated pleural effusion
Stable chronic hyperinflation

items.stem: Why can oxygenation remain severely impaired in ARDS even when a high inspired oxygen concentration is provided?
options: Pulmonary compliance becomes abnormally high
Every alveolus remains normally aerated
Fluid-filled or collapsed lung units can create substantial intrapulmonary shunt
ARDS always increases alveolar ventilation uniformly

items.stem: When classifying the severity of ARDS, which principle should guide interpretation?
options: Classify severity only from respiratory rate
Assume every patient with bilateral opacities has the same severity
Use sputum color as the primary severity measure
Use the applicable evidence-based severity framework together with oxygenation and ventilatory conditions rather than judging severity from a single symptom

items.stem: When selecting a lung-protective tidal volume for a patient with ARDS, which patient characteristic should guide the tidal-volume calculation?
options: Actual body weight should guide tidal volume because lung size increases proportionally with total body mass
Body mass index should guide tidal volume because obesity increases functional lung volume
Current minute ventilation should determine tidal volume without considering predicted body size
Predicted body weight based on height and sex should guide tidal-volume selection

items.stem: A ventilated patient with ARDS has worsening lung stiffness and excessive airway pressures despite a low tidal-volume strategy. What principle should guide reassessment?
options: Increase tidal volume until PaCO2 normalizes because high airway pressure is expected in stiff lungs
Reassess plateau/driving pressures, compliance, patient-ventilator interaction, and the overall lung-protective strategy rather than simply increasing tidal volume
Reduce PEEP to zero before evaluating plateau pressure so airway pressures can be interpreted without PEEP
Increase inspiratory flow until peak pressure falls, then assume alveolar distending pressure is acceptable

items.stem: Why might a clinician tolerate some elevation in PaCO2 during lung-protective ventilation for ARDS?
options: PaCO2 has no relationship to ventilation
Avoiding injuriously large tidal volumes or pressures may take priority over completely normalizing PaCO2
Hypercapnia always improves oxygenation and requires no monitoring
ARDS prevents carbon dioxide from entering the blood

items.stem: Why may prone positioning improve oxygenation in severe ARDS?
options: It works by intentionally creating a pneumothorax
It can improve regional ventilation and recruitment and reduce severe ventilation-perfusion mismatch in appropriately selected patients
It guarantees removal of all pulmonary edema
It eliminates the need for mechanical ventilation

items.stem: Before and during prone positioning of an intubated patient with severe hypoxemia, what should the respiratory therapist prioritize?
options: Secure the airway and respiratory equipment, monitor oxygenation and ventilation, and reassess the patient's response and complications
Leave the artificial airway unsecured during repositioning
Assume ventilator settings and tube position cannot change during the maneuver
Disconnect all monitoring so the patient can be turned more easily

items.stem: After prone positioning, which approach best evaluates whether the intervention is helping?
options: Assume prone positioning is successful whenever the patient remains prone
Avoid reassessment until the patient is returned supine
Reassess oxygenation, ventilation, respiratory mechanics, hemodynamics, and overall tolerance rather than relying on position alone
Judge response only from heart rate

items.stem: A patient with severe ARDS remains profoundly hypoxemic despite optimized conventional lung-protective support and appropriate adjunctive measures. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Continue increasing tidal volume because refractory hypoxemia indicates inadequate minute ventilation
Reduce PEEP substantially to improve venous return before considering additional rescue strategies
Recognize refractory hypoxemia and promptly evaluate escalation to advanced rescue strategies/appropriate specialty support
Delay escalation until hypercapnia develops because oxygenation failure alone does not indicate severe ARDS

items.stem: What is the best way to think about an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator used in severe refractory hypoxemia?
options: It replaces lung-protective ventilation
It permanently reverses the underlying ARDS in every patient
It may serve as a rescue strategy in selected patients while response is reassessed and definitive escalation is considered
It eliminates the need to evaluate oxygenation response

items.stem: A patient with severe ARDS continues to deteriorate despite optimized evidence-based ventilatory support and rescue measures. Which care-plan recommendation may become appropriate?
options: Early consultation or referral to an ECMO-capable center when the clinical situation meets the relevant criteria
Use progressively injurious ventilator settings instead of considering referral
Delay all referral discussions until cardiopulmonary arrest occurs
Assume ECMO is never considered for refractory respiratory failure

items.stem: During a sleep study, airflow stops but respiratory effort continues. Which type of event does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: Obstructive apnea
Normal sleep breathing
Sleep-related hypoventilation only
Central apnea

items.stem: During repeated sleep events, both airflow and respiratory effort are absent. Which mechanism should be considered?
options: Normal physiologic snoring
Central apnea caused by absent ventilatory drive during the event
Isolated bronchospasm
Upper-airway obstruction with preserved inspiratory effort

items.stem: A patient has loud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, and cardiovascular risk factors but has never had objective sleep testing. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: Arrange appropriate objective sleep testing to evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea
Begin long-term supplemental oxygen without evaluating sleep-disordered breathing
Diagnose obstructive sleep apnea from symptoms alone and start treatment without objective testing
Order routine spirometry as the definitive diagnostic test for sleep apnea

items.stem: What does the apnea-hypopnea index primarily describe?
options: The difference between IPAP and EPAP
The average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep
The patient's average daytime respiratory rate
The number of oxygen cylinders used overnight

items.stem: A sleep study shows recurrent loss of airflow with persistent thoracoabdominal effort and associated oxygen desaturation. How should the event be interpreted?
options: The event cannot be interpreted using multiple sleep-study signals
The combined airflow, effort, and oxygenation signals support obstructive sleep-disordered breathing
Oxygen desaturation makes airflow and effort signals irrelevant
The pattern proves central apnea because effort is present

items.stem: Overnight transcutaneous CO2 progressively rises while ventilation becomes inadequate during sleep. What should the therapist recognize?
options: The finding always indicates a pulse-oximeter malfunction
The trend may support sleep-related hypoventilation and should be interpreted with the rest of the study
CO2 monitoring provides no information about nocturnal ventilation
A rising CO2 proves obstructive apnea without considering effort or airflow

items.stem: A patient has uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea and needs positive airway pressure to splint the upper airway open during sleep. Which therapy is a common first-line PAP approach?
options: CPAP or an appropriate auto-adjusting PAP strategy
Continuous aerosol therapy without PAP
Chest-tube suction
Invasive mechanical ventilation for every patient

items.stem: A patient with sleep-disordered breathing also requires greater ventilatory assistance than CPAP alone can provide. Which concept should the therapist recognize?
options: A bilevel positive-airway-pressure mode may provide additional inspiratory ventilatory assistance when CPAP alone does not meet the patient's ventilatory needs
Increase fixed CPAP until it provides the same inspiratory pressure support as bilevel therapy
Replace PAP with nocturnal oxygen because supplemental oxygen provides equivalent ventilatory assistance
Use auto-CPAP because varying expiratory pressure directly provides mandatory ventilatory support

items.stem: After PAP is initiated for obstructive sleep apnea, residual obstructive events remain frequent. What should be done?
options: Stop all monitoring once a mask is fitted
Assume PAP is effective because the device is turned on
Reassess study/titration data, interface and leak, tolerance, and pressure effectiveness before selecting an appropriate adjustment
Ignore residual events if the patient is asleep

items.stem: Which sleep-study finding most directly distinguishes a central apnea from an obstructive apnea?
options: Any decrease in oxygen saturation
Presence of snoring alone
Absence of respiratory effort during the period of absent airflow
Use of a nasal interface

items.stem: A patient with neuromuscular weakness has sustained nocturnal CO2 elevation rather than repeated discrete obstructive events. Which problem should be considered?
options: Normal sleep physiology
A pleural air leak
Sleep-related hypoventilation from inadequate ventilation
Isolated obstructive apnea only

items.stem: Why might a PAP mode with backup ventilation be considered for selected patients with central events or sleep-related hypoventilation?
options: It eliminates the need to identify the cause of central events
It is identical to simple supplemental oxygen
It works only by increasing upper-airway humidity
It can provide ventilatory support when spontaneous respiratory effort is absent or inadequate

items.stem: A PAP user has high unintentional leak, dry mouth, and persistent residual events. What should be assessed first?
options: Interface fit, mouth leak when relevant, tubing/connections, and whether the leak is interfering with effective therapy
Increase pressure without checking the interface or leak
Stop PAP permanently because dryness cannot be addressed
Tell the patient that all leak is therapeutic

items.stem: A patient reports water collecting in the PAP tubing overnight. Which problem is most likely?
options: Condensation or rainout related to humidification and temperature conditions
A pneumothorax caused by humidification
A central apnea detected by the tubing
Normal intentional leak

items.stem: A patient says the PAP mask causes pressure discomfort and plans to stop therapy. What is the best respiratory-therapy response?
options: Lower PAP pressure empirically until the mask feels comfortable, regardless of prescribed settings or treatment efficacy
Recommend stopping PAP for several weeks so facial pressure sensitivity can resolve before reassessment
Replace the interface with supplemental oxygen because oxygen provides equivalent treatment for upper-airway obstruction
Assess the source of discomfort, evaluate mask fit/interface options and PAP data, correct modifiable barriers, and reassess adherence

items.stem: Before birth, why is pulmonary vascular resistance normally high?
options: The ductus arteriosus is normally closed before birth
The fetal lungs are fluid-filled and pulmonary blood flow is relatively low while placental gas exchange is active
The fetal lungs provide all gas exchange
Placental blood flow is absent

items.stem: What major cardiopulmonary change should occur as a healthy newborn establishes breathing after birth?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises sharply
Right-to-left fetal shunting must increase
Pulmonary vascular resistance falls and pulmonary blood flow increases
Placental gas exchange increases after cord separation

items.stem: Why is maternal and perinatal history important when evaluating a newborn's respiratory transition?
options: Perinatal history has no relationship to neonatal respiratory status
Only postnatal chest imaging can identify transition problems
Gestational age does not influence respiratory risk
Pregnancy and delivery factors can change the risk for abnormal cardiopulmonary transition and neonatal respiratory disease

items.stem: Which group of findings belongs in the immediate respiratory assessment of a newborn?
options: Respiratory rate and effort, color/oxygenation, heart rate, tone, airway patency, and response to initial support
Respiratory rate, birth weight, maternal age, and feeding preference
Heart rate, temperature, head circumference, and urine output
Oxygen saturation, gestational age, blood pressure, and newborn screening results

items.stem: Where is preductal pulse oximetry commonly obtained in a newborn?
options: The umbilical cord after it is discarded
The right upper extremity
The left lower extremity only
Either foot only

items.stem: A newborn has persistent apnea, poor tone, and a low heart rate rather than establishing effective breathing. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Begin chest compressions before ventilation whenever the newborn is apneic because circulation takes priority over lung inflation
Provide free-flow oxygen first for apnea and delay positive-pressure ventilation until pulse oximetry confirms hypoxemia
Provide positive-pressure ventilation when the newborn is apneic/gasping or the heart rate remains below the resuscitation threshold despite initial steps
Continue stimulation alone when the heart rate is falling as long as some respiratory effort is visible

items.stem: A newborn remains apneic with a low heart rate after initial steps. Which respiratory intervention is the central priority?
options: Delay ventilation until an arterial blood gas is available
Use routine suctioning as the primary resuscitation treatment
Establish effective positive-pressure ventilation and assess the heart-rate response
Begin chest compressions before attempting effective ventilation

items.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, positive-pressure ventilation is being delivered but the chest is not moving and the heart rate is not improving. What should the therapist do?
options: Continue ineffective ventilation unchanged
Troubleshoot ventilation and perform corrective steps to establish effective lung inflation
Assume the heart rate cannot respond to ventilation
Start feeding to stimulate breathing

items.stem: How should oxygen administration during neonatal resuscitation be approached?
options: Start every newborn at 100% oxygen because rapid normalization of saturation reduces oxidative risk
Withhold oxygen monitoring until ten minutes of life because early saturation targets are not clinically useful
Begin with the resuscitation oxygen strategy appropriate for gestational age and clinical condition, then titrate using preductal SpO2 targets and response
Adjust oxygen according to skin color alone because pulse oximetry is too delayed for neonatal resuscitation

items.stem: When should chest compressions be considered during neonatal resuscitation?
options: Whenever oxygen saturation is below the adult normal range immediately after birth
Before effective ventilation has been established in every apneic newborn
When the heart rate remains severely low despite effective ventilation according to the resuscitation sequence
For any newborn who cries weakly

items.stem: What compression-to-ventilation approach is emphasized in neonatal resuscitation when compressions are required?
options: Fifteen compressions to two ventilations
Three compressions to one ventilation
Thirty compressions to two ventilations
Continuous compressions with no coordinated ventilation

items.stem: A newborn's heart rate remains critically low despite effective ventilation and coordinated compressions. What should the team anticipate next?
options: Delaying further action until spontaneous breathing returns
Routine bronchodilator therapy as the next priority
Advanced resuscitation steps including appropriate access and epinephrine according to the neonatal resuscitation sequence
Stopping ventilation because compressions have begun

items.stem: A premature newborn develops respiratory distress soon after birth with findings consistent with surfactant deficiency. Which disorder should be suspected?
options: Stable normal transition
Chronic adult COPD
Isolated central sleep apnea
Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

items.stem: A preterm infant with RDS remains significantly distressed and hypoxemic despite appropriate noninvasive support. What should the therapist consider?
options: Stop all distending pressure because surfactant deficiency improves with alveolar collapse
Reassess for escalation, including selective surfactant and invasive ventilatory support when clinically indicated
Use adult incentive spirometry
Continue unchanged support regardless of deterioration

items.stem: Which NBRC task is directly involved when exogenous surfactant is delivered through an endotracheal airway?
options: Endotracheal instillation of a respiratory medication with evaluation of response
Chest-tube suction control
Routine expectorated sputum collection
Adult peak-flow monitoring

items.stem: A near-term infant delivered by cesarean section develops early tachypnea with relatively mild respiratory distress that improves as retained fetal lung fluid clears. Which condition best fits?
options: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
Surfactant-deficiency RDS in an extremely premature infant
Apnea of prematurity
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia

items.stem: A term newborn delivered through meconium-stained fluid develops significant respiratory distress with abnormal lung findings shortly after birth. Which diagnosis should be considered?
options: Apnea of prematurity
Chronic bronchopulmonary dysplasia
Transient tachypnea solely from retained fluid
Meconium aspiration syndrome

items.stem: A newborn has respiratory distress plus maternal/perinatal infection risk and clinical findings concerning for infection. Which diagnosis belongs high in the differential?
options: Isolated uncomplicated TTN regardless of infection risk
Normal cardiopulmonary transition
Neonatal pneumonia
Adult-onset emphysema

items.stem: A newborn has severe hypoxemia with evidence of persistent high pulmonary vascular resistance and right-to-left shunting after birth. Which disorder is most consistent?
options: Transient tachypnea without vascular involvement
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Apnea of prematurity
Stable fetal circulation after successful transition

items.stem: Why can comparing preductal and postductal oxygen saturation be useful when PPHN is suspected?
options: The comparison diagnoses surfactant deficiency by itself
Postductal saturation is always higher in PPHN
A meaningful difference can provide evidence of ductal-level right-to-left shunting in the appropriate clinical context
The values directly measure pulmonary artery pressure

items.stem: A newborn with PPHN has persistent severe oxygenation failure despite initial stabilization. Which treatment concept may be considered in the appropriate clinical setting?
options: Intentionally worsen hypoxemia to lower pulmonary vascular resistance
Support oxygenation and hemodynamics while considering selective inhaled pulmonary vasodilation
Use airway clearance as the sole treatment for pulmonary vascular disease
Avoid reassessing perfusion because PPHN affects only the lungs

items.stem: A premature infant has recurrent pauses in breathing with associated bradycardia and desaturation. What is an important respiratory-care task?
options: Ignore bradycardia because it is unrelated to apnea
Discontinue cardiorespiratory monitoring
Monitor and interpret apnea events and associated physiologic changes
Use adult spirometry to confirm each event

items.stem: A premature infant who had been stable develops a sudden increase in apnea episodes. What should the therapist recognize?
options: New apnea cannot be related to infection or physiologic deterioration
A change in apnea pattern warrants evaluation for secondary causes rather than automatically attributing every event to prematurity
Every apnea in a premature infant has the same benign cause
Monitoring results should not affect the care plan

items.stem: Which pharmacologic therapy is commonly used in the management of apnea of prematurity?
options: Continuous paralytic therapy
Long-acting inhaled anticholinergic therapy
Caffeine therapy with monitoring of clinical response
Routine inhaled nitric oxide for every apnea event

items.stem: A very premature infant has had prolonged oxygen and ventilatory support and continues to require respiratory support well beyond the acute neonatal period. Which condition should be considered?
options: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia or chronic neonatal lung disease
Isolated apnea event with no chronic lung injury
Transient tachypnea of the newborn
Normal transition

items.stem: Why must growth and nutrition be considered when evaluating an infant with chronic neonatal lung disease?
options: Nutrition has no relationship to chronic neonatal respiratory care
Chronic respiratory disease increases ongoing physiologic demands, and growth is part of the overall respiratory-management context
BPD is managed only by changing ventilator rate
Adequate growth proves oxygen is unnecessary

items.stem: An infant with BPD has changing oxygen needs and repeated respiratory symptoms over time. What is the best approach?
options: Use the highest oxygen requirement recorded during admission as the permanent home prescription
Base long-term management on a single clinic saturation because serial trends add little information
Trend oxygen need, growth, respiratory symptoms, gas exchange, and treatment response over time and adjust the care plan as the infant's status changes
Reduce follow-up once BPD is diagnosed because the disease course is predictable after discharge

items.stem: Why is apparatus dead space especially important when assembling neonatal respiratory equipment?
options: Added apparatus dead space can be large relative to neonatal tidal volume and can substantially reduce effective alveolar ventilation
Added dead space is usually beneficial because it increases carbon dioxide rebreathing and stimulates respiratory drive
Neonatal tidal volume is large enough that connectors and sensors have little effect on effective ventilation
Apparatus dead space changes oxygen concentration but has minimal effect on carbon dioxide elimination

items.stem: A ventilated neonate suddenly has poor delivered volume and worsening gas exchange. What should the therapist assess early?
options: FiO2 and respiratory rate first, because sudden low delivered volume usually reflects inadequate oxygen concentration
Blood pressure and temperature first, because circuit or airway problems rarely cause abrupt volume loss
Airway position/patency, circuit integrity, leaks or obstruction, delivered volumes/pressures, and equipment function
Chest radiograph first, before checking the airway or ventilator circuit

items.stem: Why must neonatal CPAP and ventilator interfaces be selected and monitored carefully?
options: Small size, leak, resistance, dead space, skin injury, and rapidly changing respiratory status can materially affect support
Equipment troubleshooting is unnecessary if oxygen is connected
Adult interfaces are interchangeable with neonatal interfaces
Interface fit has no effect on neonatal respiratory support

items.stem: Which monitoring location is especially useful when the goal is to assess preductal oxygen saturation in a newborn?
options: Either lower extremity only
Right upper extremity
Umbilical clamp
Abdomen

items.stem: A neonatal blood gas shows worsening respiratory acidemia while the infant's work of breathing is increasing. What should the therapist do?
options: Increase FiO2 first because respiratory acidemia is primarily corrected by raising arterial oxygen tension
Repeat the blood gas later without changing support because neonatal PaCO2 commonly rises during successful therapy
Reduce ventilatory support because increasing work of breathing indicates improving spontaneous ventilation
Integrate the blood gas with work of breathing and current support, then reassess ventilation and escalate respiratory assistance as indicated

items.stem: Why should neonatal oxygen therapy be guided by target ranges and trends rather than simply maximizing SpO2?
options: Keep SpO2 as close to 100% as possible because higher saturation consistently improves neonatal outcomes
Use a single saturation value to set FiO2 for the remainder of the shift because frequent adjustment increases risk
Base oxygen therapy on skin color once supplemental oxygen has been started because pulse oximetry is unreliable in neonates
Target oxygen within the prescribed neonatal range and follow trends because both inadequate and excessive oxygen exposure can cause harm

items.stem: A child with respiratory illness becomes less interactive, has increasing retractions, and can no longer speak or feed as well as earlier. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Retractions are expected and never indicate worsening illness
Feeding and behavior are unrelated to pediatric respiratory assessment
The child is improving because activity has decreased
The child may be deteriorating and developing respiratory fatigue

items.stem: Why must respiratory rate be interpreted using age-appropriate expectations in pediatric patients?
options: Normal respiratory rates change with age, so an adult reference range can misclassify a child's condition
Respiratory rate has no value in pediatric assessment
Only oxygen saturation should be used to assess children
All children have the same normal respiratory rate as adults

items.stem: A previously agitated child with severe respiratory distress becomes quiet with shallower breathing while work of breathing remains high. What is the most concerning interpretation?
options: Shallower breathing always indicates improved ventilation
The child may be tiring and progressing toward respiratory failure
The decrease in agitation proves the obstruction has resolved
Mental-status changes are not respiratory findings

items.stem: Why can a relatively small amount of airway narrowing cause major problems in a young child?
options: The child's smaller airway radius means edema or secretions can produce a proportionally large increase in resistance
Airway radius does not influence resistance
Pediatric airways cannot be narrowed by edema
Children have larger airways than adults relative to obstruction

items.stem: Why can infants and young children desaturate rapidly during significant airway or ventilatory compromise?
options: They consume less oxygen than adults and have unlimited reserve
Pediatric oxygen demand is unrelated to respiratory deterioration
Their smaller lungs prevent oxygen saturation from changing
They have important size-related airway limitations and relatively high oxygen consumption with less reserve

items.stem: When establishing an artificial airway in a pediatric patient, what principle is most important?
options: Once placed, pediatric airway position does not require reassessment
Use an adult-size tube for every child to minimize resistance
Use age/size-appropriate airway equipment and continually reassess position, patency, ventilation, and pressure/volume effects
Apparatus dead space is never important in small patients

items.stem: An infant with typical bronchiolitis has increased secretions and mild hypoxemia but remains adequately ventilated. Which general management approach is most appropriate?
options: Routine antibiotics for every case
Immediate invasive ventilation for all bronchiolitis
Routine aggressive bronchodilator therapy for every infant regardless of response
Supportive care with attention to oxygenation, hydration, suction needs, and reassessment

items.stem: An infant with bronchiolitis has worsening work of breathing and persistent hypoxemia despite initial oxygen therapy. What should the therapist consider?
options: Stopping oxygen because the infant remains hypoxemic
Routine chest compressions
Escalating respiratory support, including HFNC when appropriate, while reassessing the response
Ignoring work of breathing if the infant is awake

items.stem: Why should respiratory therapy for typical bronchiolitis focus on the child's clinical response rather than routinely giving multiple aerosol medications?
options: The clinical scenario emphasizes supportive care and therapies should not be used routinely when they are not indicated
Bronchiolitis is always caused by bacterial pneumonia
Every aerosol medication is required for bronchiolitis
Supportive care has no role in bronchiolitis

items.stem: A young child has a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor. Which upper-airway disorder is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Croup
Isolated apnea of prematurity
Lower-lobe pneumonia
Bronchiolitis

items.stem: A child has severe stridor at rest with increasing distress. Which principle should guide respiratory management?
options: Delay airway planning until respiratory arrest
Recognize a potentially difficult airway, minimize unnecessary agitation, provide appropriate therapy, and be prepared for airway escalation
Force repeated throat examinations regardless of distress
Assume stridor is a lower-airway wheeze

items.stem: A toxic-appearing child with high fever, drooling, difficulty swallowing, and severe upper-airway distress is suspected of having epiglottitis. What is the safest respiratory-care principle?
options: Place the child supine and force oral fluids
Treat the presentation as uncomplicated bronchiolitis
Avoid unnecessary agitation and coordinate controlled airway management with the appropriate team
Aggressively inspect the throat without airway preparation

items.stem: A child with an asthma exacerbation continues to wheeze and has significant work of breathing after initial bronchodilator therapy. What should the therapist do?
options: Avoid corticosteroid therapy under all circumstances
Assume treatment succeeded because a bronchodilator was administered
Reassess severity and response and recommend appropriate additional therapy or respiratory support
Stop monitoring once the first aerosol is complete

items.stem: A child with severe asthma becomes fatigued with decreasing air movement and a rising PaCO2. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Decreasing air movement means bronchospasm has resolved
A rising PaCO2 proves the child is recovering
These are concerning signs of worsening ventilatory failure requiring urgent escalation
Fatigue is unrelated to respiratory failure
