items.stem: A child with severe asthma remains in marked distress despite repeated appropriate initial therapy. What should the respiratory therapist anticipate next?
options: Use sputum color as the sole measure of severity
Continue the identical plan indefinitely without reassessment
Delay any care-plan change until cardiac arrest
Reassess the response and recommend escalation of the respiratory care plan based on severity and trajectory

items.stem: A previously well toddler suddenly coughs and develops unilateral decreased breath sounds after eating. What should be strongly suspected?
options: Diffuse pulmonary edema
Foreign body aspiration
Apnea of prematurity
Chronic interstitial lung disease

items.stem: A child has a convincing choking history with persistent asymmetric breath sounds and imaging findings concerning for an aspirated object. What procedure may be required?
options: Routine incentive spirometry as definitive treatment
Bronchoscopy for airway evaluation and foreign-body removal by the appropriate provider
Sleep study
Thoracentesis

items.stem: When assisting with bronchoscopy for suspected pediatric foreign body aspiration, what is an appropriate respiratory-therapy responsibility?
options: Prepare appropriate airway/respiratory equipment, assist the procedural team, monitor the patient, and reassess afterward
Leave emergency airway equipment outside the procedure area
Attempt blind removal of a distal object without visualization
Stop monitoring once bronchoscopy begins

items.stem: A child has increasing oxygen need and work of breathing but is still breathing spontaneously and does not yet require invasive ventilation. Which support may be appropriate when clinically indicated?
options: Chest-tube suction
Heated high-flow nasal cannula with age/size-appropriate setup and reassessment
Adult invasive ventilation for every child needing oxygen
No respiratory support until apnea occurs

items.stem: A cooperative older child has significant ventilatory insufficiency and needs pressure support without an immediate indication for intubation. Which option may be considered?
options: No monitoring because the child is cooperative
Simple oxygen alone as a guaranteed correction for inadequate ventilation
Routine bronchoscopy as ventilatory support
Noninvasive ventilation with an appropriate pediatric interface and close reassessment

items.stem: A child on noninvasive support has worsening gas exchange and a large mask leak. What should the therapist do first?
options: Remove monitoring to improve comfort
Assess interface fit, circuit/device function, delivered support, and the child while preparing to escalate if noninvasive support is failing
Ignore the leak because all pediatric leak is intentional
Increase pressure without evaluating the leak or patient

items.stem: When selecting invasive ventilator settings for a pediatric patient, what principle should guide tidal-volume selection?
options: Base tidal volume on actual body weight because pediatric lungs scale directly with total body mass
Use a fixed tidal volume for all children within the same age group and adjust only respiratory rate
Use an appropriate predicted/ideal body-size approach and the child's disease state to select a lung-protective tidal volume rather than basing VT on actual weight alone
Select the largest tidal volume that normalizes PaCO2 because volutrauma risk is minimal in children

items.stem: Why can unnecessary circuit connectors or added apparatus dead space be especially important in a small child?
options: Added dead space primarily increases inspired oxygen concentration and therefore causes oxygen toxicity
Added connectors decrease compressible volume and usually improve effective alveolar ventilation
Apparatus dead space matters mainly in adults because their tidal volumes are larger
Added apparatus dead space can represent a large fraction of a small child's tidal volume and reduce effective alveolar ventilation

items.stem: A ventilated child has unexpectedly poor effective ventilation after extra circuit components were added. What should the therapist evaluate?
options: Whether added apparatus dead space is large relative to the child's tidal volume and is reducing effective alveolar ventilation
Whether the extra connectors increased oxygen concentration enough to suppress ventilation
Whether the circuit length increased pulmonary compliance and caused excessive spontaneous tidal volume
Whether the added components reduced anatomic dead space and therefore caused hypocapnia

items.stem: A patient arrives after major trauma with gurgling respirations, severe hypoxemia, and an obvious leg deformity. Which problem should be addressed first?
options: The immediate airway and breathing threat
Long-term rehabilitation planning
The leg deformity
Routine nutrition assessment

items.stem: In a high-risk respiratory emergency, which approach best supports safe, effective care?
options: Use rapid clinical and available record/monitoring data to identify the most immediate respiratory threat and act
Complete every nonurgent diagnostic test before treating airway compromise
Prioritize chronic problems over acute airway threats
Wait for a final diagnosis before supporting breathing

items.stem: After an emergency respiratory intervention is performed, what should the therapist do next?
options: Focus only on the original vital signs
Immediately reassess airway, breathing, oxygenation, ventilation, and response while continuing the primary survey
Delay reassessment until discharge
Assume the intervention worked and stop monitoring

items.stem: A trauma patient has severe respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension, and rapidly worsening oxygenation. Which life-threatening thoracic injury should be suspected?
options: Uncomplicated pleural scarring
Stable simple rib fracture
Tension pneumothorax
Chronic bronchitis

items.stem: A trauma patient has an open chest wound with severe respiratory compromise. What is the respiratory therapist's priority?
options: Treat only pain and ignore breathing
Encourage unassisted ambulation
Delay respiratory support until routine imaging is complete
Recognize the life-threatening thoracic injury, support oxygenation/ventilation, and facilitate immediate definitive emergency management

items.stem: A patient with blunt chest trauma initially appears stable but develops increasing hypoxemia and respiratory distress over time. What should be considered?
options: Evolving pulmonary contusion or another thoracic injury requiring urgent reassessment
Improvement because symptoms were delayed
Only chronic obstructive lung disease
A normal expected finding after all blunt trauma

items.stem: A burn patient has facial burns, soot around the mouth, hoarseness, and progressive neck swelling. What is the most important concern?
options: Stable airway because the patient is still speaking
Isolated lower-extremity trauma
Simple bronchospasm with no airway risk
Impending difficult airway from inhalation injury and edema

items.stem: Why may early airway protection be appropriate in a patient with significant thermal airway injury?
options: Thermal injury causes immediate fixed bronchospasm that can be prevented only by early intubation
Early intubation prevents systemic carbon monoxide absorption from continuing after smoke exposure
Airway edema can progress rapidly after thermal injury, making later intubation much more difficult or impossible
Airway edema resolves after fluid resuscitation, so intubation is used mainly to reduce work of breathing

items.stem: A trauma patient has major facial injury, distorted airway anatomy, and worsening oxygenation. Which airway-management approach is most appropriate?
options: Wait for complete apnea before preparing equipment
Treat this as a difficult-airway emergency, maintain oxygenation, and prepare appropriate airway strategies and backup plans
Assume standard airway anatomy despite visible distortion
Attempt repeated blind airway maneuvers without planning

items.stem: A patient rescued from an enclosed-space fire has headache and confusion. PaO2 is normal and pulse oximetry appears acceptable. Why can significant carbon monoxide poisoning still be present?
options: Carbon monoxide always causes a low measured PaO2
A normal PaO2 directly excludes carbon monoxide exposure
Pulse oximetry directly measures carboxyhemoglobin
PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen and conventional pulse oximetry can be misleading; hemoximetry is needed to assess dyshemoglobins

items.stem: Which test is most directly useful for evaluating suspected carboxyhemoglobin after smoke exposure?
options: CO-oximetry/hemoximetry
Peak expiratory flow
Routine spirometry
Apnea-hypopnea index

items.stem: A patient from a severe enclosed-space fire has altered mental status, cardiovascular instability, and concern for both carbon monoxide and cyanide toxicity. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Treatment should wait until every toxin level is finalized
Supplemental oxygen is never indicated in smoke exposure
Normal PaO2 proves toxic hypoxia is absent
Tissue hypoxia/toxic exposure can be life threatening despite misleading routine oxygen measurements and requires immediate emergency treatment/escalation

items.stem: A patient develops urticaria, wheezing, throat tightness, and hypotension shortly after an exposure. What should be suspected?
options: Stable isolated asthma only
Uncomplicated sleep apnea
Anaphylaxis with acute airway and cardiopulmonary risk
Chronic interstitial lung disease

items.stem: What medication is the immediate priority in multisystem anaphylaxis with airway or cardiovascular compromise?
options: Intramuscular epinephrine
A mucolytic
A long-acting inhaled bronchodilator as the sole treatment
An oral antibiotic

items.stem: A patient with anaphylaxis has rapidly progressive tongue and laryngeal swelling despite initial treatment. What should the respiratory therapist anticipate?
options: Continue observation while waiting for the edema to stabilize because airway intervention is safer after swelling peaks
Use noninvasive ventilation as the definitive airway strategy because positive pressure reverses laryngeal edema
Prepare for rapid advanced airway management because progressive upper-airway edema can make ventilation and intubation increasingly difficult
Delay airway preparation until oxygen saturation falls because preserved SpO2 indicates the upper airway remains secure

items.stem: An unresponsive patient with suspected opioid overdose has very slow, inadequate respirations. What is the immediate respiratory priority?
options: Perform routine spirometry
Support ventilation while appropriate antidote and emergency care are initiated
Wait for naloxone to work before assisting ventilation
Withhold oxygen and ventilation

items.stem: Which antidote is associated with opioid-induced respiratory depression?
options: Dornase alfa
Flumazenil
Dexamethasone
Naloxone

items.stem: Which principle is most important when managing sedative overdose when a specific antidote may be indicated?
options: Naloxone is the standard reversal agent for every sedative
Flumazenil reverses all opioid overdoses
Flumazenil is associated with benzodiazepines but has important limitations; airway and ventilatory support remain priorities
Any antidote eliminates the need to support ventilation

items.stem: A patient develops sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest discomfort, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and risk factors for venous thromboembolism. Which diagnosis should be considered?
options: Stable chronic bronchitis
Isolated upper-airway edema
Uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea
Pulmonary embolism

items.stem: A hemodynamically stable patient has high clinical concern for pulmonary embolism. Which diagnostic action is most appropriate?
options: Recommend appropriate diagnostic imaging based on the clinical context while supporting cardiopulmonary status
Use sputum culture as the definitive PE test
Diagnose pulmonary embolism solely from pulse oximetry
Avoid imaging whenever PE is suspected

items.stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism becomes hypotensive with worsening hypoxemia and signs of right-heart strain. What should the therapist recognize?
options: A high-risk obstructive cardiopulmonary emergency requiring urgent support and escalation
An isolated airway-secretion problem
A reason to delay emergency management until outpatient testing
Improvement because blood pressure has fallen

items.stem: A patient with major burns has smoke exposure, increasing hoarseness, worsening oxygenation, and progressive respiratory distress. What should be prioritized?
options: Focus only on the percentage of skin burned
Integrate airway edema, inhalation injury, toxic exposure, and pulmonary injury while escalating respiratory support as needed
Delay airway assessment until edema is maximal
Assume respiratory deterioration is unrelated to the burn

items.stem: Why can a burn patient require ongoing respiratory reassessment even if the initial chest examination is not dramatic?
options: A normal initial examination permanently excludes inhalation injury
Respiratory status cannot worsen after the initial assessment
Airway edema and pulmonary injury can evolve, and toxic-gas effects may not be reflected by a single routine oxygen measurement
Smoke exposure affects only the skin

items.stem: A burn patient develops progressive hypoxemia and ventilatory failure despite initial respiratory support. What should the therapist do?
options: Recognize deterioration and promptly escalate oxygenation/ventilatory and airway support according to the evolving emergency
Wait for cardiopulmonary arrest before changing support
Stop monitoring once supplemental oxygen has been started
Continue the initial plan unchanged regardless of response

items.stem: Why does arterial oxygenation commonly fall after rapid ascent to high altitude?
options: Atmospheric oxygen concentration falls to nearly zero
Lower barometric pressure reduces inspired oxygen partial pressure
Hemoglobin immediately loses its ability to bind oxygen
Carbon dioxide concentration in room air becomes extremely high

items.stem: Which response is expected as part of acclimatization to altitude?
options: Barometric pressure rises because of acclimatization
Increased ventilation helps compensate for reduced inspired oxygen pressure
Pulmonary gas exchange becomes unnecessary
Ventilation progressively stops to conserve oxygen

items.stem: A patient with chronic cardiopulmonary disease becomes significantly more hypoxemic after traveling to high altitude. What should the respiratory therapist recommend?
options: Reassess oxygenation and recommend an appropriate change in supplemental oxygen or the respiratory care plan
Ignore the change because inspired oxygen concentration remains about 21%
Assume the patient's sea-level oxygen prescription must remain unchanged
Use bronchoscopy as the first treatment for altitude hypoxemia

items.stem: A traveler develops headache, nausea, dizziness, and fatigue several hours after rapid ascent to high altitude without pulmonary edema or neurologic dysfunction. Which condition is most consistent?
options: Acute mountain sickness
High-altitude cerebral edema
High-altitude pulmonary edema
Arterial gas embolism

items.stem: A climber at high altitude develops severe dyspnea, cough, hypoxemia, crackles, and declining exercise tolerance. Which emergency should be suspected?
options: High-altitude pulmonary edema
Isolated carbon monoxide poisoning
Simple acclimatization
Decompression sickness

items.stem: A climber develops severe headache, confusion, and ataxia at high altitude. What is the most appropriate priority?
options: Treat this as a high-altitude emergency requiring descent/evacuation and oxygen or pressure-based support as available
Delay intervention until loss of consciousness
Treat only with increased oral fluids and continue climbing
Encourage continued ascent to improve acclimatization

items.stem: According to Boyle's law, what happens to a trapped gas volume as ambient pressure decreases during ascent?
options: The gas becomes liquid
The gas expands
The gas contracts
The gas volume remains unchanged

items.stem: A diver holds the breath while ascending. Why can this cause pulmonary barotrauma?
options: Nitrogen instantly disappears from the blood
Expanding gas may overdistend and injure the lungs if it cannot escape
Inspired oxygen concentration falls because seawater enters the lungs
Increasing ambient pressure compresses the lungs during ascent

items.stem: A diver develops sudden chest symptoms during ascent after a rapid pressure change. What concept should guide the initial interpretation?
options: Rapid ascent primarily compresses intrapulmonary gas, making pressure-related lung injury less likely
Pressure-volume change and expanding trapped gas can cause pulmonary barotrauma and require emergency evaluation
Chest symptoms after ascent are most consistent with inert-gas narcosis because ambient pressure has decreased
Pulmonary barotrauma generally develops only after prolonged surface exposure rather than during ascent

items.stem: A diver develops joint pain and neurologic symptoms after surfacing following a significant dive exposure. Which mechanism is most consistent with decompression sickness?
options: Inert gas coming out of solution and forming bubbles during decompression
Simple airway mucus plugging
Progressive carbon monoxide accumulation from altitude
Surfactant deficiency

items.stem: A diver has abrupt neurologic deterioration immediately after a rapid ascent associated with suspected pulmonary barotrauma. Which emergency should be strongly considered?
options: Bronchiolitis
Arterial gas embolism
Acute mountain sickness
Chronic pulmonary fibrosis

items.stem: A diver has suspected decompression sickness or arterial gas embolism. Which respiratory-care priority is most appropriate?
options: Withhold oxygen until a definitive bubble measurement is obtained
Provide high-concentration oxygen and facilitate urgent evaluation for hyperbaric recompression while supporting cardiopulmonary status
Recommend immediate return to depth without professional evaluation
Use routine incentive spirometry as definitive therapy

items.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient is scheduled for transport to CT. Which action should occur before leaving the unit?
options: Wait until the patient is in the hallway to check oxygen supply
Disconnect monitoring to simplify transport
Assess airway security, oxygenation, ventilation, hemodynamic stability, monitoring, access, and foreseeable transport risks
Assume a stable bedside patient will remain stable during transport

items.stem: During transport preparation, a team member is assigned to bring the backup BVM. What best demonstrates closed-loop communication?
options: The request is made once with no confirmation
Everyone assumes someone else obtained the BVM
The equipment is discussed only after departure
The receiver acknowledges the request and confirms when the BVM is present and ready

items.stem: A patient has a tenuous airway and has recently required increasing ventilator support. What is the safest transport principle?
options: Calculate the available oxygen duration from cylinder contents/pressure and planned flow, then include an appropriate safety reserve for delays or increased need
Use the stated cylinder capacity as the expected transport time because flow changes are accounted for by the regulator
Plan to consume nearly all available cylinder pressure so the maximum transport range is used efficiently
Estimate duration from the patient's minute ventilation because cylinder depletion is determined primarily by spontaneous tidal volume

items.stem: A transport oxygen cylinder contains 1,800 psi. The cylinder factor is 0.28 L/psi, flow is 10 L/min, and 200 psi will be kept as reserve. Approximately how long is usable oxygen available?
options: 50 minutes
45 minutes
36 minutes
28 minutes

items.stem: A calculated cylinder duration is almost exactly equal to the expected transport time. What should the therapist do?
options: Proceed with the calculated supply because matching expected transport time provides an adequate reserve
Lower oxygen flow during transport to extend cylinder duration even if the prescribed flow is needed to maintain oxygenation
Use the full cylinder to zero pressure because the reserve is intended only for equipment testing
Arrange additional oxygen capacity because transport planning should include a safety reserve and possible delays

items.stem: A transport ventilator battery is expected to last 70 minutes and the planned trip is 55 minutes. Which additional consideration is most important?
options: Disconnect the ventilator whenever the transport pauses
Turn off ventilator alarms to conserve battery
Assume 15 extra minutes eliminates the need for backup planning
Confirm adequate reserve/backup power for delays or unexpected increased transport time

items.stem: Before moving a ventilated patient, what should be verified on the transport ventilator?
options: Correct settings and circuit plus enough oxygen for the planned trip; battery reserve can be checked at the destination
Ventilator function and battery reserve; a backup BVM is optional when transport is within the hospital
Correct settings and alarms; oxygen supply need not be verified when a full cylinder was recently installed
Correct settings and circuit, adequate oxygen and power, alarms, function, and a backup ventilation method

items.stem: Why should a functioning BVM accompany a mechanically ventilated patient during transport?
options: It replaces the need for an oxygen supply
It guarantees the artificial airway cannot become displaced
It is used only for measuring blood pressure
It provides an immediate backup method of ventilation if the transport ventilator or circuit fails

items.stem: During transport, the ventilator suddenly stops delivering breaths. What is the safest immediate response?
options: Turn off monitoring to reduce alarms
Assess the patient and airway and provide backup manual ventilation while the equipment problem is rapidly evaluated
Continue transport without ventilation if the destination is close
Spend several minutes navigating ventilator menus before supporting the patient

items.stem: Which consideration is especially important when transporting a ventilated neonate?
options: Size-appropriate airway/equipment, thermoregulation, minimal apparatus dead space, and reliable oxygenation/ventilation support
Adult-size circuits should be used whenever possible
Added apparatus dead space is insignificant in neonates
Temperature control is unrelated to respiratory transport

items.stem: Why must backup airway and ventilation equipment be selected for the child's size before pediatric transport?
options: Disconnect monitoring during movement to reduce tubing entanglement, then reconnect it after arrival
Secure the airway and equipment, verify portable oxygen/power reserves, maintain required monitoring, and prepare backup ventilation before movement
Use the transport ventilator without a backup manual ventilation device when its battery and oxygen supply are adequate
Reduce oxygen flow before departure to preserve the cylinder reserve, then restore the prescribed setting at the destination

items.stem: A critically ill infant becomes more hypoxemic during transfer. What should the therapist prioritize?
options: Assume motion artifact explains every saturation change
Wait until arrival before checking the airway
Immediate reassessment of airway, oxygenation, ventilation, equipment function, temperature, and support needs
Continue moving without reassessment to avoid delay

items.stem: During a mass-casualty event, respiratory resources are limited. Which principle should guide respiratory-care triage?
options: Use routine first-come, first-served care regardless of acuity
Reserve all respiratory equipment until every patient has a complete diagnostic workup
Use an organized triage framework to prioritize immediate life threats and allocate limited resources where they can provide meaningful benefit
Give all available oxygen equipment to the first patient encountered

items.stem: A disaster response has a constrained oxygen supply. What is the most appropriate respiratory-care approach?
options: Continue to the destination because stopping transport usually creates more risk than managing deterioration while moving
Return automatically to the point of origin before treating the problem so definitive equipment is available
Silence transport alarms and complete the trip if pulse oximetry remains measurable
Reassess the patient and transport system immediately, stabilize the problem with available backup resources, and determine whether transport can safely continue

items.stem: Several patients need respiratory support but equipment is scarce. What should the therapist do?
options: Use equipment without regard to infection-control or operational safety
Prioritize immediate respiratory threats, apply the disaster plan, reassess patients, and communicate changing resource needs
Abandon reassessment after the initial triage category is assigned
Treat only patients who already have a ventilator

items.stem: A patient is being discharged with home oxygen. Which home finding requires direct safety education before therapy begins?
options: Household smoking near the oxygen-use area
A clear path to the bathroom
A caregiver who understands the prescription
A working telephone

items.stem: A patient prescribed home respiratory equipment has limited mobility, unreliable electricity, and no nearby caregiver. What should the therapist do?
options: Proceed with the standard equipment plan because home barriers should be addressed only after the patient demonstrates difficulty
Identify the barriers and coordinate a realistic plan for power backup, mobility, equipment access, caregiver/emergency support, and safe use before discharge
Cancel home respiratory therapy because unreliable electricity and limited caregiver support are absolute contraindications to home equipment
Teach routine device operation and defer emergency-power planning to the equipment supplier after discharge

items.stem: After teaching oxygen fire safety, what is the best way to verify understanding?
options: Ask only whether they understand
Provide a brochure without discussion
Assume understanding because the patient signed discharge papers
Ask the patient or caregiver to explain and demonstrate the key safety steps in their own words/actions

items.stem: A home PAP user reports persistent mask leak and poor adherence. Which education approach is most appropriate?
options: Explain that all large leaks are normal
Advise stopping PAP whenever leak occurs
Review interface fit and setup, identify the source of leak, correct comfort barriers, and verify the patient can repeat the troubleshooting steps
Tell the patient to tighten the mask as much as possible regardless of discomfort

items.stem: Which teaching principle best fits home aerosol and airway-clearance equipment care?
options: Store equipment wet in a sealed container after every use
Clean equipment only when visible mold appears
Share respiratory equipment between family members without processing
Teach the manufacturer/facility-recommended cleaning, drying, maintenance, and replacement process and verify caregiver understanding

items.stem: A caregiver says a nebulizer takes much longer than usual and produces very little aerosol. What should the therapist teach?
options: Block the aerosol outlet to increase output
Double every medication dose to compensate
Continue using the device indefinitely because treatment time is irrelevant
Check assembly, tubing, power/gas source, medication cup and device condition, and arrange service or replacement if normal function is not restored

items.stem: Before discharge of a ventilator-dependent patient, which caregiver skill is essential?
options: Recognize and respond to ventilator alarms while assessing the patient first and using backup ventilation when needed
Change prescribed settings whenever an alarm occurs
Rely on the ventilator without learning manual backup ventilation
Silence every alarm without assessing the patient

items.stem: A caregiver of a tracheostomy-dependent patient cannot pass the suction catheter and the patient is in respiratory distress. What should the caregiver have been taught?
options: Turn off humidification and ignore the distress
Continue forcing the catheter until it passes
Treat this as a possible airway obstruction, follow the emergency airway plan, use backup equipment/support, and activate emergency help as indicated
Wait several hours to see whether the obstruction clears

items.stem: What is the strongest evidence that a caregiver is prepared to manage home ventilation and tracheostomy care?
options: Written instructions are present in the home
The equipment company delivered the devices
The caregiver has watched one demonstration
The caregiver can independently demonstrate routine care and emergency responses using teach-back/return demonstration

items.stem: A patient depends on electrically powered respiratory equipment at home. What should the emergency plan include?
options: A fully charged device battery is sufficient planning because utility outages rarely exceed expected battery duration
Emergency services should be the primary backup-power plan, so additional equipment-specific contingencies are unnecessary
Power-outage planning can be deferred until an outage occurs if the patient has used the equipment reliably at home
Backup power or alternate support, equipment-specific contingency steps, emergency contacts, and criteria for seeking emergency care

items.stem: A patient's home oxygen system stops working and the patient becomes increasingly dyspneic. Which action should the patient/caregiver plan prioritize?
options: Disassemble internal oxygen-system components during severe distress
Use the prescribed backup oxygen/support if available, assess symptoms, troubleshoot only safe basic issues, and call emergency services when indicated
Reduce all respiratory support to conserve supplies
Wait for the next routine clinic appointment

items.stem: Which method best verifies that a family understands a home respiratory emergency plan?
options: Ask them to sign the plan without discussion
Tell them to search online during an emergency
Have them describe or demonstrate what they would do during realistic scenarios such as power loss, device failure, or airway emergency
Assume they understand because emergency phone numbers are posted

items.stem: At follow-up, a patient reports improved symptoms and much greater activity than at discharge but continues the same home oxygen regimen. What should the therapist do?
options: Continue the discharge oxygen prescription unchanged because long-term oxygen settings should not be reassessed after clinical improvement
Review current symptoms/activity and objective oxygenation data and coordinate reassessment of ongoing oxygen needs rather than assuming the discharge prescription remains optimal
Stop oxygen immediately because improved activity indicates the original qualifying hypoxemia has resolved
Increase oxygen during activity because greater activity automatically increases long-term oxygen requirements

items.stem: A patient is not using prescribed home therapy because the interface is uncomfortable and equipment instructions are confusing. What is the best response?
options: Discontinue all follow-up
Identify the specific barriers, correct equipment/education problems, verify understanding, and coordinate needed changes
Label the patient noncompliant without further assessment
Tell the patient to continue without addressing the problem

items.stem: A patient's respiratory status and equipment needs change after discharge. Which transition-of-care action is most appropriate?
options: Make undocumented equipment changes without notifying anyone
Wait until the next hospitalization to address changing needs
Communicate the updated assessment to the appropriate care team, coordinate equipment/prescription changes, educate the patient/caregiver, and verify understanding
Focus only on the original discharge plan

items.stem: A blood gas analyzer repeatedly reports nearly identical control values, but they are consistently far from the known target. Which description best fits this performance?
options: The analyzer is accurate but imprecise
The results prove calibration verification is unnecessary
The analyzer is precise but inaccurate, suggesting systematic bias
The analyzer demonstrates only random error around the target

items.stem: After major analyzer maintenance, why may calibration verification be required before relying on patient results?
options: It is performed only to clean the analyzer
It confirms that the measurement system performs acceptably across the reportable range rather than assuming maintenance preserved accuracy
It replaces all future quality-control testing
It proves every future patient specimen will be collected correctly

items.stem: A device produces a value that is dramatically inconsistent with the patient's condition and prior measurements. What is the safest quality-control response?
options: Question the result and evaluate the measurement system, sample, calibration/QC status, and need for repeat testing before acting on an implausible value
Delete the result without investigating why it occurred
Accept the value automatically because the device displayed it
Change treatment immediately without verifying the measurement

items.stem: A blood gas analyzer's control material is outside the acceptable range immediately before patient testing. What should the therapist do?
options: Run patient specimens and compare them with bedside findings; report results that appear clinically plausible
Repeat the failed control until one result falls in range, then resume testing without investigating the cause
Do not report patient results from the affected system until the QC failure is investigated and acceptable performance is restored
Apply a correction factor based on the control error so patient testing can continue while troubleshooting is deferred

items.stem: A patient's blood gas values are physiologically implausible and inconsistent with bedside monitoring. Which sequence is most appropriate?
options: Discard the specimen and document nothing
Check specimen integrity/collection and handling, analyzer/QC status, and relevant device/system factors, then repeat testing when indicated
Assume bedside monitoring must be wrong
Report the result first and investigate only if someone complains

items.stem: A CO-oximeter has failed required quality-control checks when a smoke-inhalation specimen arrives. What is the safest action?
options: Estimate carboxyhemoglobin from conventional pulse oximetry
Disable the QC warning and continue routine testing
Withhold unreliable analyzer results, troubleshoot according to QC procedure, and use an appropriately verified testing pathway
Report carboxyhemoglobin because the clinical situation is urgent even though QC failed

items.stem: A Levey-Jennings chart shows several consecutive control values suddenly clustering on the same side of the mean after a reagent change. What pattern should be suspected?
options: Random analytical variation because consecutive values on one side of the mean are expected in a stable process
A trend because a shift requires values to move progressively in one direction over time
Improved precision because clustering on one side of the mean indicates tighter agreement among control results
A shift suggesting a systematic change that requires investigation

items.stem: Control values on a Levey-Jennings chart progressively move upward over several runs. What does this pattern suggest?
options: A shift because any series of abnormal control values moving in one direction represents an abrupt change in the mean
A trend that may reflect developing systematic error and should be investigated
Random error because progressive movement across several runs is typical of unpredictable analytical variation
Improved calibration because gradual movement toward a control limit indicates increasing analyzer sensitivity

items.stem: A control result is a major outlier and violates the laboratory's accepted QC rule. What should occur before affected patient results are released?
options: Delete the control and release patient results
Adjust patient results mathematically to compensate for the failed control
Repeat the same control until one acceptable value appears without investigating
Stop and investigate the QC failure, correct the problem, and demonstrate acceptable analyzer performance according to policy

items.stem: A patient has a normal PaO2 and SpO2 but a hemoglobin of 6 g/dL. What is the most important interpretation?
options: Normal PaO2 guarantees normal oxygen content
Low hemoglobin causes pulse oximetry to read zero
Oxygen content can still be markedly reduced because hemoglobin is a major determinant of oxygen-carrying capacity
Anemia always produces hypercapnia

items.stem: A patient with worsening respiratory symptoms has a rising WBC count with a differential pattern concerning for infection. How should this result be used?
options: Assume any elevated WBC proves bacterial pneumonia
Use the WBC count alone to identify the exact organism
Integrate it with the clinical assessment and other diagnostic data rather than treating the CBC as a standalone diagnosis
Ignore the CBC because it has no respiratory relevance

items.stem: A patient being considered for an invasive respiratory procedure has a markedly reduced platelet count. What should the therapist do?
options: Recognize that anemia can reduce arterial oxygen content even when PaO2 and SpO2 are acceptable
Interpret normal SpO2 as evidence that oxygen-carrying capacity is adequate regardless of hemoglobin concentration
Expect anemia to lower PaO2 directly because less hemoglobin causes less oxygen to dissolve in plasma
Use PaCO2 to estimate the reduction in oxygen content caused by low hemoglobin

items.stem: A patient has significant potassium abnormality along with new weakness and cardiac rhythm changes. Why is this important to respiratory care?
options: Potassium abnormalities directly diagnose pneumonia
The finding matters only if PaO2 is low
Electrolyte disturbance can affect muscle function and arrhythmia risk and may alter the safety of respiratory treatment
Potassium has no effect on muscle or cardiac function

items.stem: A critically ill patient has profound hypophosphatemia and difficulty sustaining spontaneous ventilation during liberation attempts. What relationship should be considered?
options: Low phosphate may contribute to muscle weakness and should be considered in the overall assessment
Phosphate has no relationship to muscle function
Low phosphate proves upper-airway obstruction
The laboratory value should be ignored during ventilator assessment

items.stem: A patient's creatinine is rising and fluid balance is increasingly positive while oxygenation worsens. What is the best interpretation?
options: Renal dysfunction and positive fluid balance may be contributing to pulmonary congestion/respiratory deterioration and should be integrated into the assessment
Rising creatinine indicates the hypoxemia is primarily caused by reduced erythropoietin production rather than fluid balance
Positive fluid balance generally improves pulmonary perfusion and therefore should improve oxygenation
Renal function is relevant only to medication dosing and does not meaningfully affect respiratory assessment

items.stem: A patient in shock has an elevated lactate that continues to rise. How should this laboratory trend be interpreted?
options: It may reflect ongoing systemic stress or impaired perfusion and should be integrated with the patient's hemodynamic and clinical status
It is a direct measure of PaCO2
It independently proves bacterial pneumonia
A rising lactate always means perfusion is improving

items.stem: A patient with severe hyperglycemia and metabolic acidosis develops deep, rapid breathing. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The patient should be encouraged to slow breathing solely to normalize respiratory rate
The increased ventilation may be respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis such as DKA
Hyperglycemia eliminates the need to evaluate acid-base status
The breathing pattern proves primary respiratory alkalosis is the only disorder

items.stem: A patient becomes acutely confused and diaphoretic during respiratory treatment. Which laboratory/bedside measurement should be considered promptly as part of the assessment?
options: Platelet count only
Glucose
Troponin only
INR only

items.stem: A patient scheduled for an invasive respiratory procedure has a markedly elevated INR. What should the therapist recognize?
options: Coagulation testing has no relevance to invasive procedures
An elevated INR lowers bleeding risk
The abnormal coagulation result may increase bleeding risk and should be addressed before the procedure proceeds
INR evaluates oxygen-carrying capacity

items.stem: After an invasive procedure, a patient develops unexpected bleeding. Which laboratory data are especially relevant to review?
options: Serum sodium and potassium to assess electrolyte-related bleeding
Platelet count and coagulation studies such as PT/INR and aPTT
BNP and troponin to assess whether cardiac strain caused the bleeding
Creatinine and BUN to determine whether renal function explains the bleeding

items.stem: A patient's history suggests abnormal bleeding risk, but the available record lacks current coagulation data before an invasive procedure. What diagnostic testing should be recommended?
options: Recommend appropriate laboratory evaluation when needed to clarify procedure-related bleeding risk
Proceed without additional information because the procedure is respiratory
Use pulse oximetry to estimate INR
Assume absence of visible bleeding proves normal coagulation

items.stem: A dyspneic patient has an elevated troponin. How should this finding be interpreted?
options: Treat troponin as evidence of myocardial injury that must be interpreted with symptoms, ECG findings, trends, and the broader clinical picture
Use an elevated troponin to diagnose acute myocardial infarction without considering ECG findings or serial change
Interpret troponin primarily as a marker of left-ventricular filling pressure when evaluating dyspnea
Use a normal initial troponin to exclude evolving myocardial injury regardless of symptom timing

items.stem: A patient with dyspnea has an elevated BNP/NT-proBNP. What is the best use of this result?
options: Use an elevated BNP alone to distinguish cardiogenic from every noncardiogenic cause of pulmonary edema
Interpret BNP primarily as a marker of myocardial necrosis rather than ventricular wall stress
Use BNP/NT-proBNP as contextual evidence that may support cardiac strain or heart-failure assessment when integrated with the clinical picture
Use a low BNP value to exclude all cardiac contributions to dyspnea regardless of timing or comorbidities

items.stem: A patient has unexplained acute dyspnea, chest symptoms, and concerning cardiovascular findings. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?
options: Avoid additional testing once any laboratory abnormality is found
Assume all acute dyspnea is pulmonary in origin
Select treatment solely from one biomarker value
Integrate available biomarkers with the patient record and recommend additional appropriate diagnostic evaluation when the cause remains uncertain

items.stem: A respiratory specimen has findings suggesting heavy upper-airway contamination rather than a high-quality lower-respiratory sample. How should the result be handled?
options: Question specimen quality and interpret culture/Gram stain results cautiously rather than assuming they represent the lower airway
Treat every organism recovered as the definite cause of pneumonia
Assume contamination proves tuberculosis
Ignore specimen quality because culture results are always definitive

items.stem: A respiratory culture identifies a pathogen and provides susceptibility results. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Use organism identification and susceptibility in the clinical context to help guide antimicrobial decision-making
A susceptibility report proves the specimen was collected correctly
Susceptibility results are unrelated to treatment selection
Any cultured organism requires the same antibiotic

items.stem: A patient has chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and a significant TB exposure history. What diagnostic approach is most appropriate?
options: Exclude TB if conventional pulse oximetry is normal
Use sputum color alone to diagnose TB
Use a routine CBC as the definitive test for tuberculosis
Recommend appropriate TB testing and respiratory specimen studies while interpreting results with the clinical context

items.stem: A smoke-exposed patient has neurologic symptoms despite a normal PaO2 and apparently acceptable conventional SpO2. Which specialty test is most relevant?
options: Platelet count
Serum sodium
CO-oximetry measurement of carboxyhemoglobin
Peak expiratory flow

items.stem: A patient has persistent cyanosis and an oxygen saturation that does not respond as expected to supplemental oxygen after an oxidant exposure. Which dyshemoglobin should be considered?
options: Fetal hemoglobin
Methemoglobin
Myoglobin
Oxyhemoglobin only

items.stem: A specialty blood test is abnormal in a patient with respiratory symptoms. How should the therapist use the result?
options: Change therapy without confirming what the test measures
Interpret the specialty test with the patient's history, clinical findings, and other laboratory/monitoring data before recommending changes or additional testing
Treat any isolated abnormal specialty result as a complete diagnosis
Ignore specialty tests because only ABGs affect respiratory care

items.stem: A therapist is comparing sources to guide a respiratory-care decision. Which source generally provides stronger evidence for practice than a single expert opinion?
options: A vendor advertisement
An undocumented personal preference
A single social-media post
A well-conducted systematic review or evidence-based guideline

items.stem: A national guideline recommends an intervention for a defined patient population, but the current patient has a listed contraindication. What is the best response?
options: Follow the guideline recommendation because population-level recommendations generally take precedence over individual contraindications
Discard the guideline entirely because one contraindication means none of its recommendations apply to this patient
Apply the guideline thoughtfully to the individual patient and recognize that the contraindication may require a different approach
Use the recommended intervention at a reduced intensity without evaluating whether the contraindication still applies

items.stem: Which approach best represents evidence-based respiratory care?
options: Replace clinical assessment entirely with published guidelines
Use the newest publication regardless of quality or applicability
Use the same intervention for every patient with the same diagnosis
Combine high-quality evidence and guideline recommendations with patient-specific findings, contraindications, goals, and clinical judgment

items.stem: A patient meets all criteria in an approved respiratory-driven oxygen protocol for a stepwise reduction in oxygen. What should the therapist do?
options: Wait for a new physician order for every protocol-defined adjustment
Ignore the protocol and make an unrelated change
Apply the protocol as authorized and reassess the patient's response
Discontinue all monitoring after the adjustment

items.stem: A patient being managed under an aerosol protocol develops findings outside the protocol's defined safety limits. What is the appropriate action?
options: Continue the protocol unchanged because protocols cannot be overridden
Stop relying on routine protocol progression, reassess the patient, and escalate to the appropriate provider/team according to policy
Skip the abnormal findings if the scheduled treatment is due
Make unlimited changes outside the protocol without communication

items.stem: A ventilated patient meets the institution's protocol criteria for a spontaneous breathing trial. What best reflects respiratory-driven protocol practice?
options: Perform the trial without monitoring because criteria were met
Ignore the protocol until the patient has been ventilated for a predetermined number of weeks
Extubate immediately without conducting the protocol assessment
Initiate the protocol-authorized trial, monitor tolerance using defined criteria, and act on the response according to the protocol

items.stem: Why are structured disease-severity tools useful in respiratory care?
options: They eliminate the need for clinical assessment
They guarantee the same treatment is appropriate for every patient
They support consistent classification and help guide assessment, intervention, and escalation when applied to the correct patient population
They replace all diagnostic testing

items.stem: A patient's calculated severity category appears low, but the therapist observes rapidly worsening work of breathing and mental status. What should the therapist do?
options: Recalculate the score repeatedly without assessing the patient
Ignore the bedside findings because the score is low
Prioritize the concerning clinical deterioration and escalate assessment/care rather than allowing the score to replace clinical judgment
Wait until the score changes before responding

items.stem: Before using a disease-severity framework to guide care, what should the therapist verify?
options: That the patient has no laboratory or clinical data
That every respiratory disease uses the same severity scale
That the tool is appropriate for the patient's condition/population and is being applied using the required variables and intended interpretation
That the tool produces the treatment the therapist already prefers

items.stem: After an accidental ventilator disconnection causes transient severe hypoxemia, the patient is stabilized. What should the team do next to support quality improvement?
options: Conduct a structured debrief focused on what happened, contributing system factors, and changes that could reduce recurrence
Identify one individual to blame before reviewing the event
Change multiple policies immediately without first examining contributing factors
Avoid discussing the event because the patient recovered

items.stem: A therapist catches an incorrectly assembled respiratory device before it reaches a patient. Why should the near miss still be reviewed?
options: Only events causing permanent injury warrant review
No harm occurred, so the event provides no useful information
Near misses should be hidden to protect departmental metrics
It can reveal system vulnerabilities and opportunities to prevent a future patient-safety event

items.stem: A department notices repeated oxygen-delivery setup errors across different staff members and shifts. Which response best reflects root-cause thinking?
options: Track the number of errors without investigating why they occur
Examine workflow, equipment, training, communication, environment, and other system contributors rather than assuming repeated individual carelessness
Discipline the most recent therapist and end the review
Assume the errors are unrelated because different staff were involved

items.stem: After changing respiratory support under an authorized protocol, what documentation is most appropriate?
options: Wait until the end of the week and reconstruct the event from memory
Document only that the patient was seen
Chart an intervention that was planned but not actually performed
Record the relevant assessment, intervention, patient response, and required communication accurately and objectively

items.stem: A patient's condition requires a decision that is outside the therapist's scope or protocol authority. What should the therapist do?
options: Provide appropriate care within scope, communicate the concern, and escalate to the authorized interdisciplinary team member
Make the out-of-scope decision independently because the patient is ill
Ask a family member to authorize the clinical decision
Delay all care until the next shift

items.stem: A decision has been made through the appropriate process to withdraw ventilatory support. What best reflects the respiratory therapist's professional role?
options: Participate within scope in the interdisciplinary plan, clarify orders and goals, support comfort-focused respiratory care, communicate respectfully, and document accurately
Continue current ventilatory support until the family specifically asks the respiratory therapist to discontinue it
Remove ventilatory support once the care team discusses withdrawal, even if the final plan and orders have not been clarified
Limit participation to equipment removal because symptom management and communication belong exclusively to nursing and medicine

items.stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis requires a respiratory procedure. Which precaution category is most appropriate in addition to standard precautions?
options: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask for staff entering the room
Airborne precautions with appropriate respiratory protection
Contact precautions with gown and gloves as the primary transmission-based strategy
Protective isolation to reduce the patient's exposure to environmental organisms

items.stem: Before performing a respiratory procedure likely to generate exposure to secretions, how should the therapist select PPE?
options: Use the same gown-glove-mask combination for all respiratory procedures to avoid underprotection
Select PPE from the patient's oxygen requirement because higher respiratory support predicts greater infection risk
Match PPE to the anticipated exposure and required standard/transmission-based precautions
Base PPE on whether secretions are visible before the procedure rather than the expected exposure during care

items.stem: After a procedure, respiratory equipment is visibly contaminated with blood or secretions. What is the safest action?
options: Place it with clean ready-to-use equipment
Carry it uncovered through clean areas
Rinse it briefly and return it directly to service
Handle and contain the contaminated equipment according to biohazard and infection-control procedures while protecting staff from exposure

items.stem: Why is respiratory equipment classified as critical, semicritical, or noncritical before reprocessing?
options: The classification determines oxygen flow rate
The classification is based only on equipment cost
All respiratory equipment requires exactly the same processing
The classification helps determine the required level of disinfection or sterilization based on how the device contacts the patient

items.stem: Why must reusable equipment generally be cleaned before high-level disinfection or sterilization?
options: Disinfection works best when visible soil remains
Cleaning is needed only for equipment used with oxygen
Cleaning permanently sterilizes every device
Organic material and soil can interfere with effective processing, so cleaning is a necessary first step

items.stem: A therapist is unsure whether a reusable respiratory component can tolerate a particular disinfectant and contact time. What should guide the decision?
options: The device manufacturer's instructions and the facility's validated reprocessing policy
The strongest chemical available for every device
A shorter contact time chosen to speed turnover
The therapist's preferred method regardless of device instructions

items.stem: After a flexible bronchoscope is used, which sequence best reflects safe reprocessing?
options: Dry the contaminated scope before any cleaning
Thorough cleaning first, followed by required high-level disinfection/processing, rinsing as applicable, drying, storage, and documentation
Rinse with water only and immediately reuse
High-level disinfection first, then cleaning after storage

items.stem: Why must bronchoscope channels receive the required cleaning and processing rather than treating only the external surface?
options: Channel contamination cannot survive after a procedure
Internal channels can retain contamination and transmit infection if they are not adequately processed
Processing internal channels damages every bronchoscope
Only the outside of a bronchoscope contacts patient material

items.stem: A reprocessed bronchoscope has incomplete documentation and there is uncertainty whether required drying and channel processing occurred. What should the therapist do?
options: Use it because the external surface appears clean
Remove it from use until proper reprocessing status is verified or the device is reprocessed according to policy
Wipe the insertion tube and assume the channels are safe
Use it only for a short procedure

items.stem: Which practice best supports prevention of ventilator-associated infection and device-associated events?
options: Avoid unnecessary circuit breaks and manipulate airway/ventilator equipment using appropriate hand hygiene and infection-control practices
Change equipment solely because a new shift begins
Drain condensate toward the patient
Disconnect the circuit routinely even when there is no clinical need

items.stem: Condensate has collected in a ventilator circuit. What is the safest principle when managing it?
options: Ignore large amounts of condensate because it cannot affect the patient
Handle and drain condensate according to infection-control policy while preventing contaminated fluid from entering the patient's airway
Drain condensate toward the endotracheal tube
Open the circuit repeatedly without regard to contamination

items.stem: A ventilated patient is stable, but staff are repeatedly breaking the circuit for nonessential reasons. What should the therapist recommend?
options: Remove all humidification regardless of indication
Reduce unnecessary circuit breaks and reinforce appropriate device and hand-hygiene practices to lower preventable exposure and complications
Continue routine disconnections because more circuit openings reduce infection risk
Stop monitoring the ventilator to reduce staff contact

items.stem: A patient with chronic lung disease has persistent exertional dyspnea and reduced activity despite appropriate medical management. Which intervention should the therapist discuss?
options: Pulmonary rehabilitation with exercise training, education, symptom management, and multidisciplinary support
Routine invasive ventilation
Avoidance of all physical activity
Strict bed rest to avoid dyspnea

items.stem: Which combination best reflects a comprehensive pulmonary rehabilitation program?
options: Exercise training, education, behavior change, symptom-management strategies, and multidisciplinary support
Oxygen therapy alone
One exercise test with no follow-up
Medication refills without exercise or education

items.stem: A pulmonary rehabilitation patient has documented inspiratory muscle weakness. Which adjunct may be considered when appropriately indicated?
options: Continuous sedation
Inspiratory muscle training as part of an individualized rehabilitation plan
Elimination of all exercise training
Routine chest compressions

items.stem: Which data should be monitored during a 6-minute walk assessment to evaluate activity tolerance safely?
options: Distance and SpO2 only, because symptoms and cardiovascular response do not affect test interpretation
Heart rate and blood pressure only, because functional distance is not part of a 6-minute walk assessment
Distance, respiratory rate, and spirometry measured continuously during the walk
Symptoms, distance, SpO2, heart rate, blood pressure as appropriate, and oxygen response

items.stem: During a supervised walk test, a patient develops clinically significant exertional desaturation. What best matches the mapped NBRC task?
options: Evaluate the response and use the prescribed testing/titration process to determine appropriate oxygen needs during activity
Ignore the saturation because only resting oxygenation matters
Stop recording oxygen data once exercise begins
Immediately prescribe long-term invasive ventilation

items.stem: A patient's repeat 6-minute walk shows improved distance with less dyspnea and stable oxygenation compared with the prior test. What is the best interpretation?
options: The test is invalid because a valid repeat 6-minute walk should produce nearly the same distance as the baseline test
The increased distance proves pulmonary function has normalized even without repeat physiologic testing
Stable oxygenation means the change in walking distance cannot reflect a meaningful rehabilitation response
The findings suggest improved functional exercise tolerance and should be interpreted with the full clinical context

items.stem: A patient becomes very dyspneic while dressing and bathing. Which teaching strategy is most appropriate?
options: Complete every task as quickly as possible before dyspnea starts
Use pacing, planned rest, task modification, and coordinated breathing to reduce unnecessary energy demand
Hold the breath during difficult portions of the activity
Avoid all activities of daily living

items.stem: A patient with obstructive lung disease becomes breathless during activity. How should pursed-lip breathing generally be taught?
options: Forcefully exhale as fast as possible
Use a relaxed inspiration followed by a slower exhalation through gently pursed lips
Perform repeated breath holds during exertion
Take rapid shallow breaths through tightly closed lips

items.stem: A patient says energy-conservation strategies feel like 'giving up.' What is the best educational response?
options: Advise ignoring severe symptoms to build endurance faster
Tell the patient to stop all difficult activities permanently
Explain that pacing and task modification are tools to preserve function and help the patient complete meaningful activities with less symptom burden
Explain that rehabilitation should eliminate all dyspnea immediately

items.stem: A patient who smokes says, 'I know I should quit, but I'm not ready to set a quit date.' What is the best response?
options: Recommend switching completely to vaping as proven cessation therapy
Use supportive evidence-based counseling, assess readiness and barriers, and continue offering cessation help at future contacts
Refuse further counseling until the patient chooses a quit date
Tell the patient relapse means treatment has failed

items.stem: Which approach is consistent with evidence-based tobacco cessation care?
options: Counseling only once with no follow-up
Avoiding medication discussion for all patients
Behavioral counseling combined with appropriate recognition/use of approved cessation medications when indicated
E-cigarettes presented as universally proven first-line cessation therapy

items.stem: A patient stopped smoking for two months but has resumed smoking. What should the therapist emphasize?
options: Avoid discussing tobacco use again
Treat relapse as an opportunity to reassess triggers, reinforce effective strategies, and support another quit attempt
Tell the patient no further cessation treatment is useful
Recommend abandoning all prior successful strategies

items.stem: A patient with chronic respiratory disease reports increasing symptoms that match the warning signs in the written action plan. What should the patient have been taught?
options: Wait for symptoms to persist for a predetermined number of days before using the action plan so transient changes are not overtreated
Increase every respiratory medication at the first warning sign because written action plans are intended mainly to confirm self-directed dose changes
Follow the action plan promptly, use prescribed therapies as directed, and seek appropriate clinical help based on the plan's escalation criteria
Use the action plan only after home pulse oximetry becomes abnormal because symptom changes alone are insufficient for escalation

items.stem: Which education package best supports chronic respiratory disease self-management?
options: Medication adherence, vaccination, trigger avoidance, symptom recognition, follow-up, and a clear plan for worsening symptoms
Avoiding all exercise and follow-up
Using emergency services as the only symptom-management plan
Changing prescribed therapy whenever symptoms fluctuate without guidance

items.stem: A patient says, 'I usually wait several days after my breathing worsens before I tell anyone.' What is the most important self-management teaching?
options: Use oxygen flow changes as the only response to every symptom
Stop maintenance therapy whenever symptoms worsen
Recognize personal warning signs early and follow the established action/escalation plan rather than waiting for severe deterioration
Delay reporting symptoms until home treatments have failed for a week

items.stem: Before teaching a patient how to use a new inhaler, what should the respiratory therapist assess first?
options: The patient's literacy, language, sensory or cognitive needs, readiness to learn, access barriers, and available caregiver support
Only the patient's diagnosis
Whether the device has been advertised to the patient
Whether the therapist prefers written or verbal teaching

items.stem: A patient with limited English proficiency needs education about home oxygen safety. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Use a qualified interpreter and adapt teaching to the patient's communication needs while verifying understanding
Ask a young family member to translate all safety instructions
Skip education because an interpreter may take additional time
Provide English-only instructions and obtain a signature

items.stem: A patient appears overwhelmed immediately after receiving a serious diagnosis and cannot focus on detailed equipment teaching. What should the therapist do?
options: Recognize the readiness barrier, prioritize essential immediate information, adapt timing and teaching, and reassess learning when the patient can participate
Assume lack of attention means the patient is refusing care
Deliver all teaching rapidly so the checklist is complete
Document education as successful without verifying learning

items.stem: Which statement best demonstrates teach-back after explaining an asthma action plan?
options: 'Sign here to confirm you were taught.'
'I want to be sure I explained this clearly. Can you tell me what you will do if your symptoms move into the yellow zone?'
'Do you understand everything I just told you?'
'Read this again at home if you forget.'

items.stem: After teaching a patient to use a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer, what is the best way to verify psychomotor learning?
options: Give the patient a written handout only
Ask the patient to demonstrate the complete technique while the therapist observes and corrects errors
Ask whether the instructions were clear
Have the therapist repeat the demonstration without patient participation

items.stem: During return demonstration, a patient performs most steps correctly but repeatedly actuates the inhaler before sealing the lips around the spacer. What should the therapist do?
options: Take the device away and end teaching
Correct the specific error, demonstrate or explain the step again, and have the patient repeat the skill until understanding is verified
Document successful competency because most steps were correct
Repeat the entire lecture without addressing the observed error

items.stem: Which information is most important during a respiratory handoff for a patient whose oxygen requirement has increased rapidly?
options: A complete chronological review of the hospitalization so the receiving clinician can independently identify the important respiratory issues
The current oxygen device and latest saturation only, because other respiratory information can be obtained from the chart
Concise current status, relevant background, respiratory assessment, interventions and response, immediate concerns, and needed follow-up
The admitting diagnosis, medication list, and scheduled treatments, with acute changes deferred to the next bedside assessment

items.stem: A therapist reports sudden severe desaturation and requests immediate assistance. Which response best demonstrates closed-loop communication?
options: The therapist assumes someone heard the request
The team waits until the event is over to clarify responsibilities
The receiver nods but gives no verbal confirmation
The receiver repeats or confirms the request and reports back when the requested action has been completed

items.stem: A patient's respiratory status is worsening despite initial interventions, but the first team member contacted has not responded. What should the therapist do?
options: Wait indefinitely because one notification attempt fulfills the communication responsibility
Continue appropriate immediate care and escalate through the established chain or emergency response process until the deterioration is addressed
Delay escalation until the next scheduled rounds
Document the concern and leave the bedside

items.stem: A patient expresses a treatment preference that differs from what the therapist expected. What is the best response?
options: Explore the patient's goals and preferences without assumptions, provide understandable information, and support appropriate shared decision-making
Assume the preference is based on poor health literacy
Tell the patient the clinician's preference automatically overrides theirs
Avoid discussing the preference because it may complicate care

items.stem: A patient becomes visibly distressed when several clinicians enter the room and begin a procedure discussion. Which response best supports psychologically safe communication?
options: Require the patient to discuss prior trauma before providing respiratory care
Tell the patient there is no reason to feel distressed
Explain what is happening, ask permission when appropriate, offer choices where possible, respect boundaries, and avoid unnecessary loss of control
Continue without explanation because efficiency is the priority

items.stem: During a goals-of-care discussion involving possible withdrawal of ventilatory support, what is the respiratory therapist's most appropriate communication role?
options: Use technical terminology without checking understanding
Make the final goals-of-care decision independently
Persuade the family toward the therapist's preferred outcome
Communicate respectfully within the interdisciplinary plan, clarify respiratory information in understandable terms, respect patient/family values, and avoid imposing personal beliefs

items.stem: An ABG shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Which component most directly indicates inadequate alveolar ventilation?
options: PaO2 not provided
Elevated PaCO2
Low pH alone
HCO3- of 26 mEq/L

items.stem: Which ABG value is used most directly to evaluate arterial oxygen tension rather than ventilation?
options: HCO3-
Base excess
PaO2
PaCO2

items.stem: A patient's ABG is substantially different from prior values. Before recommending a major treatment change, what should the therapist do?
options: Interpret pH, PaCO2, oxygenation, and metabolic values together with the patient's condition and verify that the sample/context are credible
Prioritize PaCO2 because ventilation abnormalities determine whether the other ABG values are clinically meaningful
Compare the pH with the reference range and make the treatment decision before considering oxygenation or metabolic data
Use the newest ABG value as definitive even when it conflicts sharply with the patient's condition and prior results

items.stem: An ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 55 mm Hg, and HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Which primary disorder is most consistent?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis

items.stem: An ABG shows pH 7.36, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and HCO3- 32 mEq/L. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
Normal ventilation because the pH is within reference range
Acute respiratory alkalosis
A compensated or chronic respiratory acidosis pattern should be considered

items.stem: Why should a therapist question a simple single-disorder explanation when pH, PaCO2, and HCO3- changes do not fit the expected compensation pattern?
options: A mixed acid-base disorder may be present and requires systematic interpretation
The sample is most likely venous because arterial samples should follow expected compensation relationships exactly
Compensation has normalized the pH, so the remaining PaCO2 and HCO3- abnormalities can be considered clinically insignificant
The bicarbonate value should be disregarded because PaCO2 alone determines the primary acid-base disorder

items.stem: A patient has pH 7.22, PaCO2 68 mm Hg, and only a small increase in HCO3-. Which pattern is most consistent?
options: Primary metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory acidosis from acute ventilatory failure
Fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis
Primary metabolic acidosis

items.stem: A stable patient with chronic hypoventilation has an elevated PaCO2, elevated HCO3-, and a pH close to normal. What does this pattern suggest?
options: Normal ventilation
Acute uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Pure metabolic acidosis

items.stem: A patient with known chronic CO2 retention develops worsening somnolence. ABG now shows a much higher PaCO2 and a newly acidemic pH despite an elevated HCO3-. What should be suspected?
options: Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis without an acute change
Primary metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Acute respiratory alkalosis superimposed on chronic hypercapnia
Acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure

items.stem: An arterial blood gas sample contains a visible air bubble before analysis. Why is this a problem?
options: The sample becomes venous blood
Air bubbles improve specimen accuracy
Contact with air can alter measured gas tensions and make the specimen unreliable
Only bicarbonate can be affected by air

items.stem: An ABG specimen cannot be analyzed promptly. What principle is most important?
options: Add extra liquid heparin after collection
Handle and transport the specimen according to approved procedures because delay and improper storage can change results
Open the syringe to room air before transport
Leave the sample at room temperature indefinitely

items.stem: Why should the patient's oxygen device and FiO2 or flow at the time of ABG collection be documented accurately?
options: Oxygenation results must be interpreted in the context of the oxygen support being delivered when the sample was obtained
PaO2 can be compared directly across samples even when FiO2 changes because arterial oxygen tension is independent of inspired oxygen
Documenting the oxygen device is mainly needed to interpret PaCO2 because FiO2 has little effect on oxygenation assessment
Current SpO2 provides enough context to interpret PaO2, so documenting oxygen support adds little value

items.stem: Which sequence best represents the path oxygen must successfully travel to reach tissues?
options: Inspired gas to alveoli to arterial blood to circulation to tissue delivery
Arterial blood to inspired gas to alveoli to tissues
Tissues to alveoli to atmosphere to circulation
Inspired gas directly to tissues without blood transport

items.stem: A patient has adequate inspired oxygen but impaired transfer of oxygen from alveoli into arterial blood. Which part of the oxygen pathway is failing?
options: Atmospheric oxygen availability
Tissue extraction only
Pulmonary gas exchange
Cardiac rhythm generation only

items.stem: A patient has acceptable PaO2 and saturation but profound anemia and poor perfusion. Why can tissue oxygen delivery still be inadequate?
options: Normal PaO2 guarantees normal tissue oxygen delivery
Adequate oxygen tension does not guarantee adequate oxygen content and blood flow to tissues
Hemoglobin and cardiac output do not influence oxygen delivery
Only alveolar oxygen determines tissue delivery

items.stem: A patient has hypoxemia from regions with low ventilation relative to perfusion and improves substantially with supplemental oxygen. Which mechanism is most consistent?
options: Complete right-to-left shunt only
Isolated anemia
V/Q mismatch
Metabolic acidosis

items.stem: A patient has severe hypoxemia that responds poorly to increasing FiO2 because blood is passing perfused but nonventilated lung units. Which mechanism is most consistent?
options: Shunt
Low V/Q mismatch with preserved ventilation to all perfused units
Diffusion limitation that improves substantially as FiO2 rises
Alveolar hypoventilation with an otherwise normal A-a oxygen gradient

items.stem: A patient with interstitial lung disease desaturates more during exercise as capillary transit time shortens. Which gas-exchange problem should be considered?
options: Primary metabolic alkalosis
Diffusion limitation
Excessive hemoglobin concentration
Anatomic dead space only

items.stem: Which description best defines alveolar dead space?
options: Blood that bypasses ventilated alveoli
Air remaining only in the conducting airways
Perfused alveoli with no ventilation
Ventilated alveoli that receive little or no effective perfusion

items.stem: If carbon dioxide production is stable and effective alveolar ventilation falls, what generally happens to PaCO2?
options: PaCO2 falls
PaCO2 rises
PaCO2 becomes unrelated to ventilation
PaCO2 always remains exactly 40 mm Hg

items.stem: Two patients have the same minute ventilation, but one has substantially more physiologic dead space. Which patient is likely to have less effective alveolar ventilation?
options: Dead space affects oxygen content but not effective ventilation
Both must have identical alveolar ventilation
The patient with greater physiologic dead space
The patient with less physiologic dead space

items.stem: Which variable contributes most to arterial oxygen content under usual conditions?
options: Hemoglobin-bound oxygen
PaCO2
Dissolved oxygen alone
Serum bicarbonate

items.stem: Why can a patient with normal arterial oxygen content still have inadequate systemic oxygen delivery?
options: A normal arterial oxygen content guarantees adequate tissue oxygen delivery unless PaCO2 is elevated
Oxygen delivery also depends on cardiac output
Cardiac output changes oxygen extraction but does not alter the amount of oxygen delivered to tissues per minute
Systemic oxygen delivery depends primarily on PaO2 rather than blood flow once hemoglobin is adequately saturated

items.stem: A falling mixed venous oxygen saturation can indicate what general imbalance?
options: Hemoglobin concentration must be high
Oxygen delivery may be inadequate relative to tissue oxygen consumption
Tissue oxygen extraction has stopped
Arterial PaO2 must be increasing

items.stem: A patient with carbon monoxide exposure has a normal PaO2. Why does this not exclude impaired oxygen carriage?
options: PaO2 measures dissolved oxygen and does not quantify carboxyhemoglobin-bound hemoglobin
Normal PaO2 guarantees normal hemoglobin function
PaO2 directly measures carboxyhemoglobin
Carbon monoxide always lowers PaO2 to zero

items.stem: A patient remains cyanotic with an SpO2 that behaves unexpectedly despite supplemental oxygen after an oxidant exposure. What additional measurement should be considered?
options: An arterial PaO2 alone because dissolved oxygen directly identifies methemoglobin concentration
Conventional pulse oximetry repeated on another finger because a second SpO2 measurement distinguishes dyshemoglobinemia
Peak expiratory flow because oxidant exposure primarily produces reversible airflow obstruction
CO-oximetry/hemoximetry to evaluate dyshemoglobins such as methemoglobin

items.stem: Which principle is most important when dyshemoglobinemia is suspected?
options: PaO2 measures functional hemoglobin saturation directly
A normal pulse-oximeter value excludes all dyshemoglobins
Conventional pulse oximetry and PaO2 may be misleading, so the clinical context and appropriate hemoximetry matter
Dyshemoglobins affect ventilation but not oxygen carriage

items.stem: A patient has PaO2 80 mm Hg while receiving FiO2 0.40. What is the P/F ratio?
Why can the A-a oxygen gradient help evaluate hypoxemia?
options: It directly measures hemoglobin concentration
It measures airway resistance
It compares calculated alveolar oxygen with arterial oxygen and can help distinguish impaired gas exchange from some other causes of low PaO2
It is identical to the P/F ratio

items.stem: Two patients have the same PaO2 and saturation, but one has much lower hemoglobin. Which calculation would best demonstrate the difference in blood oxygen-carrying capacity?
options: Respiratory rate
A-a gradient alone
P/F ratio alone
Arterial oxygen content
